# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R172.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R172.md -->

# R172 — Fixed-Turn Quiet-Lineage Lex Descent

## Statement
Fix a retained proper tight turn J=(a,b,c) and enter its pair-bearing lineage. Let A_J subseteq {a,c} be the turn endpoints already captured as historical signed anchors by selected-incidence actualizations; set epsilon_J=2-|A_J|. Let M be the current balanced-pair mass. Define delta_J=0 when M>2. When M=2, let S be the current floor pair and set delta_J=2-|S intersect {a,c}|. Define Psi_J=(epsilon_J,M-2,delta_J) in ordinary lexicographic order on nonnegative integer triples. Along the chosen quiet, nonclosing, non-exit continuation that retains the fixed turn J, every macro step strictly decreases Psi_J. Hence no infinite quiet recurrence is possible in one fixed-turn lineage.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1) smallest-counterexample setting; J=(a,b,c) is a fixed retained proper tight turn; the pair-bearing fixed-turn continuation uses the accepted retained-turn pair-mass tax above the floor, Complete Floor Pair Steering at M=2, Pair-Deletion Rigidity at the target-aligned floor, selected predecessor/successor incidence at b, endpoint-anchored signed-dimer actualization, Historical Anchor Protection / General Tight-Path Contact, and Cross-Generation Two-Pair Collision. Quiet means the chosen continuation has not taken a spanning two-cover or one of the accepted explicit productive historical pair/contact exits.

## Scope
History-relative / lineage-relative Strong theorem. It is a rank on one chosen proof lineage retaining the same graph-intrinsic turn J and its ancestry ledger. Representative changes are allowed only through the designated accepted fixed-turn macros that preserve that lineage data. It is not a graph invariant and not a monotone across arbitrary proof operations or switches to an unrelated turn.

## Applicability
Use to rule out free remint / recurrence after choosing one proper turn as a retained lineage coordinate. At M>2 the second coordinate pays; at the mass-two floor steering pays delta_J; at the aligned floor a fresh endpoint capture pays epsilon_J even if pair mass is subsequently reminted.

## Persistence
Retain throughout the lineage: J=(a,b,c); the active historical pair and mass M; floor-steering certificates when at M=2; the target pair {a,c}; captured endpoint set A_J; selected-incidence certificate at b; and all historical pair/contact exits. Witness names may change under accepted signed-support rebirth, but the fixed turn and endpoint-capture history are retained. A later remint may increase M only after epsilon_J has already strictly decreased.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Not a global well-founded rank for the Strong project. Does not control arbitrary operations after an explicit exit, deliberate abandonment of J, or switching to another turn lineage. Does not assert that every explicit pair/contact exit closes. Does not require or use CW-freeness, state-DAG height, scalarization, or finite repetition as contradiction. Proper cycles remain constructive outputs. The fixed-turn clock does not count historical capture events that occurred before entry unless they are part of A_J by the theorem's selected-incidence lineage definition.

## Proof
Fix the retained proper tight turn J=(a,b,c) and one chosen pair-bearing lineage satisfying the R172 quiet/nonclosing/non-exit fences. At the macro boundaries retain the historical captured-endpoint set A_J subseteq {a,c}, epsilon_J=2-|A_J|, the active balanced-pair mass M, and when M=2 the current singleton floor pair S and delta_J=2-|S intersect {a,c}|; set delta_J=0 above the floor. We choose the accepted macro granularity exactly as follows.

(1) Above-floor regime M>2. Apply the fully reconstructible certificate-retaining descent R415 to the active ancestry-bearing pair, retaining J as a fixed graph-intrinsic lineage coordinate and not abandoning its history. If a spanning two-cover occurs, this is a closing output and is outside the quiet continuation. Otherwise R415 reaches mass two through finitely many certified strict mass decreases. End the present macro at the first such decrease. Historical capture data cannot be lost, so epsilon_J cannot increase. If epsilon_J has already decreased during the segment, Psi_J decreases in its first coordinate. Otherwise epsilon_J is unchanged and M strictly decreases, so the second coordinate M-2 strictly decreases. If the new mass is two, delta_J may become positive, but lexicographic order has already decreased in the second coordinate. Thus every nonclosing above-floor macro strictly lowers Psi_J.

(2) Misaligned mass-two regime M=2 and S != {a,c}. Apply one nonclosing singleton-replacement macro from fully reconstructible Complete Floor Pair Steering R432 with target T={a,c}. R432 retains the incoming ancestry ledger and keeps pair mass two, while every nonclosing replacement lowers delta_T(S)=2-|S intersect T| by exactly one. Historical captured endpoints are retained, so epsilon_J does not increase. Hence either epsilon_J decreases first, or epsilon_J and M-2 remain unchanged and delta_J strictly decreases. Therefore Psi_J strictly decreases.

(3) Aligned-floor regime M=2 and S={a,c}, so the second and third coordinates are both zero. Work in the aligned pair-deletion frame and apply fully reconstructible R434. A selected predecessor or successor incidence at b yields an endpoint-anchored signed dimer at one outer endpoint e in {a,c}. If e has already completed a previous quiet selected-incidence episode, R434 gives an explicit anchor-contact/strict-growth event, hence a nonquiet exit. Therefore in a quiet nonclosing episode the endpoint e is fresh. Actualization either closes/exits or captures e as a new historical signed anchor. Immediately designate the protected return continuation as in R434. If a first contact is exposed, that is again an explicit nonquiet exit. Otherwise the continuation returns to a both-singleton floor retaining e and restores the opposite target endpoint, reaching the next aligned checkpoint with e recorded in the completed endpoint budget. Thus at the next quiet macro boundary A_J has strictly enlarged and epsilon_J has dropped by one. This remains a strict lexicographic decrease even if the episode temporarily or subsequently remints the active pair above mass two, because epsilon_J is the first coordinate.

These three regimes exhaust the chosen macro boundaries. The small difference between R172's historical wording 'already captured as historical signed anchors' and R434's stricter completed-return budget causes no gap: on a quiet lineage, a capture that has not yet completed its protected return is still inside the same macro; failure to complete quietly is an explicit contact/exit. Hence at successive quiet aligned macro boundaries every credited capture is exactly a completed retained endpoint episode. Therefore every quiet, nonclosing, non-exit macro retaining J strictly decreases the nonnegative lexicographic triple Psi_J. Ordinary lexicographic order on N^3 is well founded, so an infinite quiet recurrence in one fixed-turn lineage is impossible. The argument is lineage-relative and makes no claim across explicit exits, abandonment of J, or unrelated remints.

# R175 — One-Rail Unsigned-End Refund

## Statement
Let (alpha;(p)) and (T;beta) be a balanced opposite-sign historical pair in a smallest Strong counterexample, where the singleton support is (p) and T=(t_0,t_1,...,t_m) is nontrivial, m>=1, with its displayed signed end at t_0. Suppose a current literal outside frame contains a nontrivial tight path U=(u_0,u_1,...) vertex-disjoint from (p) and T, so u_0u_1 is a selected boundary. Then before any fresh recompletion or unrelated marker reset there is a proper tight trimer C_U equal to either (t_0,u_0,u_1) or (u_1,u_0,t_0). Its vertex set is exactly {t_0,u_0,u_1}; deleting it from the historical pair leaves the singleton support unchanged and the signed suffix T^-=(t_1,...,t_m), so historical pair mass drops exactly by one. The original tail witness beta remains valid. The exact head/tail dual also holds.

## Hypotheses
Smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample; an ancestry-bearing balanced opposite-sign pair with one singleton support (p) and one nontrivial tail-signed support T=(t_0,...,t_m); a current literal outside nontrivial path U=(u_0,u_1,...) disjoint from both historical supports, with selected state u_0u_1.

## Scope
Strong-safe one-turn refund in the singleton/nontrivial historical-pair layer. The construction is performed in the current literal outside frame before fresh recompletion. Head/tail duality gives the corresponding refund at the opposite unsigned end.

## Applicability
Use to peel a nontrivial historical support by exactly one vertex while keeping the singleton side fixed. This is the certificate-preserving final layer of the chosen singleton/nontrivial pair descent.

## Persistence
The singleton support (p) survives literally. The descendant support is the historical suffix T^- and retains beta as its original tail witness. The trimer orientation may be either displayed orientation and must be retained if later orientation-sensitive calculations need it. The outside selected boundary u_0u_1 is the physical provenance of the refund.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not close the both-singleton floor. Does not make arbitrary pair mass globally monotone across unrelated marker resets. Does not automatically close richer growth, cycle, or bounded-contact exits if one deliberately takes those branches. The witness beta is graph-intrinsic but need not lie in every residual induced subsystem. No CW-specific inference is used.

## Proof
Let (alpha;(p)) and (T;beta) be the literal historical pair of R175, with T=(t_0,t_1,...,t_m), m>=1, and let U=(u_0,u_1,...) be the displayed outside path, so u_0u_1 is selected. Apply Boundary Antisymmetry R3 to the triple (t_0,u_0,u_1). Exactly one of t_0u_0u_1 and u_1u_0t_0 is tight. In either case the resulting tight trimer C_U has vertex set {t_0,u_0,u_1}; hence it meets the historical pair exactly at the unsigned head t_0 of T and is disjoint from the fixed singleton (p). Delete V(C_U) from the active historical-support bookkeeping. By Signed-Interval Rebirth R425, the surviving suffix T^-=(t_1,...,t_m) is still tail-signed by the same old witness beta, while (p) is untouched. Therefore the descendant historical pair is (alpha;(p)),(T^-;beta) and its mass is exactly one less. The head/tail dual is identical after reversing the displayed roles. No recompletion, voluntary truncation, or hidden marker reset is used.

# R176 — Spare-Vertex Cross-State Pair Upgrade

## Statement
Let H be a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament, let W be a proper vertex subset, and let R,T be literal path covers of W. Suppose T selects a state xy whose endpoints lie in two distinct components of R. Then H contains a graph-intrinsic balanced opposite-sign pair.

## Hypotheses
Arbitrary Level-(1); W is a proper subset of V(H), so at least one spare vertex d exists outside W; R and T are literal path covers of W; T contains a selected cross state xy between distinct R-components. The accepted Cross-State Sign-or-Reverse-Trimer theorem is available for xy.

## Scope
Strong-safe generic parent. No smallest-counterexample minimality, endpoint role, component-count drop, deleted marker, extremality, or CW assumption is required. Punctured Component-Drop Pair is the specialization where r<c guarantees such a cross state.

## Applicability
Use whenever two covers of a proper induced subsystem exhibit one current cross-state. It eliminates the bounded reverse-trimer as a sign-free branch by using any spare ambient vertex as an opposite singleton support.

## Persistence
The resulting balanced pair is graph-intrinsic in H. In the good/good seam case retain the original cross-witness provenance. In a bad-seam case retain the explicit reverse-trimer orientation and the chosen spare vertex d; the singleton support uses d and the reverse trimer supplies the opposite nontrivial signed support.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Without a spare vertex outside W, the reverse-trimer branch does not automatically carry an opposite singleton sign by this proof. The theorem does not preserve current selection of the pair supports in a common cover and does not itself pay the pair or close the conjecture. No endpoint, minimality, or component-drop conclusion is part of the parent statement.

## Proof
Let xy be the selected directed state of T, with x and y in distinct components of R, and choose any spare vertex d in V(H)-W. Let R_x be the R-component containing x. First suppose R_x has at least two vertices. Choose a vertex p adjacent to x along the literal path R_x. Since y lies in a different R-component, p,x,y are distinct. Apply boundary antisymmetry R3 with middle x to the triple {p,x,y}. Exactly one of (y,x,p) and (p,x,y) is tight. If (y,x,p) is tight, then the tested oriented dimer (x,p) is head-signed by witness y. By the standard singleton signed-support convention made explicit in R444, the automatic ordered two-vertex path (d,y) makes singleton (d) tail-signed by the same witness y. The supports {x,p} and {d} are disjoint because {x,p} is contained in W and d is outside W; y lies in a different R-component and is outside both supports. Hence these two supports form a graph-intrinsic balanced opposite-sign pair. If instead (p,x,y) is tight, then oriented dimer (p,x) is tail-signed by witness y. The automatic two-vertex path (y,d) makes singleton (d) head-signed by y, again giving a disjoint balanced opposite-sign pair. Now suppose R_x is the singleton path (x). The selected state xy is itself an ordered two-vertex path and therefore makes singleton (x) tail-signed by witness y. The automatic path (y,d) makes singleton (d) head-signed by the same witness y. Since d lies outside W, the two singleton supports are disjoint, and again we obtain a balanced opposite-sign pair. These cases exhaust the R-component containing x. In every case the pair birth retains the selected cross-state endpoint y as the common witness, the crossed R-component containing x, and, when nontrivial, the exact old R-neighbor p used in the signed dimer. Thus the conclusion and cross-state provenance of R176 follow without the lost historical Cross-State Sign-or-Reverse-Trimer lemma.

# R19 — Universal internal-vertex graft

## Statement

If a retained tight path contains a vertex internally and a current cover contains that vertex while covering everything outside the rest of the path, insert the two missing path states at the vertex. The complete blocker set is exactly the currently selected states incident with the vertex. If its selected incidence degree is zero, one, or two, the gain is respectively two, one, or zero, with no cycle debt. The resulting representative contains the whole retained path and every component of the old cover after removing that vertex.

## Hypotheses


## Scope
This is the parent of older fixed-vertex graft and local four-vertex surgery theorems. Specializations remain useful only when they retain a boundary role, chosen side, or ancestry not present in the parent.


## Applicability


## Persistence


## Exclusions / nonclaims


## Proof
Let K=(...,a,x,b,...) be the retained tight path, with x internal, and let T be the current path cover in the R19 setup: T contains x and covers every vertex outside V(K)\\{x}, while the other vertices of K are not present in T. The graft inserts the two retained-path selected states ax and xb through x and restores all of K as one tight path component. Because every vertex of K\\{x} is absent from T, neither inserted state can conflict with any old selected state away from x. The only possible blockers are therefore exactly the old selected states of T incident with x. Since T is a path cover, the selected incidence degree d_T(x) is 0,1,or 2. Remove precisely these d_T(x) blocker states and remove x from its old T-component; keep every resulting component of T-x unchanged. Then add the entire retained path K. The resulting selected-state system is the disjoint union of K with the components of T-x, because those old components use only vertices outside K. Hence it is already a path cover and creates no physical tight-cycle component: cycle debt is zero. The exchange inserts two selected states and removes d_T(x) blockers, so its raw gain is 2-d_T(x). By reconstructed gain-minus-cycle-debt identity R17, the actual path-cover improvement is also 2-d_T(x). Therefore incidence degree zero gives gain two, incidence degree one gives gain one, and incidence degree two gives gain zero. The final representative contains all of K and every component of the old cover after deleting x, exactly as stated. No other blocker or cycle correction exists because the vertex sets are disjoint after x is removed.

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R191.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R191.md -->

# R191 — No order-ten smallest boundary-tournament counterexample

## Statement
There is no order-ten smallest counterexample to the Strong Level-(1) two-cover conjecture.

## Hypotheses
Standing project definitions; accepted R4, R8, R128, R183 and R184.

## Scope
Parent closure of the entire order-ten smallest-counterexample case. The only remaining minimum-overlap branch is m=1, which is excluded by structural four-core clique counting.

## Applicability
Use as the order-ten closure theorem. Any global reduction whose terminal hypothetical counterexample has order ten may consume this directly.

## Persistence
Global contradiction in the standing order-ten smallest-counterexample setting.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not assert that every hypothetical smallest counterexample has order ten; that is a separate global reduction if available.

## Proof

Assume for contradiction that H is an order-ten smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample. Let F be the family of all five-element vertex sets that support a tight Hamilton P5. We deliberately do not define F using global-longest paths.

1. Clean support-family geometry.

First, union F=V(H). Fix v in V(H) and choose any six-set E containing v. By R195, at least four of the six five-subsets E-{e} support a P5. Only one of those six subsets omits v, namely E-{v}; hence at least one good five-subset contains v.

Second, intersection F is empty. Fix v. Since H has ten vertices, choose a six-set E contained in V(H)-{v}. R195 supplies a P5 support inside E, hence a member of F avoiding v.

Third, any two members of F intersect. If A,B in F were disjoint, then because |A|=|B|=5 and |H|=10 they would be complementary. Choosing a tight Hamilton P5 on A and one on B would give a spanning two-cover of H, contradiction.

Finally, some two members meet in at most three vertices. Suppose instead that every two distinct members of F meet in at least four vertices. Since union F has ten vertices and every member has size five, F has two distinct members A,B. Their intersection has size exactly four; write C=A cap B, A=C union {a}, B=C union {b}. Consider any D in F. If C is contained in D, call D star-type. Otherwise D misses some c in C. It cannot miss two vertices of C, because then |D cap A|<=3. Thus it misses exactly one c. The inequalities |D cap A|>=4 and |D cap B|>=4 force A-{c} and B-{c} both into D, and their union already has five vertices. Hence D=(C-{c}) union {a,b}, a top-type member contained in A union B. If any top-type member exists, then a star-type member C union {d} with d outside {a,b} would meet it in only the three vertices C-{c}. Therefore the only star-type members are A and B, and every member of F is contained in A union B, contradicting union F=V(H). If no top-type member exists, every member contains C, contradicting intersection F=empty. Hence, writing m for the minimum intersection of two distinct members of F, we have 1<=m<=3.

2. Minimum intersection three is impossible.

Suppose A,B in F have minimum intersection S=A cap B of size three. By R8 orient S as a tight trimer. Minimality R4 gives pc(H-S)<=2. If H-S were Hamiltonian, a Hamilton path on H-S together with the tight trimer on S would two-cover H, impossible. Thus H-S has an exact two-cover P|Q.

If one rail has order five, it itself is a member of F disjoint from S. If one rail has order six, R195 applied to its six-vertex support supplies a five-vertex Hamilton support D contained in that rail and disjoint from S. Either case contradicts minimum intersection three, since A-S has only two vertices and therefore |D cap A|<=2. Consequently both rails have order at most four. Since they cover seven vertices, their profile is 4+3. The three-rail is a tight trimer and the four-rail is a disjoint tight P4, so R126 forces a tight P5 contained in H-S, giving the same contradiction. Thus m is not three.

3. Minimum intersection two is impossible.

Suppose A,B in F have minimum intersection S of size two. Put U=A-S, V=B-S, and R=V(H)-(A union B), so |U|=|V|=3 and |R|=2. Apply clean Pair-Deletion Rigidity R429 to S. It gives an exact two-cover P|Q of H-S and both rails are nontrivial. If a rail has order five it is a P5 support; if a rail has order six, R195 supplies a P5 support inside it. If both rails have order at most four, then because they are nontrivial and cover eight vertices they have profile 4+4; taking a consecutive tight trimer from one rail and the other P4, R126 again supplies a P5. Therefore in every case there is D in F with D cap S empty.

Minimum intersection two with A and B forces |D cap U|>=2 and |D cap V|>=2. Since |D|=5, the profile of D across U,V,R is one of (2,2,1), (2,3,0), (3,2,0). Choose L from {A,B} so that |L cap D|=2, and let M be the other one. Put X=L cap M=S, Y=L cap D, and Z=M cap D. Then X and Y are disjoint two-subsets of L. Any vertex of Z cap L would belong to both X and Y, so Z is disjoint from L. Minimum intersection gives |Z|>=2, while Z is contained in M-L, a three-set, so |Z| is two or three.

If |Z|=2, write
L=X union Y union {p},
M=X union Z union {b},
D=Y union Z union {d},
and let e be the unique vertex outside L union M union D. Orient P0={p,b,e} as a tight trimer by R8. This trimer is disjoint from D. Write X={x1,x2} and choose any r in D. R146 applied to P0 and the three exterior vertices x1,x2,r forces a P5 on one of P0 union {x1,x2}, P0 union {x1,r}, P0 union {x2,r}. Each candidate meets D in at most one vertex. It is therefore a member of F intersecting D in fewer than two vertices, contradicting minimality of m.

If |Z|=3, write
L=X union Y union {p},
M=X union Z,
D=Y union Z,
and let e,f be the two vertices outside L union M union D. Orient P0={p,e,f} as a tight trimer. For any distinct u,v in X union Y union Z, the five-set P0 union {u,v} cannot support a P5. Indeed, if it did, minimum intersection two with both M and D would force u,v to lie in M cap D=Z, because P0 is disjoint from M and D. But then this P5 support would meet L only in p, contradicting m=2. Now choose any three distinct u,v,w from the seven-set X union Y union Z. R146 applied to P0 and u,v,w forces one of the three pair-extensions to support a P5, contradiction. Hence m is not two.

4. Minimum intersection one is impossible.

Suppose m=1. Fix A in F and let E=V(H)-A. The five-set E is not in F, because otherwise the P5s on A and E would be a spanning two-cover. Fix a in A. For z in E put B_z=(E-{z}) union {a}. We claim at most one of the five B_z fails to lie in F. If two distinct B_x,B_y were bad, put P0=E-{x,y}, a three-set, and orient P0 as a tight trimer using R8. R146 applied to P0 and the exterior vertices x,y,a forces one of
E=P0 union {x,y},
B_y=P0 union {x,a},
B_x=P0 union {y,a}
to support a P5, contradicting the assumed badness of all three. Thus for each a in A at least four of the five B_z belong to F. As a ranges over A, these give at least twenty distinct members of F meeting A in exactly one vertex.

Let barF={V(H)-B : B in F}. The families F and barF are disjoint, since a set lying in both would be complementary to another member of F and the two corresponding P5s would span H. Work in the Johnson graph J(10,5). For every successful replacement B_z, its complement is C_{a,z}=(A-{a}) union {z}, which lies in barF and is a Johnson neighbor of A. The twenty distinct successful pairs (a,z) therefore give at least twenty F-to-barF Johnson edges incident with every A in F. Summing from the F side gives
 e_J(F,barF) >= 20|F|.

For the opposite bound, for every four-set C let K_C={C union {v}: v notin C}; this is a K6 in J(10,5), and every Johnson edge belongs to exactly one such clique, indexed by the four-set intersection of its endpoints. Put r_C=|F cap K_C| and s_C=|barF cap K_C|. Since F and barF are disjoint, r_C+s_C<=6. Hence
 r_C s_C <= (r_C+s_C)^2/4 <= (3/2)(r_C+s_C).
Summing over all four-sets C counts every F-to-barF Johnson edge exactly once. Each five-set contains five four-subsets, so sum_C r_C=5|F| and sum_C s_C=5|barF|=5|F|. Therefore
 e_J(F,barF) <= (3/2)(10|F|)=15|F|,
contradicting the lower bound 20|F|.

All possible minimum intersections m=1,2,3 are impossible. This contradiction proves that no order-ten smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample exists, exactly the conclusion of R191.

The proof uses only current clean R4, R8, R126, R146, R195, and R429. It does not use R9, R10-R15, R24, R5, R127-R131, R141, R147, R168, R169, R183, R184, R189, R190, or any singleton-order-floor descendant. The historical P191 route is preserved separately.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R191.md -->

# R195 — Four-of-six Hamilton-five density

## Statement
Every six-vertex subset E of a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament has at least four vertices e such that E\\{e} supports a tight five-vertex path.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1) boundary antisymmetry; E is any six-element vertex set.

## Scope
Order-free local path-density strengthening of the six-set P5 fact.

## Applicability
Use whenever a six-vertex exterior or residual cell appears. It supplies at least four distinct Hamilton five-subsets, hence at least four choices of omitted marker.

## Persistence
The four-or-more Hamilton five-subset supports are graph-intrinsic on E.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not assert all six five-subsets are Hamiltonian and does not prescribe which at most two omissions fail.

## Proof
Let M={e∈E : E\\{e} supports a tight five-path}. Fix any three-subset T⊂E and put P=E\\T. By R8, P admits a tight trimer orientation. The three vertices of T are distinct and exterior to P, so R146 implies that at least one of the three five-sets obtained by adjoining two vertices of T to P is Hamiltonian. Those three sets are exactly E\\{t} for t∈T. Hence M∩T≠∅ for every three-subset T⊂E. If |E\\M|≥3, choosing T⊂E\\M of size three contradicts this. Therefore |E\\M|≤2, so |M|≥4.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R195.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R20.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R20.md -->

# R20 — Cover-puncture fragmentation identity

## Statement

Delete any proper set from a historical spanning cover and split what remains into maximal historical runs. In an exact cover of the deletion, the number of selected states joining different runs equals the number of run-color blocks in the current rails minus the number of current rails. It is at least the number of historical runs minus the number of current rails. Equality means each historical run occurs in one contiguous block.

## Hypotheses


## Scope
This controls how many crossings exist, but not which crossings, their orientations, endpoint roles, or ancestry.


## Applicability


## Persistence


## Exclusions / nonclaims


## Proof
Delete the prescribed proper vertex set from the historical spanning cover and split every surviving historical component at the deleted vertices into its maximal nonempty historical runs. Give every surviving vertex the color of the unique historical run containing it. Let the current exact cover of the deletion have q nonempty rails. On one current rail, compress consecutive vertices of the same historical-run color into maximal color blocks. If that rail has b color blocks, then exactly b-1 selected adjacent states of the rail join two different historical runs: these are precisely the adjacencies at the boundaries between consecutive color blocks, and no other selected adjacency changes run color. Summing over all q rails, the total number N of selected states joining different historical runs is therefore N=(sum of block counts)-q. This is the asserted identity. If the deletion leaves r nonempty historical runs, every such run contains at least one surviving vertex and hence appears in at least one current color block. Therefore the total number of blocks is at least r, so N>=r-q. Equality holds exactly when the total number of blocks is r. Since all r run colors appear at least once, this occurs exactly when each historical run appears in one and only one contiguous color block across the current rails. Conversely, if every historical run occurs in a single contiguous current block, the total block count is r and equality holds. The argument counts only current selected adjacencies and historical run membership; it determines neither their orientation nor any additional ancestry roles, exactly as fenced in R20.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R20.md -->

# R2001 — Later OUT-v first loss reduces to three exact first-open residuals

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789410868.203179`

## Statement

Retain the non-loop OUT-`v` first-loss setting with `j>t+1`, and put `c=b_{t+1}` for the first R1033-open spectator slot.

A later first loss can survive that first-open slot only if at least one of the following occurs:

1. the normalized pre-loss prefix is not a literal tight three-path forest;
2. at least one spectator split-copy at `c` has already left its `J` state;
3. the explicit first-open detour reaches the tight three-forest supplied by R1061, but the final source-gated closure `b_t->s` has a bad endpoint seam or closes a same-rail directed cycle.

If none of these residuals occurs, there is an earlier literal tight two-path cover of the underlying `G` support.

## Proof

Let `M=hat M_{r-1}` be the normalized prefix immediately before the putative later OUT-`v` first loss, with far free source copy `s,in` as in R1051.

Assume none of the three residuals occurs. Then `M` is a literal tight three-path forest and both spectator split-copies at the first-open slot remain in their J-state. By R1061,

`M' = M-{b_t->b_{t+1}}+{v->b_{t+1}}`

is a literal tight three-path forest whose free copies are exactly `b_t,out` and `s,in`.

The unique direct closure is therefore

`k=b_t->s`.

Because the third residual is assumed absent, neither endpoint seam of `k` is bad and the two endpoints lie on different rails. Hence `k` joins the terminal of one path component to the source of another. It creates no directed cycle, and its only new turns are precisely the two endpoint seams already assumed tight. Thus `M'+k` is a literal tight two-path cover of the G-support.

Therefore any surviving later `j>t+1` first-loss cell must exhibit at least one of the three stated residuals.

## Dependencies

- `A7C3/RESULTS/INTERESTING/R1033.md`
- `A7C3/RESULTS/INTERESTING/R1051.md`
- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R1059.md`
- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R1060.md`
- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R1061.md`
- normalized-prefix mechanics in `A7C3/WORKSPACE/D17/416-g35-neutral-normalization-forward-blocker-transport.md`

## Scope

This is an exact local physical reduction on the G-support. It does not claim that transition count three is a strict old-source descent, and it does not by itself close O4 in H. R24 and R5 are unused.

# R2002 — Exact cycle criterion for the first-open source closure

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789410954.532749`

## Statement

Retain the physical first-open detour state of R1061. The final source closure

`b_t->s`

is cyclic if and only if `s` is the source of the spectator-prefix component created by cutting `b_t->b_{t+1}`.

Equivalently, in the original normalized pre-loss forest, cyclicity occurs exactly when the rail contains the directed segment

`s -> ... -> b_t -> b_{t+1} -> ...`.

## Proof

Let `M` be the normalized pre-loss tight three-path forest, with

`d=b_t->b_{t+1}`

selected. Put

`M' = M-{d}+{v->b_{t+1}}`.

By R1061, `M'` is a tight three-path forest with free copies `b_t,out` and `s,in`.

Deleting `d` from its M-rail splits that rail into a prefix `P` ending at `b_t` and a suffix `Q` beginning at `b_{t+1}`. By R1060, `v` was an isolated singleton in M, so adding `v->b_{t+1}` only changes the suffix component, replacing Q by the path obtained by attaching v in front. The prefix P is unchanged.

The source spoke `s` is not incident with either modified edge, so it remains the source of the same component as before. The closure `b_t->s` creates a directed cycle exactly when its terminal endpoint `b_t` and source endpoint `s` lie on the same M'-rail. The M'-rail containing `b_t` is precisely P. Hence the closure is cyclic exactly when s is the source of P.

That condition is equivalent, in the original forest M, to the directed rail segment

`s -> ... -> b_t -> b_{t+1} -> ...`.

Conversely, if M contains this segment, cutting d leaves `P=(s,...,b_t)`, and adding `b_t->s` closes P into a directed cycle.

- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R1061.md`

This theorem localizes the same-rail cycle branch only. It does not consume that cycle or by itself force a spanning two-cover. R24 and R5 are unused.

# R2003 — First-open predecessor transport preserves a tight three-forest

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789411207.095289`

## Statement

Retain the later non-loop OUT-`v` first-loss setting, let `c=b_{t+1}` be the first R1033-open spectator slot, and let `M=hat M_{r-1}` be a literal tight normalized pre-loss three-path forest. Suppose the canonical successor `c->b_{t+2}` is selected and some selected predecessor `y->c` is present.

Then

`M_y=M-{y->c}+{v->c}`

is again a literal tight three-path forest. Its free copies are exactly `y,out` and the same far source copy `s,in`.

If `y!=s`, the unique direct closure of those defects is `y->s`. If `y=s`, the two free copies belong to the same physical vertex, and this is the unique split-copy coincidence in the transport statement.

## Proof

By R1060, `v` is an isolated singleton component of M. Deleting the selected predecessor edge `y->c` cuts one path component into a prefix ending at y and a suffix beginning at c. Adding `v->c` joins the isolated singleton v to that suffix, so it creates no directed cycle and no turn at v.

The successor `c->b_{t+2}` remains selected. Therefore the only new turn is

`(v,c,b_{t+2})`.

Since c is the first R1033-open slot, this is exactly the first-open comparison and is tight. Every other selected turn is inherited from M. Hence `M_y` is a literal tight three-path forest.

The deletion makes `y,out` free, while the fixed far free IN-copy remains `s,in`. If `y!=s`, these are distinct physical vertices and their unique direct matching closure is `y->s`. If `y=s`, the two free split copies are the OUT and IN copies of the same source vertex, so the direct closure would be the forbidden loop `s->s`. No other coincidence is possible.

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789411244.407239`

## Statement

Let `c=b_{t+1}` be the first R1033-open spectator in the later non-loop OUT-`v` pre-loss state `M=hat M_{r-1}`. Suppose the selected predecessor of `c` is the far source spoke `s`, so `s->c` is selected while `s,in` is the fixed free copy.

Then `s` is the source of that rail, and the old closure

`M+{v->s}`

has exact two-cover matching cardinality, is acyclic, and has transition count `1`. Its only new turn is

`(v,s,c)`.

Therefore either this turn is tight and the closure is a literal tight two-path cover of the current `G` support, or R3 forces the reverse tight trimer

`(c,s,v)`.

## Proof

Because `s,in` is unmatched in M, the physical vertex s has no selected predecessor. Since `s->c` is selected, s is the first vertex of its path component, which therefore begins

`s -> c -> ...`.

By R1060, v is an isolated singleton component of M. Adding `v->s` joins that singleton to the s-starting rail. Hence matching cardinality rises by one to the exact two-cover cardinality, no directed cycle is created, and there is no new turn at v.

At s, the selected successor is c, so the only new turn is `(v,s,c)`. The closure edge `v->s` is X-X. The preceding normalized closure in the first-loss packet has transition count one by R1036, so

`tau(M+{v->s})=1`.

If `(v,s,c)` is tight, every turn of the resulting selected graph is tight and the two components form a literal tight two-path cover of the G-support.

If `(v,s,c)` is bad, the vertices v,s,c are pairwise distinct: `v!=s` in the non-loop branch and `c∈B` while `v,s∈X`. R3 therefore gives the reverse tight trimer `(c,s,v)`.

# R2005 — First-open local failure is exactly an occupied replacement successor

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789411321.831759`

## Statement

Let `c=b_{t+1}` be the first R1033-open spectator in a later non-loop OUT-`v` cell, and let `M=hat M_{r-1}` be a literal tight normalized pre-loss three-path forest.

Local interception at c can fail only if c has an occupied selected successor

`c->z`

with

`z!=b_{t+2}`,

and in that case R3 forces the reverse tight trimer

`(z,c,v)`.

Thus every genuine first-open local availability blocker is an occupied replacement successor. If no such bad successor turn occurs, adding or exchanging in `v->c` is physically tight at c; in the occupied-predecessor case this merely transports the free OUT defect to the actual predecessor.

## Proof

By R1060, v is an isolated singleton component of M. Let `c->z` denote the actual selected successor of c when one exists.

If `c,in` is free, add `v->c`. This joins the isolated singleton v to the c-starting component, raises matching cardinality by one, and cannot create a directed cycle. There is no turn at v. If `c,out` is also free, there is no new turn at c. Otherwise the only new turn is `(v,c,z)`.

If `c,in` is occupied by a selected predecessor `y->c`, delete that edge and add `v->c`. Deleting the predecessor cuts one path into a prefix ending at y and a suffix beginning at c; adding `v->c` joins the singleton v to that suffix. The result is again an acyclic three-path forest. There is no new turn at v, and the only possible new turn is again `(v,c,z)`. If that turn is tight, the exchange is physically tight and the free OUT defect has moved from v to y.

Therefore local physical failure at c is possible only when c has a selected successor and `(v,c,z)` is bad. The selected vertices v,c,z are distinct: v is isolated before the exchange, c is a spectator vertex, and a selected successor is not c. R3 then gives the reverse tight trimer `(z,c,v)`.

Finally, if the selected successor is the canonical spectator edge `c->b_{t+2}`, the defining R1033 first-open comparison makes `(v,c,b_{t+2})` tight. Hence a bad successor must satisfy `z!=b_{t+2}`. It is therefore a genuine occupied replacement successor.

## Scope

This is a local physical normal form at c, conditional on the normalized pre-loss prefix already being a literal tight three-path forest. Successful occupied-predecessor exchanges may still leave a transported defect requiring a later closure or consumer. The reverse trimer is exported but not consumed here. R24 and R5 are unused.

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789412894.171249`

## Statement

Retain the first-open blocker geometry of R2005. Put

`b=b_t`, `c=b_{t+1}`,

and suppose the occupied replacement successor `c->z` produces the reverse tight trimer

`(z,c,v)`.

Then a tight Hamilton P4 is forced in every R1033 star-triangle or reverse-spoke-hook case except exactly two local no-P4 residues:

1. **Star-triangle residue.** Here `t>=2`, `z=b_{t-1}`, and the four-set `{b_{t-1},b_t,b_{t+1},v}` is exactly R516 signature `00`.
2. **Reverse-spoke-hook residue.** Here `t=1`, `z=b_1`, and the four-set `{b_1,b_2,b_3,v}` is exactly R516 signature `11`.

Both R516 rows are genuine no-P4 cells, so the list is exact at the local four-vertex level.

## Proof

Write `u=b_{t-1}` in the star-triangle branch. R1033 gives the tight turns

`(v,b,u)`, `(u,b,c)`, `(c,b,v)`.

If `z=b`, the blocker `(b,c,v)` concatenates with `(u,b,c)` to give the tight P4 `u,b,c,v`.

Assume `z` is distinct from `u,b`. Apply R3 to the triple `{z,c,b}`. Either `(z,c,b)` is tight, giving the P4 `z,c,b,v`, or `(b,c,z)` is tight, giving `u,b,c,z`.

Thus only `z=u` can remain. If `(u,c,b)` is tight, then `u,c,b,v` is a P4. Otherwise R3 gives `(b,c,u)`. Suppose there is still no P4. For the tight base trimer `(u,b,c)`, no-P4 forces the same-polarity terminal contacts needed by R516: `(b,u,v)` must be tight, since otherwise R3 gives `(v,u,b)` and hence `v,u,b,c`; and `(v,c,b)` must be tight, since otherwise R3 gives `(b,c,v)` and hence `u,b,c,v`. The star turns `(v,b,u)` and `(c,b,v)` force the R516 alignment bits

`A=0`, `B=0`.

Therefore R516 gives exactly signature `00` on `{u,b,c,v}`. Conversely the R516 `00` row contains all these required turns and has no tight Hamilton P4.

Now take the reverse-spoke-hook branch. R1033 gives

`(c,v,b)` and `(c,b,v)`.

If `z!=b`, the blocker `(z,c,v)` concatenates with `(c,v,b)` to give the tight P4 `z,c,v,b`. Hence only `z=b` remains, so the blocker is `(b,c,v)`.

If `t>1`, the spectator turn `(b_{t-1},b,c)` gives the P4 `b_{t-1},b,c,v`. Therefore a no-P4 residue requires `t=1`. Since the live later-loss setting has `b_3`, put `d=b_3`. Tightness of the spectator path gives `(b,c,d)`, while the R1033 hook right flank gives `(v,c,d)`. Relative to the R516 base trimer `(b,c,d)` with fourth vertex v, the blocker `(b,c,v)` and the hook flank `(v,c,d)` give alignment bits

`A=1`, `B=1`.

The same-polarity terminal hypotheses are therefore satisfied, and R516 gives exactly signature `11` on `{b_1,b_2,b_3,v}`. Conversely that row contains the required blocker/hook turns and has no tight Hamilton P4.

No other occupied-successor no-P4 case survives.

# R2007 — The two no-P4 first-open residues force earlier spectator-support escape

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789413290.258349`

## Statement

In the two exact no-P4 occupied-successor residues of R2006, acyclicity of the physical normalized pre-loss three-path forest forces loss of an earlier canonical spectator support.

- In the star-`00` residue, with `u=b_{t-1}`, `b=b_t`, `c=b_{t+1}` and selected replacement successor `c->u`, at least one of `u->b` and `b->c` is absent.
- In the hook-`11` residue, with `t=1` and selected replacement successor `b_2->b_1`, the canonical spectator support `b_1->b_2` is absent.

By R1049 and F-normalization, each such absent spectator support is explained by endpoint truncation, passage behind the `C_*` frontier, or membership in an off-`C_*` component normalized to its F-state. Thus neither R516 residue is a new local first-open blocker class.

## Proof

In the star-`00` residue, suppose both canonical spectator edges

`u->b`, `b->c`

were selected together with the replacement successor

`c->u`.

Then the physical selected graph would contain the directed cycle

`u->b->c->u`,

contradicting the hypothesis that the normalized pre-loss state is a three-path forest. Hence at least one spectator support is absent.

The star branch has `t>=2`, and the later-loss hypothesis `j>t+1` gives `t<=m-2`, so `b->c` is an internal spectator adjacency rather than the right endpoint-truncated edge. The edge `u->b` is likewise a canonical J-rail edge unless `t=2` and the unique omitted endpoint adjacency is the left edge. R1049 describes the endpoint-truncated J[B] rail, while F-normalization says every noncommon J-edge disappears only after its C_* copy passes behind the toggled frontier or when its off-C_* neutral component is placed in F-state. A common F∩J edge cannot disappear. This exhausts the support-loss mechanisms.

In the hook-`11` residue, the replacement successor is `b_2->b_1`. If `b_1->b_2` were also selected, the physical selected graph would contain the directed 2-cycle

`b_1->b_2->b_1`,

again impossible in a path forest. Hence `b_1->b_2` is absent. R1049 gives the same exhaustive alternatives: it is either the explicitly omitted endpoint adjacency of J[B], or, if it belongs to J[B], its split support is behind C_* or off C_* under normalization.

Thus the two R516 no-P4 cells immediately export to the already-classified endpoint/frontier/component topology.

- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R1049.md`

# R2008 — Exceptional first-open blockers are already old-F successor states

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789413354.661259`

## Statement

Each of the two exceptional no-P4 occupied-successor blockers from R2006 is itself an old-F successor state.

- In the star-`00` residue the selected blocker is the nonconsecutive edge `b_{t+1}->b_{t-1}`.
- In the hook-`11` residue the selected blocker is the reverse spectator edge `b_2->b_1`.

Neither edge can belong to canonical `J[B]`. Since it is selected in the normalized pre-loss prefix, it lies in `F\J`. Consequently the first-open OUT copy is either already behind the `C_*` frontier, hence in its F-state on the augmenter, or lies on an off-`C_*` component already normalized to F.

Thus the two R516 residues are not new endpoint-only local obstructions: their blocking edge itself certifies the previously isolated old-F successor topology.

## Proof

A normalized prefix selects only edges from `F∪J`: on `C_*` the passed prefix is in its F-state and the untouched suffix in its J-state, while every off-`C_*` symmetric-difference component is normalized to its F-state.

In the star-`00` residue, the replacement successor is

`b_{t+1}->b_{t-1}`.

R1049 proves that every selected B-B edge of J is a forward consecutive spectator edge. The displayed backward two-step edge is therefore not in J. Since it is selected in the normalized prefix, it must lie in `F\J`. If its split copies belong to `C_*`, selection of this F-edge means the frontier has already passed that position; otherwise the edge lies on an off-`C_*` component in its normalized F-state.

In the hook-`11` residue, the replacement successor is

`b_2->b_1`.

Again R1049 allows only the displayed forward spectator edge `b_1->b_2` in J[B], possibly with that endpoint adjacency omitted altogether. The reverse directed edge `b_2->b_1` is never a selected J-edge. Its presence in the normalized prefix therefore makes it an `F\J` edge, with the same behind-frontier versus off-component dichotomy.

# R2009 — Off-component first-open blockers reduce to physical obstruction

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789413782.426479`

## Statement

If an exceptional first-open blocker `c->z∈F\J` from R2008 lies on an off-`C_*` symmetric-difference component `D`, then either `c` is terminal on the endpoint-truncated rail `J[B]`, or toggling the delta-zero component `D` from its F-state to its J-state preserves matching cardinality and replaces the blocker at `c,out` by the canonical successor `c->b_{t+2}`.

Hence the nonterminal off-component residue is purely a physical seam/cycle obstruction, not a matching-availability obstruction.

## Proof

Let `M=hat M_{r-1}` be the normalized pre-loss matching and let `D` be an off-`C_*` component of `F triangle J` containing the selected exceptional blocker `c->z` at `c,out`. By R2008, `c->z∈F\J`; by normalized-prefix convention, every off-`C_*` component is in its F-state in `M`.

Because `C_*` is the unique nonzero-cardinality symmetric-difference component between the exact-two-cover matching `F` and the three-forest matching `J`, every off-`C_*` component is delta-zero. Thus `D` contains equally many `F\J` and `J\F` edges. Replacing all selected `F\J` edges of `D` by all `J\F` edges of `D` therefore preserves matching cardinality and yields another matching.

Suppose now that `c` is nonterminal on the endpoint-truncated spectator rail `J[B]`. Audited R1049 says that the selected J-successor at `c=b_{t+1}` is exactly the forward spectator edge `c->b_{t+2}`. This edge cannot lie in `F∩J`, because the selected blocker `c->z∈F\J` already occupies the same split copy `c,out`. Hence `c->b_{t+2}∈J\F`, and since it is adjacent at `c,out` to `c->z`, it lies on the same symmetric-difference component `D`.

Toggling `D` therefore removes `c->z` and installs `c->b_{t+2}` at `c,out`. The new successor is precisely the R1033 first-open successor, so the local turn `(v,c,b_{t+2})` is already tight whenever the first-open edge `v->c` is tested.

Thus no matching-level obstruction remains in the nonterminal off-component branch. Any surviving failure after the toggle must come from physical realization of the toggled state, such as a bad inherited seam, a directed cycle/component collision, or another physical obstruction elsewhere on `D`.

If `c` is terminal on `J[B]`, R1049 supplies no canonical successor and this argument stops exactly at the stated endpoint-truncated residue.

## Dependencies

- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2008.md`
- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R1049.md`
- `A7C3/WORKSPACE/D17/421-g35-normalized-shortcut-transition-frontier.md`

## Scope

This is a matching-state reduction. It does not assert that the whole J-state of `D` is a tight acyclic physical forest. The surviving nonterminal obstruction is exactly physical. R24 and R5 are unused.

# R2010 — The first-open spectator cannot be terminal in a later OUT-v loss

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789413886.871229`

## Statement

In a later non-loop OUT-`v` first-loss cell with `j>t+1`, the first-open spectator `c=b_{t+1}` cannot be terminal at `c,out` on the endpoint-truncated rail `J[B]`.

Indeed, terminality would force `c=b_{m-1}`, omission of `b_{m-1}->b_m` from `J[B]`, and `j=m`, while R1051 simultaneously makes the selected first-loss edge `f_r` exactly `b_{m-1}->b_m∈J`, a contradiction.

## Proof

Write `B=(b_1,...,b_m)` and `c=b_{t+1}`. Because the putative first loss is later, `j>t+1`, so `t+1<m` and therefore `c!=b_m`.

Audited R1049 says `J[B]` is exactly the displayed spectator path with one endpoint adjacency deleted. If the deleted edge is the left endpoint edge `b_1->b_2`, then the nontrivial rail is `b_2->...->b_m`; every `b_i` with `2<=i<m` has a selected successor. Since `c=b_{t+1}` has index at least `2` and strictly less than `m`, `c,out` is not terminal.

Thus terminality at `c,out` can only occur when the deleted endpoint adjacency is the right edge `b_{m-1}->b_m`. Then the nontrivial rail is `b_1->...->b_{m-1}`, and among vertices of index `<m` its unique terminal OUT-copy is `b_{m-1},out`. Hence `c=b_{m-1}` and `t=m-2`.

The later-loss inequality now gives `j>m-1`; since `b_j` is a spectator vertex, `j<=m`, so `j=m`.

Apply audited R1051 to the same non-loop OUT-`v` literal first-loss cell. It identifies the selected deleted same-side J-edge as

`f_r=b_{j-1}->b_j`.

With `j=m`, this is exactly `b_{m-1}->b_m`, and R1051 derives it as a selected edge of the canonical `J`. But terminality forced that same right endpoint adjacency to be the unique edge omitted from `J[B]`. Contradiction.

Therefore a putative later first loss `j>t+1` cannot escape first-open interception merely because `c,out` is terminal on the endpoint-truncated spectator rail.

## Dependencies

- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R1049.md`
- `A7C3/RESULTS/INTERESTING/R1051.md`

## Scope

This eliminates only the terminal-`c,out` alternative in the later non-loop OUT-`v` branch. It does not consume an off-`C_*` component whose J-state is matching-valid but fails physical tightness or acyclicity. R24 and R5 are unused.

# R2011 — Neutral-component toggles transport off-component physical obstruction to C_*

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789414372.145159`

## Statement

In a physically tight later-loss normalized prefix, after an off-`C_*` first-open blocker component is toggled to its `J`-state, further whole neutral-component `F→J` toggles can be chosen monotonically so that either a tight three-forest with the canonical first-open successor is obtained or every remaining bad turn, backtrack, or directed cycle meets the flipped `F`-prefix of `C_*`.

Thus the physical off-component obstruction cannot remain trapped entirely among neutral components.

## Proof

Let `M=hat M_{r-1}` be the physically tight normalized pre-loss three-forest and let `D` be the off-`C_*` neutral component carrying the exceptional first-open blocker. By R2009 and R2010, toggling `D` from its F-state to its J-state is matching-valid, preserves cardinality, and installs the canonical successor `c->b_{t+2}` at `c,out`; terminality at `c,out` is impossible. Keep the partial state of `C_*` fixed: its already-flipped prefix stays in F-state and its future suffix stays in J-state.

For any set `S` of neutral components containing `D`, let `M(S)` be the matching obtained from `M` by putting exactly the components in `S` into J-state and every other neutral component into F-state. Every neutral component has delta zero, so all `M(S)` have the same three-forest matching cardinality. Split-graph components are disjoint, so toggling one component never changes the already-installed successor at `c,out` unless it is `D`; since `D` remains in `S`, the canonical successor persists throughout.

Take a physical blocker of `M(S)` that avoids the flipped F-prefix of `C_*`.

For a bad turn or two-edge backtrack, if both selected incidences at its middle physical vertex are J-like (a common edge, a component in `S`, or the unflipped J-suffix of `C_*`), the same two incidences occur in the tight forest `J`, impossible. If both are F-like neutral incidences from components outside `S`, the same two incidences occur in the original physically tight normalized prefix `M`, impossible. Hence the blocker is mixed: one incidence is J-like and the other lies on some neutral component `E` outside `S` still in F-state. Toggle `E` to J. The exact local blocker disappears, and at that vertex the two incidences now agree with J.

For a directed cycle, suppose it uses no selected edge from an F-state neutral component outside `S`. Since it also avoids the flipped F-prefix of `C_*`, every selected edge on the cycle is then a J-edge or common edge. The identical directed cycle would occur in `J`, impossible. Therefore the cycle contains an F-selected edge from some neutral component `E` outside `S`; toggling `E` removes that edge and destroys the exact cycle.

Thus every blocker avoiding the flipped `C_*` prefix permits a toggle of a new neutral component, strictly enlarging `S` and destroying that exact blocker. There are finitely many neutral components, so the process terminates. If no blocker remains, the matching is an acyclic tight matching of three-forest cardinality and hence a tight three-forest. Otherwise every remaining bad turn, backtrack, or cycle meets the flipped F-prefix of `C_*`.

# R2012 — At most one neutral component can capture the isolated singleton v

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789414485.925629`

## Statement

In the later non-loop OUT-`v` pre-loss state, there is at most one neutral symmetric-difference component `D_v` whose `F→J` toggle can destroy the isolated-singleton status of `v`.

If it exists, `D_v` is an alternating path with `v,in` as its J-only endpoint and the toggle merely transports that free IN defect to the opposite F-only endpoint. Consequently the R2011 neutral transport can avoid changing `v` until it either reaches `D_v`, reaches the flipped F-prefix of `C_*`, or produces a tight three-forest with the canonical first-open successor and `v` still isolated.

## Proof

Let `M=hat M_{r-1}` be the physically tight normalized pre-loss state. Audited R1060 gives both `v,out` and `v,in` unmatched in `M`. Its proof gives the stronger split-graph fact that F has no incidence at `v,in`; any noncommon J-incidence there, if one exists, lies on a delta-zero off-`C_*` component.

Because J is a matching, there is at most one selected edge at `v,in`. Hence there is at most one neutral component containing a `J\F` edge incident with `v,in`; call it `D_v`. If no such edge exists, no neutral toggle changes `v,in`.

Suppose `D_v` exists. At the split vertex `v,in`, the component has degree one in `F triangle J`, and its unique incident edge is J-colored because F has no incidence there. A delta-zero symmetric-difference component has equally many F-only and J-only edges. Thus `D_v` cannot be an alternating cycle. It is an alternating path whose opposite endpoint is F-only: an alternating path with equal color counts has oppositely colored terminal edges.

In the normalized F-state, `v,in` is free and the opposite endpoint is matched by its terminal F-edge. Toggling the whole component to J selects the J-edge at `v,in` and deletes the terminal F-edge at the opposite endpoint. Matching cardinality is unchanged; the free split copy is transported from `v,in` to that opposite endpoint.

Every other neutral component is disjoint from `v,in`, so toggling it leaves `v,in` free. Neutral components are also disjoint from `v,out`, whose unmatched status is carried by the distinguished component `C_*` at the pre-loss position. Hence every collection of neutral toggles avoiding `D_v` preserves both free copies of `v`.

Run the monotone blocker-transport procedure of R2011 but stop before toggling `D_v`. If the initial blocker component is already `D_v`, record immediate `D_v` contact. Otherwise toggle any required neutral component `E != D_v`; if the only required neutral component is `D_v`, stop and record that contact. Since each accepted step strictly enlarges the toggled neutral set, the procedure terminates in one of three states: no blocker remains, a blocker meets the flipped F-prefix of `C_*`, or the next forced neutral component is `D_v`. In the first state the result is a tight three-forest with the canonical first-open successor and, because `D_v` was never toggled, `v` remains isolated.

## Dependencies

- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R1060.md`
- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2011.md`
- `A7C3/WORKSPACE/D17/416-g35-neutral-normalization-forward-blocker-transport.md`

## Scope

This does not consume the `D_v` case or the returned `C_*`-prefix blocker. Its gain is structural: arbitrary neutral-component topology can affect the key singleton `v` through at most one distinguished alternating path, and that path has exact defect-transport behavior. R24 and R5 are unused.

# R2013 — The distinguished D_v residue admits transition-neutral defect transport

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789414610.662149`

## Statement

The distinguished `D_v` residue can be made transition-ledger neutral. If `w(D_v) != 0`, R1039 supplies a unique opposite-weight neutral partner, so toggling the pair transports the free IN defect from `v,in` while preserving `tau=1`; thereafter every remaining neutral toggle has weight zero.

Thus continued neutral blocker transport either reaches the flipped `C_*` prefix or yields a tight three-forest with the canonical first-open successor, `tau=1`, and free copies `v,out` and `u,in`, where the direct closure `v->u` has exact two-cover cardinality and transition count at most two.

## Proof

Let `M=hat M_{r-1}` be the physical F-normalized pre-loss state. By R1060, `v,out` and `v,in` are free. The old same-side closure at this pre-loss state has transition count one, and because that closure is X-X, `tau(M)=1`.

Use R1039 to batch neutral toggles by transition weight. In the `(3F,1J)` branch every neutral component has weight zero. In the `(2F,0J)` branch the only possible nonzero neutral weights are one unique split pair `+1,-1`; every other neutral component has weight zero.

Modify the monotone R2011 blocker transport from its first required off-component toggle onward. Whenever a forced untoggled neutral component `E` has `w(E)=0`, toggle `E`. Whenever `w(E)=+1` or `-1`, toggle simultaneously the unique untoggled opposite-weight component `E'` with `w(E')=-w(E)`. The forced blocker loses its offending F-incidence on `E`; the extra toggle may create another blocker, but that blocker is simply processed next. Each batch strictly enlarges the set of J-state neutral components, preserves matching cardinality, and has total transition weight zero. Hence `tau=1` is preserved throughout.

If the balancing partner is `D_v`, that is exactly the moment the distinguished residue is reached. By R2012, `D_v` is an alternating path with J-only endpoint `v,in` and opposite F-only endpoint, say `u,in`. The opposite endpoint lies on the IN shore because the path has equal F-only and J-only edge counts, hence even length. Toggle `D_v`, together with its unique opposite-weight partner if `w(D_v)!=0`. The batch has total weight zero. It matches `v,in` and frees `u,in`; `v,out` remains free because it lies on the fixed pre-loss state of `C_*`.

The split endpoint `u,in` stays free under all later neutral toggles. It is an F-only endpoint of `F triangle J`, so it has no J-incidence, and distinct symmetric-difference components are split-vertex disjoint. Once the unique nonzero pair has been toggled, all remaining neutral components have weight zero, so the monotone R2011 repair continues without changing `tau=1`.

Consequently either the repair reaches a blocker meeting the flipped F-prefix of `C_*`, or it terminates in a literal tight three-forest `N` with the canonical successor at the first-open spectator, `tau(N)=1`, and free copies `v,out,u,in`.

Since `u!=v`, add the ordinary nonloop edge `h=v->u`. It joins two free matching copies, so `N+h` has exact two-cover matching cardinality. Because `v in X`, the edge contributes either zero transitions when `u in X` or one when `u in B`; hence `tau(N+h)<=2`.

Physically, the only new obligations of this final closure are the predecessor seam at `v`, the successor seam at `u` when defined, and the possibility that the two endpoints lie on the same rail, in which case the edge closes a directed cycle. A failed endpoint seam exports its R3 reverse trimer.

# R2014 — The distinguished D_v path exposes a canonical v-to-endpoint closure

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789414626.763839`

## Statement

If the distinguished neutral path `D_v` of R2012 exists, its opposite F-only endpoint is an IN-copy `w,in` with `w!=v`. After toggling `D_v` to its J-state, `v,out` and `w,in` are free, so `v->w` is a canonical nonloop exact-two-cover-cardinality closure candidate.

Whenever the toggled state is a literal tight three-forest, the only new physical obligations of this closure are the endpoint seams at `v,w` and the possibility that `v,w` lie on the same rail.

## Proof

R2012 gives `D_v` as a delta-zero alternating path in the split bipartite graph `OUT union IN`, with one endpoint `v,in` incident only to a J-only edge and the opposite endpoint incident only to an F-only edge.

Delta zero means that `D_v` has equally many F-only and J-only edges, hence even length. An even path in the OUT/IN bipartite graph has both endpoints on the same shore. Since one endpoint is `v,in`, the opposite endpoint is therefore some `w,in`. The two endpoints of the path are distinct split vertices, so `w!=v`.

Start from the F-normalized pre-loss matching `M`. R1060 gives `v,out` free. Toggling `D_v` from its F-state to its J-state preserves matching cardinality, matches `v,in`, frees `w,in`, and does not touch `v,out`. Thus in the toggled matching `M'`, both `v,out` and `w,in` are free.

Adding the ordinary nonloop edge `v->w` raises the matching cardinality by exactly one, from three-forest cardinality to exact two-cover cardinality.

Assume now that `M'` is a literal tight three-path forest. Since `v,out` is free, `v` is terminal on its rail; since `w,in` is free, `w` is the source of its rail. Adding `v->w` creates new turns only at the two endpoints: the predecessor seam at `v`, and the successor seam at `w` when a successor is selected. If those seams are tight and the endpoint rails are distinct, the new edge joins two path components and yields a literal tight two-path forest. If the endpoints lie on the same rail, it closes exactly that rail into a directed cycle.

# R2015 — Balanced two-dimensional transport returns every neutral/C_* obstruction to a low-transition closure

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789414749.430689`

## Statement

A balanced two-dimensional transport consumes the returned `C_*`-prefix obstruction. Maintain neutral J-state components in total transition weight zero, repair off-prefix blockers by zero-weight or opposite-weight neutral batches, and repair prefix-touching blockers by retreating the zipper frontier past one participating F-edge.

A finite monotone measure forces a physically tight earlier prefix with `tau<=1`. Unless its two zipper free copies coincide physically, the canonical closure to the fixed source endpoint has exact two-cover cardinality and `tau<=2`. In the sole coincidence `a_q=b_m=s`, the two boundary old-F edges at `s` exhaust its F-degree, so either a source gate is exposed or `s` is the middle spoke of the three-source X-block.

## Proof

Use zipper notation

`e_i=a_{i-1}->b_i` (F-only), `f_i=a_i->b_i` (J-only),

with first-positive index `r`. In the OUT-v cell the fixed far free IN copy is `b_m,in=s,in` for a source spoke `s` by R1051, and every standard prefix before `r` has transition count at most one.

For `0<=q<=r-1` and a set `S` of neutral components, let `M(q,S)` use the F-state on the first `q` steps of `C_*`, the J-state on the remaining suffix, the J-state on neutral components in `S`, and the F-state on every other neutral component. Require `S` to contain the R2009 blocker component so the canonical successor at the first-open spectator remains installed, and maintain

`sum_{D in S} w(D)=0`.

R1039 permits this balance. Every nonzero neutral weight belongs to the unique split pair `+1,-1`, so whenever one member must be toggled, toggle its opposite-weight mate in the same batch. Every such batch preserves matching cardinality and preserves the standard prefix transition ledger.

Start at `q=r-1` after the required balanced batch containing the R2009 blocker component. While `M(q,S)` is not physical, choose a bad turn, backtrack, or directed cycle.

If the blocker uses no selected F-prefix edge of `C_*`, the R2011 argument applies at the current frontier. A bad turn whose two incidences are J-like would occur in physical `J`; one whose two incidences are F-like neutral/common would occur in the original physical F-normalized pre-loss state. Hence a bad turn or backtrack avoiding the prefix is mixed and contains an F-state neutral incidence from some `E` outside `S`. Similarly, a directed cycle avoiding the prefix either contains an F-state neutral edge outside `S`, or else consists entirely of J/common edges and would be a cycle in `J`. Toggle such an `E`, together with its opposite-weight mate when necessary. The chosen blocker disappears and `S` strictly grows.

If instead the blocker uses a selected F-prefix edge `e_i`, retreat the frontier to some `q'<i`, for instance `q'=i-1`. Then `e_i` leaves the matching, so the exact chosen blocker disappears. Matching cardinality is unchanged and `q` strictly decreases; neutral balance is untouched.

The integer measure

`q + (# neutral components outside S)`

strictly decreases at every move. Therefore the process terminates. It cannot terminate nonphysically: at `q=0` there is no F-prefix, so any remaining blocker triggers the neutral repair move; and if no neutral component remains outside `S`, the state is literally `J`, which is physical. Hence some terminal `N=M(q,S)` is a tight three-forest.

Because `q<r` and the total toggled neutral weight is zero, `tau(N)` equals the standard pre-first-positive prefix count and is at most one. Its `C_*` endpoint copies `a_q,out` and `s,in` are free and cannot be touched by neutral toggles.

If `a_q!=s`, add the ordinary closure

`g_q=a_q->s`.

It raises matching cardinality by one to exact two-cover cardinality and adds at most one transition, so the result has `tau<=2`. Its remaining physical obligations are exactly the two endpoint seams and the same-rail directed-cycle possibility.

Finally suppose `a_q=s=b_m`. Then

`e_{q+1}=s->b_{q+1}` and `e_m=a_{m-1}->s`

are two distinct old-F incidences at `s`. If `q+1=m`, the edge `e_m` would be the forbidden loop `s->s`, so `m>=q+2`. R1037 gives `d_F(s)=2`, hence these two edges exhaust the old-F incidences of the source spoke. In the three-spoke X-block, an endpoint spoke has one source gate and one X-X mate, whereas the middle spoke has two X-X mates. Therefore the loop residue exposes a source gate unless `s` is exactly the middle source spoke.

# R2016 — The transported endpoint side is determined by the neutral-path transition weight

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789414783.157869`

## Statement

For the distinguished neutral path `D_v` with transported endpoint `u,in`, one has `u∈X` exactly when `w(D_v)=0`, and `u∈B` exactly when `|w(D_v)|=1`.

Consequently, in the physical terminal branch of R2013 the canonical closure `v->u` has transition count exactly `1` in the zero-weight case and exactly `2` in the nonzero split-neutral case. When `w(D_v)=0`, the endpoint `u` is a source spoke in `{p,q,r}`.

## Proof

Traverse `D_v` in the split bipartite graph from its J-only endpoint `v,in` to its F-only endpoint `u,in`. Label each physical vertex by its side, X or B. Traversing a selected symmetric-difference edge changes the side label exactly when that edge is a transition, and preserves the label for a same-side edge. Hence parity of the total number of transition edges on `D_v` equals whether the physical endpoint changes side from `v` to `u`.

Audited R1039 exhausts the neutral transition placements in the sharp cell. If `w(D_v)=0`, then `D_v` is transition-free or, in the PAIRED NEUTRAL case, carries exactly one F-transition and one J-transition. Thus it contains an even number, zero or two, of transition edges. Since `v∈X`, also `u∈X`.

If `w(D_v)=+1`, the SPLIT NEUTRAL branch of R1039 makes `D_v` the unique neutral component carrying the lone off-`C_*` F-transition and no J-transition. If `w(D_v)=-1`, it carries the lone J-transition and no F-transition. In either case `D_v` contains exactly one transition edge, so `u∈B`. These are the only nonzero neutral weights permitted by R1039.

Now take the physical terminal branch of R2013. The repaired tight three-forest `N` has `tau(N)=1` and free split copies `v,out` and `u,in`; its direct closure is `v->u`. If `w(D_v)=0`, then `u∈X`, so `v->u` is X-X and adds no transition, giving `tau(N+v->u)=1`. Because `u≠v` and `X={v,p,q,r}`, necessarily `u∈{p,q,r}`. If `|w(D_v)|=1`, then `u∈B`, so `v->u` is X-B and adds exactly one transition, giving `tau(N+v->u)=2`.

# R2017 — The zipper loop coincidence exposes four one-seam endpoint closures

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789414880.350229`

## Statement

In the physical R2015 loop case `a_q=s=b_m`, the source spoke `s` is a singleton rail. If the other two rails are

`P=(p_0,...,p_k)` and `Q=(q_0,...,q_l)`,

then each of

`s->p_0`, `p_k->s`, `s->q_0`, `q_l->s`

is an acyclic exact-two-cover-cardinality closure candidate of transition count at most two, with at most one new seam.

Hence if no strict-descent closure succeeds, both rails are nontrivial and R3 forces the four tight reverse trimers

`(p_1,p_0,s)`, `(s,p_k,p_{k-1})`, `(q_1,q_0,s)`, `(s,q_l,q_{l-1})`.

## Proof

Let `N` be the physical tight three-forest supplied by R2015 in the loop case `a_q=s=b_m`. By zipper construction, `a_q,out` and `b_m,in` are the two distinguished free split copies. Therefore both `s,out` and `s,in` are unmatched in `N`, so `s` is an isolated singleton rail.

Attach `s` to the source or sink of either other rail. For example, `N+{s->p_0}` joins the singleton rail to the distinct rail `P`, so it cannot create a directed cycle and raises matching cardinality by one to exact two-cover cardinality. There is no new turn at `s`; the only possible new turn is `(s,p_0,p_1)` when `k>=1`. Since `tau(N)<=1` and the added edge contributes at most one transition, the candidate has transition count at most two. The same argument applies to `p_k->s`, `s->q_0`, and `q_l->s`.

If `P` were a singleton, either attachment between `s` and `p_0` would be seam-free and would immediately give a literal tight two-forest. Hence under failure of every strict-descent candidate, `k>=1`; similarly `l>=1`.

If none of the four candidates succeeds physically, cardinality and cycle failure are impossible, so each unique new seam is bad. Boundary antisymmetry R3 gives the complete reversed trimer tight in each case:

- bad `(s,p_0,p_1)` gives tight `(p_1,p_0,s)`;
- bad `(p_{k-1},p_k,s)` gives tight `(s,p_k,p_{k-1})`;
- bad `(s,q_0,q_1)` gives tight `(q_1,q_0,s)`;
- bad `(q_{l-1},q_l,s)` gives tight `(s,q_l,q_{l-1})`.

# R2018 — Balanced nonloop closures are parity-locked at transition count one

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789414941.561289`

## Statement

Every nonloop balanced closure produced by R2015 is parity-locked at transition count exactly `1`.

For its terminal index `q<r`, one has `tau(N)=1+S_q` with `S_q∈{-1,0}`. D17.421 zipper parity gives `chi(a_q->s)≡S_q (mod 2)` because `w(C_*)=2`. Hence the closure contributes `0` when `S_q=0` and `1` when `S_q=-1`, so

`tau(N+{a_q->s})=1`

in both cases.

## Proof

Let `N=M(q,S)` be a physically tight terminal state produced by R2015 in the nonloop case `a_q!=s`, with `q<r` and balanced neutral set `S`, so `sum_{D in S} w(D)=0`.

For the F-normalized standard prefix at index `q`, D17.421 gives

`tau(hat M_q)=1+S_q+W_0`,

where `S_q=sum_{i<=q}(chi(e_i)-chi(f_i))` and `W_0` is the total neutral transition weight. Audited R1039 gives `W_0=0`. Passing from `hat M_q` to `N=M(q,S)` toggles exactly the neutral components in `S` from F-state to J-state, changing transition count by `-sum_{D in S} w(D)=0`. Therefore

`tau(N)=1+S_q`.

R2015 gives `tau(N)<=1`, while transition count is nonnegative. Hence `1+S_q∈{0,1}`, so `S_q∈{-1,0}`.

For the closure `g_q=a_q->b_m=a_q->s`, put `gamma_q=chi(g_q)`. D17.421 gives

`gamma_q = (S_q mod 2) xor (w(C_*) mod 2)`.

In the sharp cell `w(C_*)=2`, so the second parity bit is zero. Thus `gamma_q` is exactly the parity of `S_q`: zero for `S_q=0` and one for `S_q=-1`. Therefore

`tau(N+g_q)=1+S_q+gamma_q=1`

in both possibilities.

## Dependencies

# R2019 — Ordinary J-neutral prefixes give a physical pre-pivot baseline

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789414942.180039`

## Statement

The stale componentwise neutral-weight step in D17.416 can be bypassed completely before the first positive pivot. In the sharp cell of R1039 the total neutral weight is exactly zero, so the ordinary zipper prefixes `M_q` with every neutral component in its `J`-state have the same transition count as the F-normalized prefixes.

Since `M_0=J` is physical, either every `M_q` through `q=r-1` is a tight three-forest, or at the first physical failure `h<r` the preceding `M_{h-1}` is a tight three-forest with `tau<=1` and every blocker of `M_h` uses the single newly installed edge `e_h`.

Thus, before `r`, a physical low-transition prefix always exists with no neutral-component obstruction debt. Unless its two free physical labels coincide, its canonical zipper closure has exact two-cover cardinality and `tau<=2`, and all remaining physical failure is carried by that closure edge.

## Proof

Use the zipper notation of D17.421. The ordinary prefix matching `M_q` selects `e_1,...,e_q` on the prefix of `C_*`, the J-edges on its remaining suffix, and the J-state on every neutral symmetric-difference component. The F-normalized prefix `hat M_q` is obtained by toggling every neutral component from J to F.

R1039 repairs the stale componentwise claim from D17.416 and proves the exact aggregate identity

`W_0 = sum_D w(D) = 0`.

D17.421 records

`tau(hat M_q)=tau(M_q)+W_0`.

Therefore `tau(hat M_q)=tau(M_q)` for every q. By the first-positive definition used there, `tau(M_q)<=1` for every `q<r`.

Now `M_0=J`, hence is a literal tight acyclic three-forest. If every `M_q` for `0<=q<r` is physical, choose the last available pre-pivot prefix. Otherwise let `h<r` be the least index for which `M_h` is not physical. Then `M_{h-1}` is physical and has `tau(M_{h-1})<=1`.

Consecutive ordinary prefixes differ only by

`M_h = M_{h-1} - {f_h} + {e_h}`.

Any bad selected turn, two-edge backtrack, or directed cycle of `M_h` that avoided `e_h` would use only edges already selected in `M_{h-1}`. Deleting `f_h` cannot create any of those configurations. Hence every blocker at the first physical failure contains the newly installed edge `e_h`. In particular there is no hidden neutral-component obstruction at this frontier.

For either chosen physical prefix `M_q` with `q<r`, its unmatched split copies are the standard zipper defects `a_q,out` and `b_m,in`. If `a_q!=b_m`, adding the canonical closure `g_q=a_q->b_m` raises matching cardinality by one to exact two-cover cardinality and contributes at most one transition. Thus

`tau(M_q+g_q)<=2<tau(F)=3`.

Because `M_q` itself is already tight and acyclic, any bad turn, backtrack, or directed cycle in the closure must contain the sole new edge `g_q`. Hence all remaining physical debt is closure-edge debt.

If `a_q=b_m`, this is the unique zipper loop coincidence already isolated in D17.421 and subsequent results.

## Dependencies

- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R1039.md`
- `A7C3/WORKSPACE/D17/421-g35-normalized-shortcut-transition-frontier.md`

## Scope

This replaces only the physical-prefix existence role of the stale componentwise neutral-weight argument. It does not consume the physical closure seam, same-rail cycle, or unique loop coincidence. R24 and R5 are unused.
