# R2020 — Same-rail source-closure cycles are X-only

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789415193.316479`

## Statement

In any physical pre-first-positive prefix covered by R2018/R2019, a nonloop canonical source closure `g_q=a_q->s` can close a same-rail directed cycle only when the base prefix has `tau=1` and `g_q` is same-side. In that case the entire rail from source `s` to terminal `a_q` is transition-free and lies inside `X={v,p,q,r}`.

If the base prefix has `tau=0`, then `g_q` is cross-side and the endpoints must lie on different rails, so the same-rail cycle obstruction is impossible.

## Proof

Let `N` be a physical three-forest at some `q<r`, either a balanced terminal state from R2015/R2018 or an ordinary physical prefix from R2019, and suppose `g_q=a_q->s` is nonloop.

In either setting the neutral contribution has total transition weight zero. The R2018 parity calculation therefore applies: `tau(N)∈{0,1}` and `tau(N+g_q)=1`. Hence

`chi(g_q)=1-tau(N)`.

Thus the closure is cross-side exactly when `tau(N)=0`, and same-side exactly when `tau(N)=1`.

Assume first `tau(N)=0`. Every selected edge of every rail of `N` is then same-side. Since the fixed free IN endpoint `s` is a source spoke in `X`, every vertex on the rail beginning at `s` lies in `X`. If the free OUT endpoint `a_q` lay on that same rail, then `a_q∈X`, so `g_q=a_q->s` would be same-side. This contradicts `chi(g_q)=1`. Hence `a_q` and `s` lie on distinct rails, and adding `g_q` cannot create a directed cycle.

Now suppose a same-rail cycle occurs. The preceding paragraph forces `tau(N)=1`; parity then gives `chi(g_q)=0`, so `a_q` and `s` lie on the same side. Since `s∈X`, also `a_q∈X`. Along their common rail the parity of the number of X|B transitions equals the endpoint-side change, hence is even. But the entire forest `N` contains only one transition edge. Therefore the common rail contains zero transitions. Starting at `s∈X`, every vertex of the rail lies in X.

Since the retained source block is `X={v,p,q,r}`, the entire same-rail cycle support is contained in those four vertices.

## Dependencies

- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2018.md`
- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2019.md`
- retained source partition `X={v,p,q,r}` from the active D17 frame

## Scope

This does not yet consume the bounded X-only cycle. It removes every spectator-bearing or mixed-side same-rail cycle from the nonloop closure obstruction. R24 and R5 are unused.

# R2021 — Exact physical classification of a nonloop closure

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789415321.282239`

## Statement

Let `N` be any literal tight directed three-forest with free split copies `a,out` and `b,in`, `a!=b`, and let `g=a->b`. Then every physical failure of the exact-two-cover-cardinality matching `N+g` is one of exactly three local types:

1. the left endpoint trimer `(x,a,b)` is bad when `x->a` exists in `N`;
2. the right endpoint trimer `(a,b,y)` is bad when `b->y` exists in `N`;
3. `a,b` lie on the same rail, in which case `g` closes the unique directed cycle consisting of that rail and `g`.

If `a,b` lie on distinct rails, cycle failure is impossible. Any bad endpoint trimer is converted by R3 into the corresponding tight reverse trimer `(b,a,x)` or `(y,b,a)`.

## Proof

Because `a,out` and `b,in` are free in the path-forest matching, `a` is a rail terminal and `b` a rail source. Adding `g=a->b` changes no old adjacency except at those two endpoints.

Hence every newly created selected length-two walk must be `(x,a,b)`, using the unique old predecessor `x->a` if it exists, or `(a,b,y)`, using the unique old successor `b->y` if it exists. Every old trimer was already tight in `N`. Thus these are the only possible new seam failures.

For cycles, `N` is acyclic and only `g` is new, so any new directed cycle contains `g`. Deleting `g` from such a cycle leaves a directed path from `b` to `a` in `N`. Such a path exists if and only if `a,b` lie on the same rail. Since a path forest has a unique directed path inside each rail, the resulting cycle is unique. If the endpoints lie on distinct rails, `g` simply concatenates the two rails and no cycle occurs.

Finally, when the relevant vertices are distinct, R3 converts bad `(x,a,b)` to tight `(b,a,x)`, and bad `(a,b,y)` to tight `(y,b,a)`. Degenerate endpoint cases have no corresponding seam and require no clause.

## Dependencies

- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R3.md`

## Scope

This is a physical closure taxonomy. It does not itself consume the endpoint reverse trimers or the same-rail cycle. R24 and R5 are unused.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2021.md -->

# R2022 — Same-rail closure cycles convert to a finite endpoint-cap packet

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789415408.280639`

## Statement

In the R2020 same-rail cycle branch, write the X-only cyclic rail of the physical base `N` as

`R=(s=r_0,...,r_h=a)`

and the other two rails as

`P=(p_0,...,p_k)`, `Q=(q_0,...,q_l)`.

Then each cross-rail edge

`a->p_0`, `p_k->s`, `a->q_0`, `q_l->s`

is an acyclic exact-two-cover-cardinality candidate with transition count at most `2<tau(F)=3`. Hence any physical one gives strict descent.

If none succeeds, R3 forces, for each of the four candidates, at least one reverse endpoint trimer from its two possible seams. Thus the bounded same-rail cycle is convertible into a finite four-clause endpoint-cap packet and is not an independent cycle residue.

## Proof

By R2020, in the same-rail source-closure cycle branch the physical base `N` has `tau(N)=1`, and the rail `R` from source `s` to terminal `a` is X-only. The other two components are disjoint rails `P,Q`.

Every displayed candidate joins the terminal of one rail to the source of a distinct rail. Therefore its matching cardinality rises by one to exact two-cover cardinality, and no directed cycle can be created. Its added edge contributes at most one X|B transition, so every candidate has transition count at most two, strictly below `tau(F)=3`.

Apply R2021 to each cross-rail candidate.

For `a->p_0`, physical failure can only occur at `(r_{h-1},a,p_0)` when `h>=1`, or at `(a,p_0,p_1)` when `k>=1`. R3 therefore forces at least one of the reverse tight trimers

`(p_0,a,r_{h-1})`, `(p_1,p_0,a)`.

For `p_k->s`, failure forces at least one of

`(s,p_k,p_{k-1})`, `(r_1,s,p_k)`

where the corresponding seam exists.

Likewise `a->q_0` forces at least one of

`(q_0,a,r_{h-1})`, `(q_1,q_0,a)`,

and `q_l->s` forces at least one of

`(s,q_l,q_{l-1})`, `(r_1,s,q_l)`.

If an indicated neighbor is absent because a rail is a singleton, that seam simply does not exist, so failure must occur at the other endpoint. If both seams are absent, the candidate is automatically physical. Thus absence of strict descent leaves exactly the finite four-clause endpoint-cap packet above.

## Dependencies

- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2020.md`
- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2021.md`
- `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R3.md`

This removes same-rail cyclicity as an independent obstruction but does not yet consume the resulting endpoint-cap disjunctions. R24 and R5 are unused.

# R2023 — six cross-rail concatenation candidates and endpoint-cap packet

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** workspace root `1789417922.758179`

## Statement

In the sharp cell, let `N` be a literal tight directed three-forest with `tau(N)<=1`, with rails

`P_i=(s_i,...,t_i)`, `i=1,2,3`.

For every ordered pair `i!=j`, the cross-rail edge `g_{ij}=t_i->s_j` gives an acyclic exact-two-cover-cardinality concatenation candidate `N+g_{ij}` with `tau<=2`. Hence there are six such candidates.

If none of the six candidates is physical, then for each ordered pair `i!=j`, R3 forces one of the two reverse endpoint caps associated to the failed seams:

- `(s_j,t_i,t_i^-)` when the left seam `(t_i^-,t_i,s_j)` exists and is bad;
- `(s_j^+,s_j,t_i)` when the right seam `(t_i,s_j,s_j^+)` exists and is bad.

Thus failure of all six candidates yields a six-clause reverse-endpoint-cap packet, one disjunction per ordered rail pair. If one seam is absent because the relevant rail is a singleton, the other cap is forced; if both seams are absent, the concatenation is automatically physical.

## Proof

For distinct rails `P_i,P_j`, the split copies `t_i,out` and `s_j,in` are free and the physical labels are distinct because the rails of a path forest are vertex-disjoint. Adding `g_{ij}=t_i->s_j` therefore joins two distinct directed paths, reducing three rails to exact two-cover cardinality. Since the joined vertices lie on distinct rails, the added edge cannot create a directed cycle.

The base satisfies `tau(N)<=1`. The single new edge contributes at most one transition, so `tau(N+g_{ij})<=2`.

If `N+g_{ij}` is not physical, audited R2021 leaves only failure of one of the two endpoint seams. Writing `t_i^-` for the predecessor of `t_i` when defined and `s_j^+` for the successor of `s_j` when defined, the possible bad seams are exactly `(t_i^-,t_i,s_j)` and `(t_i,s_j,s_j^+)`. R3 converts a bad seam into the corresponding tight reverse trimer `(s_j,t_i,t_i^-)` or `(s_j^+,s_j,t_i)`. This gives one binary cap clause for each ordered pair `i!=j`.

If one seam is absent, only the other seam can fail and its reverse cap is forced. If both are absent, there is no changed turn to violate tightness, so the cross-rail concatenation is physical.

## Dependencies and scope

Trusted dependencies: `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2021.md`, R3, and the sharp-cell inequality `tau(F)=3` when interpreting `tau<=2` as numerically below the old source cover.

This result is a local matching-to-physical boundary test, not a global descent theorem. In applications from the marked R2019/D17.421 frontier, retain the literal rail orders, X/B labels, prefix index `q`, the next exchange pair `f_{q+1},e_{q+1}`, old-F/source incidences, short-rail coincidences, and source turns. A cap includes its inward neighbor. Arbitrary rail reversal is not a proved symmetry.

# R2024 — low-transition top-fiber covers expose a source spoke

## Statement

In the retained G13 source frame, let `G=H-{A,C}=X union B` with `X={v,p,q,r}`, and let `F` be the retained source exact two-cover in which `p,q,r` are internal. If `T` is any literal physical exact two-cover of `G` with `tau_{X|B}(T)<=2`, then at least one source spoke `s in {p,q,r}` is a physical rail endpoint of `T`.

Consequently, for `W=G-{s}`, deleting `s` from `T` leaves a literal two-cover while deleting the internal occurrence of `s` from `F` leaves a literal three-cover. Active R159 therefore gives a graph-intrinsic balanced opposite-sign pair. More concretely, after choosing a selected edge of `T-s` crossing two distinct components of `F-s`, active R176 permits its opposite singleton support to be instantiated at any chosen spare vertex `d in {A,C,s}`.

This is a source-exposure/component-drop export. It is not by itself a strict source-fiber descent or global closure theorem.

## Proof

Let `b_X,b_B` be the total numbers of maximal `X`- and `B`-blocks on the two rails of `T`. Since both rails are nonempty,

`tau(T)=b_X+b_B-2`.

The retained fact that `X` has no tight Hamilton four-vertex path gives `b_X>=2`: if `b_X=1`, the unique `X`-block contains all four vertices of `X` and is such a path. Also `b_B>=1`. Hence `tau(T)<=2` leaves exactly

- `(b_X,b_B)=(2,1)`;
- `(3,1)`;
- `(2,2)`.

Accepted R429 says every exact two-cover of this pair-deleted residue has both rails nontrivial.

For `(2,1)`, the only block shape is one mixed `X-B` rail (up to direction) and one isolated `X` rail. The isolated rail is nontrivial, so at least one of its endpoints is in `{p,q,r}`.

For `(3,1)`, the shape is `X-B-X` plus an isolated `X` rail. Again the isolated nontrivial `X` rail has a source-spoke endpoint.

For `(2,2)`, the possibilities are: two mixed `X-B` rails; `X-B-X` plus an isolated `B` rail; or `B-X-B` plus an isolated `X` rail. In the first two cases there are two distinct outer `X` endpoints, at least one of which is a source spoke because only one vertex of `X` is `v`. In the third case the nontrivial isolated `X` rail has a source-spoke endpoint.

Choose such an endpoint `s`. Its `T`-rail is nontrivial, so deleting `s` leaves exactly two nonempty `T` components. Thus `T-s` is a literal two-cover of `W=G-{s}`. Since `s` is internal in `F`, deleting it splits its `F`-rail into two nonempty paths while the other `F`-rail survives, giving a literal three-cover of `W`. Active R159 applies.

For the more explicit provenance statement, some selected edge of `T-s` crosses two distinct `F-s` components, otherwise two `T-s` components could not cover all three `F-s` components. Active R176 applies to such a cross-state and explicitly allows any spare vertex outside `W`; each of `A,C,s` is spare.

## Dependencies and scope

Dependencies: retained G13 source frame and non-Hamiltonicity of `X`, accepted R429, active R159, active R176.

The balanced pair is graph-intrinsic historical information only. R444's degeneracy warning remains in force; no payment, current selection, strict descent, or closure follows from the balanced pair alone.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2024.md -->

# R2025 — source-exposure anchor lift to a spanning cap packet

## Statement

In the retained smallest-counterexample source frame, let `T` be a literal exact two-cover of `G=H-{A,C}` exposing a source spoke `s in {p,q,r}` as a rail endpoint, and retain the tight source trimer `(A,s,C)`.

Delete `s` from its nontrivial `T`-rail, preserving that rail's original direction, and adjoin `(A,s,C)`. The result is a literal tight spanning three-forest `N` of `H`.

For every ordered pair of distinct rails of `N`, the terminal-to-source join is an acyclic exact-two-cover-cardinality candidate. Since `H` is a counterexample and therefore has no physical spanning exact two-cover, all six joins fail physically. Active R2021 and R3 consequently give one reverse-endpoint-cap clause for each ordered rail pair.

Thus source exposure has an ancestry-bearing physical consumer on all of `H`, without passing through an anonymous balanced-pair witness.

## Proof

Let the `T`-rail containing `s` be `P`. If `s` is initial, write `P=(s,u_0,...,u_k)`; if `s` is terminal, write `P=(u_0,...,u_k,s)`. Do not reverse the rail. Accepted R429 gives nontriviality of both `T`-rails, so `P-s=(u_0,...,u_k)` is nonempty and remains tight in its original orientation. Let the other `T`-rail be `Q`.

The three paths

`(A,s,C) | (P-s) | Q`

are pairwise vertex-disjoint and cover all vertices of `H`. Hence they form a literal tight spanning three-forest `N`.

Take distinct rails `R_i=(r_i^0,...,r_i^m)` and `R_j=(r_j^0,...,r_j^n)` of `N`, and add `g_{ij}=r_i^m -> r_j^0`. The two matching copies are free and the physical endpoints lie on distinct rails. Therefore the join cannot create a directed cycle and reduces the three rails to exact two-cover cardinality.

If it were physical, it would be a spanning exact two-cover of `H`, contrary to counterexample status. By active R2021, with cycle failure impossible, at least one newly created endpoint seam is bad. Boundary antisymmetry R3 reverses any such bad seam to a tight reverse trimer. This yields six cap clauses, one for each ordered pair of distinct rails.

If one seam is absent because the relevant rail is a singleton, the other seam must be bad and its reverse cap is forced. If both seams were absent, the join would be automatically physical, impossible. In particular the two nonanchor rails cannot both be singletons.

Writing `R=P-s=(u_0,...,u_k)`, the two joins touching the anchor rail `S=(A,s,C)` give especially explicit clauses:

- failure of `C->u_0` forces `(u_0,C,s)` tight, or when `k>=1`, `(u_1,u_0,C)` tight;
- failure of `u_k->A` forces `(s,A,u_k)` tight, or when `k>=1`, `(A,u_k,u_{k-1})` tight.

The identical two clauses hold for `Q`. The remaining two clauses are the directed joins between `P-s` and `Q`.

## Dependencies and scope

Dependencies: retained tight source trimer `(A,s,C)`, accepted R429 nontriviality, smallest-counterexample no-spanning-two-cover hypothesis, active R2021, and R3.

This result converts source exposure into a spanning ancestry-bearing cap packet. It does not by itself prove that one cap-guided exchange closes the conjecture; the next consumer must use these caps to construct a legal recompletion or a genuinely monotone exchange while preserving the marked data required by G13.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2025.md -->

# R2026 — Cap-guided one-cut/two-join surgery from a source-anchor lift

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** Slack workspace R2026

## Statement

In the audited R2025 source-anchor lift

`N=(A,s,C) | R | Q`,

let the nonanchor rail be `R=(u_0,...,u_k)` with `k>=1`. Then counterexample status forces at least one of the following:

1. the source-facing seam `(s,C,u_0)` is bad;
2. the source-facing seam `(u_k,A,s)` is bad;
3. `k>=2` and both rail-facing endpoint seams `(C,u_0,u_1)` and `(u_{k-1},u_k,A)` are bad.

By R3 these alternatives yield, respectively, the tight reverse cap `(u_0,C,s)`, the tight reverse cap `(s,A,u_k)`, or both tight reverse rail-facing caps `(u_1,u_0,C)` and `(A,u_k,u_{k-1})`.

## Proof

The audited R2025 lift is a literal tight spanning three-forest of `H` whose anchor rail is the retained source trimer `(A,s,C)`. Fix an edge `u_i->u_{i+1}` of `R`, delete it, and add the two cross joins

`u_k->A` and `C->u_0`.

The resulting non-`Q` component has the literal directed order

`u_{i+1},...,u_k,A,s,C,u_0,...,u_i`.

Thus the operation is acyclic. Together with the untouched rail `Q`, it has exact two-cover cardinality and spans `H` whenever every newly created seam is tight.

Write the two source-facing seams as

`L=(s,C,u_0)` and `R_s=(u_k,A,s)`.

If `k=1`, cut the sole edge `u_0->u_1`. Both rail-facing seams disappear: `u_1` begins the left fragment and `u_0` ends the right fragment. The only new seams are `R_s=(u_1,A,s)` and `L=(s,C,u_0)`. If both were tight, the displayed recombination together with `Q` would be a spanning exact two-cover of `H`, contradicting counterexample status. Hence at least one of `L,R_s` is bad.

Now suppose `k>=2` and, toward the third alternative, that both source-facing seams are tight. Cut the first edge `u_0->u_1`. Then the `C->u_0` side has no rail-facing seam because `u_0` is terminal, while the `u_k->A` side retains exactly the additional seam `(u_{k-1},u_k,A)`. If that seam were tight too, the surgery would give a spanning exact two-cover, impossible. Hence `(u_{k-1},u_k,A)` is bad.

Dually, cut the last edge `u_{k-1}->u_k`. Then `u_k` begins the left fragment, so the `u_k->A` side has no rail-facing seam, while the `C->u_0` side retains `(C,u_0,u_1)`. Counterexample status forces `(C,u_0,u_1)` bad.

This proves the trichotomy. In each bad seam all three physical vertices are distinct by the three-forest decomposition, so boundary antisymmetry R3 gives the stated complete-reversal tight cap.

## Dependencies and scope

Trusted dependencies: `A7C3/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2025.md`, R3, and the smallest-counterexample hypothesis that `H` has no spanning exact two-cover.

Provisional dependencies: none.

This is a genuine cap-guided physical surgery. It applies to either nonanchor rail of an R2025 lift whenever that rail contains an edge. It does not by itself close the remaining branch when the third alternative occurs; there the two reverse rail-facing caps become structured input for a subsequent exchange or recompletion.

# R2027 — Source-source singleton exclusion

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** Slack workspace R2027

## Statement

In the audited R2025 source-anchor lift

`N=(A,s,C) | R | Q`,

suppose the nonanchor rail `R` is the singleton `(t)` and `t` is a second retained source spoke, distinct from `s`. Then `H` has a spanning exact two-cover, contradiction. Consequently no singleton nonanchor rail in an R2025 lift can be another source spoke.

In particular, if the source exposed by R2024 lies on an isolated two-vertex X-rail `{s,t}`, then the other vertex is `v`.

## Proof

Let `S=(A,s,C)` and `R=(t)`, with `t!=s` another retained source spoke. The retained source turn `(A,t,C)` is tight.

Consider the ordered cross-rail join `t->A` from the singleton rail `R` into the anchor rail `S`. By the audited R2025 lift, this is an acyclic exact-two-cover-cardinality candidate. Because `R` is a singleton, its only possible new seam is `(t,A,s)`.

If `(t,A,s)` were tight, the joined path together with `Q` would be a spanning exact two-cover of `H`, impossible in the retained counterexample. Hence `(t,A,s)` is bad. Boundary antisymmetry R3 gives the complete reversal `(s,A,t)` tight.

Now `(s,A,t,C)` is a literal tight four-vertex path: its consecutive trimers are `(s,A,t)` and the retained source trimer `(A,t,C)`. It uses exactly the vertices of `S union {t}`. The untouched rail `Q` covers every remaining vertex, so

`(s,A,t,C) | Q`

is a spanning exact two-cover of `H`, contradiction.

Thus the singleton nonanchor rail cannot be a second source spoke. If an exposed T-rail is an isolated two-vertex X-rail, its other vertex belongs to `X={v,p,q,r}`. The three source-spoke possibilities are excluded, leaving only `v`.

## Dependencies and scope

Trusted dependencies: `R2025`, R3, the retained source trimers `(A,x,C)` for `x in {p,q,r}`, and the smallest-counterexample assertion that `H` has no spanning exact two-cover.

Provisional dependencies: none.

The symmetric ordered join `C->t` yields the same contradiction but is unnecessary.

# R2028 — Three-vertex isolated-X endpoint cap packet

**Status:** PASS_ADJUSTED
**Source:** Slack workspace R2028 re-audit

## Repaired statement

In the retained R2024/R2025 source frame, suppose a low-transition exact two-cover `T` has an isolated three-vertex X-rail `P`. Choose a retained source endpoint `s` of `P`. After deleting `s`, preserve the residual rail orientation and write

`R=(u_0,u_1)`.

Then counterexample status forces at least one of the two source-facing seams

`(s,C,u_0)` and `(u_1,A,s)`

to be bad. Equivalently, R3 forces at least one of the reverse caps

`(u_0,C,s)` and `(s,A,u_1)`

to be tight.

No stronger conclusion that `P` must contain `v`, or that a unique v-anchor cap is forced, is certified by the original argument.

## Proof

Delete `s` and apply audited R2025. The resulting literal spanning three-forest is

`N=(A,s,C) | (u_0,u_1) | Q`,

where `Q` is the other T-rail.

Cut the sole edge `u_0->u_1` and add `u_1->A` and `C->u_0`. The non-`Q` component has the literal vertex order

`u_1,A,s,C,u_0`.

The inherited middle turn `(A,s,C)` is tight. The only new seam turns are exactly

`(u_1,A,s)` and `(s,C,u_0)`.

If both were tight, this path together with `Q` would be a literal spanning exact two-cover of `H`, contradicting counterexample status. Hence at least one is bad. Complete-reversal antisymmetry R3 converts the two possible bad seams respectively to the tight caps `(s,A,u_1)` and `(u_0,C,s)`.

This is exactly the `k=1` case of R2026.

## Removed overclaims

The former proof attempted to exclude the all-source three-vertex rail and then force a unique cap at `v`. Those steps repeatedly treated cyclic rotations of a tight ordered turn as automatically tight. R3 does not provide cyclic-rotation invariance: it relates only `(x,m,y)` to its complete reversal `(y,m,x)`. Therefore those stronger conclusions are withdrawn rather than promoted.

## Dependencies and scope

Trusted dependencies: R2025, R2026 (or the direct `k=1` surgery reproduced above), R3, and counterexample status of `H`.

Provisional dependencies: none.

The surviving result is an orientation-sensitive endpoint-cap disjunction. It does not classify the three vertices of the isolated X-rail.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2028.md -->

# R2029 — Canonical triple-exposure cap packet

**Status:** PASS_ADJUSTED
**Source:** Slack workspace R2029 re-audit

## Repaired statement

In the retained source frame, suppose a low-transition exact two-cover of `G=H-{A,C}` has literal rails

`(s,v)` and `Q=(t,b_1,...,b_m,r)`,

where `{s,t,r}={p,q,r}` and `B=(b_1,...,b_m)` is nontrivial.

Lift at `s` as in R2025. Then both v-anchor caps

`(s,A,v)` and `(v,C,s)`

are tight.

Applying R2026 to `Q` forces at least one of the following orientation-sensitive alternatives:

1. `(s,C,t)` is bad, hence `(t,C,s)` is tight by R3;
2. `(r,A,s)` is bad, hence `(s,A,r)` is tight by R3;
3. both B-facing endpoint seams `(C,t,b_1)` and `(b_m,r,A)` are bad, hence both reverse caps `(b_1,t,C)` and `(A,r,b_m)` are tight by R3.

The former stronger assertions that both source-facing seams are tight and that `(r,A,s,C,t)` is a forced tight P5 are withdrawn.

## Proof

Deleting `s` from the two-vertex rail `(s,v)` leaves the singleton `(v)`, so R2025 gives the literal spanning three-forest

`N=(A,s,C) | (v) | Q`.

Join the singleton to the anchor rail by `v->A`. The resulting non-`Q` path is `(v,A,s,C)`, whose only new seam is `(v,A,s)`. If that seam were tight, this path together with `Q` would be a spanning exact two-cover of `H`. Hence `(v,A,s)` is bad, and R3 gives `(s,A,v)` tight.

Dually, join the anchor rail to the singleton by `C->v`. The path `(A,s,C,v)` has only new seam `(s,C,v)`. Counterexample status makes it bad, so R3 gives `(v,C,s)` tight.

Now apply R2026 to the edge-bearing rail `Q=(t,b_1,...,b_m,r)`. Its two source-facing seams are exactly `(s,C,t)` and `(r,A,s)`. R2026 says that at least one of these is bad, or else both rail-facing endpoint seams `(C,t,b_1)` and `(b_m,r,A)` are bad. Applying complete-reversal R3 gives precisely the three displayed cap alternatives.

No cyclic rotation of any tight turn is used.

## Removed overclaims

The previous proof tried to rule out each bad source-facing seam by combining an R3 cap, a source turn, and a cyclic rotation of one v-anchor cap. Cyclic rotation is not an axiom of Strong Level-(1) boundary tournaments. Those exclusions therefore fail, and the claimed simultaneous tightness of `(s,C,t)` and `(r,A,s)` is not certified. The downstream R2031 closure was independently falsified for the same reason.

## Dependencies and scope

Trusted dependencies: R2025, R2026, R3, the literal rail data, and counterexample status of `H`.

Provisional dependencies: none.

The surviving packet is still a concrete ancestry-bearing consumer: two deterministic v-anchor caps plus one exact R2026 trichotomy on the long rail.

# R2030 — Two-vertex source-rail anchor caps

**Status:** PASS_ADJUSTED
**Source:** Slack workspace R2030 re-audit

## Repaired statement

Let `T` be a literal exact two-cover of `G=H-{A,C}` in the retained smallest-counterexample source frame. Suppose one T-rail has exactly two vertices `{s,u}`, where `s` is a retained source spoke.

Then the four-set `{A,C,s,u}` is P4-free and both

`(s,A,u)` and `(u,C,s)`

are tight.

The original claim for an arbitrary longer rail with source endpoint `s` is withdrawn.

## Proof

Let `Q` be the other T-rail. If `{A,C,s,u}` contained any tight Hamilton P4, that P4 together with `Q` would be a literal spanning exact two-cover of `H`, contradicting counterexample status. Thus the four-set is P4-free.

The retained source turn `(A,s,C)` is tight.

If `(s,A,u)` were bad, complete-reversal R3 would make `(u,A,s)` tight. Then

`(u,A,s,C)`

would be a tight P4 because its consecutive turns are exactly `(u,A,s)` and `(A,s,C)`. Contradiction. Hence `(s,A,u)` is tight.

If `(u,C,s)` were bad, R3 would make `(s,C,u)` tight. Then

`(A,s,C,u)`

would be a tight P4 because its consecutive turns are exactly `(A,s,C)` and `(s,C,u)`. Contradiction. Hence `(u,C,s)` is tight.

No cyclic rotation of a tight turn is used.

## Removed overclaim

For a longer rail beginning `(s,u,...)` or ending `(...,u,s)`, the former proof tried to extend the rail using `(C,A,s)` or `(s,C,A)` as a cyclic rotation of the retained source turn `(A,s,C)`. Such rotations are not automatic under R3. Therefore the arbitrary-length endpoint claim is not certified and is removed.

## Dependencies and scope

Trusted dependencies: retained source turn `(A,s,C)`, R3, and counterexample status of `H`.

Provisional dependencies: none.

This repaired result is exactly the two-vertex endpoint-cap fact needed in the short-rail geometry and is independent of rail orientation.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2030.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2032.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2032.md -->

# R2032 — Two-vertex source-rail normal form, repaired

**Status:** PASS_ADJUSTED
**Source:** Slack workspace R2032 re-audit

## Statement

If a literal exact two-cover of `G=H-{A,C}` has a two-vertex rail on `{s,u}` with retained source spoke `s`, then:

- the four-set `{A,C,s,u}` is `P4`-free;
- `(s,A,u)` is tight;
- `(u,C,s)` is tight;
- `(C,u,A)` is tight;
- `u` cannot be another retained source spoke.

The formerly claimed turn `(A,C,u)` is **not** forced; the correct complete-reversal consequence is `(C,u,A)`.

## Proof

Let `Q` be the other rail of the exact two-cover. If `{A,C,s,u}` had a tight Hamilton `P4`, that `P4` together with `Q` would be a spanning exact two-cover of `H`, contradicting counterexample status. Hence the four-set is `P4`-free.

The retained source turn `(A,s,C)` is tight.

If `(s,A,u)` were bad, R3 would make its complete reverse `(u,A,s)` tight. Then `(u,A,s,C)` would be a tight Hamilton `P4`, contradiction. Thus `(s,A,u)` is tight.

If `(u,C,s)` were bad, R3 would make `(s,C,u)` tight. Then `(A,s,C,u)` would be a tight Hamilton `P4`, contradiction. Thus `(u,C,s)` is tight.

If `(A,u,C)` were tight, then the already forced `(s,A,u)` followed by `(A,u,C)` would make `(s,A,u,C)` a tight Hamilton `P4`, contradiction. Hence `(A,u,C)` is bad, and complete-reversal R3 gives `(C,u,A)` tight.

Finally, if `u` were another retained source spoke, its retained source turn `(A,u,C)` would be tight, contradicting the preceding badness. Therefore `u` is not another source spoke.

## Removed overclaim

The original version asserted `(A,C,u)` tight by treating a complete reversal as though it could also be cyclically rotated. That is not valid. The correct forced orientation on the unordered triple `{A,C,u}` is `(C,u,A)`.

For example, a globally edge-ordered four-set can satisfy the other hypotheses while `(A,C,u)` is bad, so the distinction is real rather than notational.

## Dependencies and scope

Trusted dependencies: counterexample status of `H`, retained source turn `(A,s,C)`, and R3.

Provisional dependencies: none.

The source-source exclusion used downstream remains valid. The repaired theorem also retains the exact forced orientation `(C,u,A)`, which may be useful in later short-rail recompletions.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2032.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2034.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2034.md -->

# R2034 — Low-transition export normal form

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** Slack workspace root `1789422532.306899`

## Statement

Let `T` be any literal exact two-cover of `G=H-{A,C}` with `tau_{X|B}(T)<=2` in the retained source frame `X={v,p,q,r}`.

Then either some source spoke `s` is an endpoint of a `T`-rail of order at least three, so the R2025 lift at `s` has both nonanchor rails edge-bearing and R2026 applies to each; or `tau(T)=2` and `T` has one of two rigid exceptional forms:

- **(E_X)** a two-vertex X-rail on `{s,v}` and a `B-X-B` rail whose X-block is the other two source spokes `{t,r}`;
- **(E_B)** a two-vertex mixed rail on `{s,b}`, `b in B`, and an `X-B` or `B-X` rail whose X-block is `{v,t,r}`, with `v` the X-side rail endpoint.

In either exception `t,r` are consecutive internal vertices of the long rail. Deleting them leaves exactly three nonempty tight residual paths, while `{A,C,t,r}` has a tight Hamilton `P4`. Hence the exceptional branch reduces exactly to a two-seam recompletion of those three residual paths.

## Proof

For the two rails of `T`, let `b_X,b_B` be the total numbers of maximal X- and B-blocks. Audited R2024 gives `b_X>=2`, `b_B>=1`, and

`tau(T)=b_X+b_B-2<=2`.

Thus only

`(tau;b_X,b_B)=(1;2,1),(2;3,1),(2;2,2)`

occur, with the R2024 rail shapes:

- `(2,1)`: an `X-B` or `B-X` rail plus an isolated X rail;
- `(3,1)`: an `X-B-X` rail plus an isolated X rail;
- `(2,2)`: either two mixed rails, an `X-B-X` rail plus an isolated B rail, or a `B-X-B` rail plus an isolated X rail.

Every `T`-rail is nontrivial.

If a source endpoint lies on a rail of order at least three, delete it and insert the retained source anchor `(A,s,C)` as in R2025. The shortened rail still contains an edge and the other `T`-rail is nontrivial, so both nonanchor rails in the lift are edge-bearing and R2026 applies to each.

Assume now that no source endpoint lies on a rail of order at least three.

The `(2,1)` shape cannot survive. Its isolated X rail either has order at least three, yielding a long source endpoint, or has order two. In the latter case R2032 forces it to be `{s,v}` rather than a source-source pair. The remaining two sources lie in the mixed rail's unique X-block, forcing a source at its X-side endpoint on a long rail, contradiction.

The `(3,1)` shape cannot survive because the long `X-B-X` rail has two X endpoints and at most one is `v`, so one is a source endpoint. The same argument excludes the `(2,2)` shape `X-B-X` plus isolated B.

In the two-mixed-rails case, at least one X-side endpoint is a source `s`. Its rail must therefore have order exactly two, hence is `{s,b}` for some `b in B`. All remaining X-vertices `{v,t,r}` lie in the other rail's unique X-block. Since that rail is long, its X-side endpoint cannot be `t` or `r`, else there is a long source endpoint. Therefore its X-side endpoint is `v`, giving `(E_B)`.

In the `B-X-B` plus isolated-X case, the isolated X rail cannot have order at least three, so it has order two. R2032 excludes a source-source pair, hence the rail is exactly `{s,v}`. The other two sources form the complete internal X-block of the `B-X-B` rail, giving `(E_X)`.

Both exceptions have `tau(T)=2`.

Let `{t,r}` be the two sources not on the short rail. In `(E_X)`, the long `B-X-B` rail has nonempty B-blocks on both sides of the X-block `{t,r}`, so `t,r` are consecutive internal vertices and deleting them splits that rail into two nonempty B-paths; the short `{s,v}` rail survives. In `(E_B)`, the long rail has X-block `{v,t,r}` with `v` at the X-side endpoint, so `t,r` are consecutive internal vertices; deleting them leaves singleton `(v)`, the nonempty B-block, and the short mixed rail `{s,b}`. Thus in either case exactly three nonempty residual paths remain.

Finally, retained source turns `(A,t,C)` and `(A,r,C)` force a Hamilton `P4` on `{A,C,t,r}`. If `(t,A,r)` is tight, use `(t,A,r,C)`; otherwise R3 gives `(r,A,t)` tight and use `(r,A,t,C)`. Consequently any legal two-seam reconnection of the three residual paths into one tight Hamilton path, together with this source `P4`, is a spanning exact two-cover of `H`.

## Dependencies and scope

Dependencies: audited R2024, R2025, R2026, R2032, retained source turns, and R3. No R24 or R5 is used.

This is an export normal form. It does not assert that the two required recompletion seams exist.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R2034.md -->

# R2035 — Tau=1 two-vertex isolated-X normal form

**Status:** PASS_ADJUSTED
**Source:** Slack workspace R2035 re-audit

## Repaired statement

In the retained source frame, suppose a literal exact two-cover `T` of `G=H-{A,C}` has block shape `X-B | X` and its isolated X-rail has exactly two vertices. Then the isolated rail is `{s,v}` for a retained source spoke `s`; both anchor caps

`(s,A,v)` and `(v,C,s)`

are tight. The other two retained source spokes lie in the unique X-block of the mixed rail, so that mixed rail has a source at its X-side endpoint.

The former claim that this entire tau=1 subcase is impossible is withdrawn.

## Proof

The isolated two-vertex X-rail contains at least one source spoke because `X={v,p,q,r}` contains only one non-source vertex `v`. Choose such a source `s` and call the other vertex `u`.

Corrected R2032 applies to this two-vertex source rail. It gives `u` non-source, hence within X necessarily `u=v`, and forces `(s,A,v)` and `(v,C,s)` tight.

The mixed rail contains every remaining X-vertex, namely the two source spokes other than `s`. Because its block pattern is `X-B` or `B-X`, its unique X-block lies at one rail endpoint. Therefore one of those two sources is the X-side endpoint of the mixed rail.

No cyclic rotation of any turn is used.

## Removed overclaim

The previous elimination proof tried to turn the two anchor caps and source turns into Hamilton P5/P6 paths using cyclic rotations of tight turns. R3 gives only complete reversal, so those recompletions are not certified. The exact normal form above is what survives.

## Dependencies

Trusted dependencies: corrected R2032 and the `X={v,p,q,r}` block shape.

Provisional dependencies: none.

**Status:** PASS_ADJUSTED
**Source:** Slack workspace R2039 re-audit

Let a literal exact two-cover rail contain consecutive internal retained source spokes

`(...,x,t,r,y,...)`.

Then the anchor/source four-set `{A,C,t,r}` has a literal tight Hamilton P4. More precisely:

- if `(t,A,r)` is tight, use `(t,A,r,C)`;
- otherwise R3 gives `(r,A,t)` tight, and use `(r,A,t,C)`.

The retained source turns `(A,t,C)` and `(A,r,C)` are tight.

If `(t,A,r)` is tight, the consecutive turns of `(t,A,r,C)` are exactly `(t,A,r)` and `(A,r,C)`, so this is a tight P4.

If `(t,A,r)` is bad, complete-reversal R3 gives `(r,A,t)` tight. The consecutive turns of `(r,A,t,C)` are then exactly `(r,A,t)` and `(A,t,C)`, so this is a tight P4.

## Removed overclaim

The former proof inserted the detour `t->C->A->r` by treating `(t,C,A)` and `(C,A,r)` as cyclic rotations of retained source turns. R3 provides no such rotation. It also rotated the complete-reversal caps obtained from failed boundary seams. Those steps are invalid, so the insertion and cap conclusions are withdrawn.

## Dependencies

Trusted dependencies: retained source turns at `t,r` and R3.

Provisional dependencies: none.

This is the orientation-correct anchor interface used in the exceptional normal forms of R2034: the source pair can be absorbed as a P4 once the complementary residual paths are legally recompleted.

## Statement

The repaired two-vertex source-rail packet does not locally force the former R2036 six-vertex absorber. There is a globally edge-ordered Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament on `{A,C,s,t,r,u}` in which

- `(A,s,C)`, `(A,t,C)`, `(A,r,C)` are tight;

- corrected R2032 turns `(s,A,u)`, `(u,C,s)`, `(C,u,A)` are tight;
- the six-set has no tight Hamilton P6.

Hence any elimination of the surviving short-rail branch must use additional anchored, rail, or global structure.

## Counterexample

Use the R887 edge-order model and order the 15 ordinary edges increasingly as

`ur < At < rs < us < Ct < rt < st < AC < Cu < ut < Ar < As < Cr < Cs < Au`.

A turn `(x,m,y)` is tight exactly when edge `xm` precedes `my`.

The required turns follow from

`As<Cs`, `At<Ct`, `Ar<Cr`, `As<Au`, `Cu<Cs`, `Cu<Au`.

The four-set `{A,C,s,u}` has no tight Hamilton P4. Exhaustive increasing-edge enumeration on the six-set gives no Hamilton P6 and exactly the following 12 Hamilton P5 orders:

`A t r C s`; `C t s A u`; `C t r A s`; `C t r A u`; `s r t u A`; `t A r C s`; `t r A s C`; `r s t u A`; `r t s A u`; `u r A s C`; `u r t s A`; `u r t s C`.

Each fails extension by its omitted vertex at both ends. Since every Hamilton P6 would yield a Hamilton P5 after deleting an endpoint, no Hamilton P6 exists.

An independent audit re-enumerated the edge-order model and confirmed exactly 0 P4s on `{A,C,s,u}`, exactly these 12 P5s on the six-set, and 0 P6s.

## Dependencies and scope

Trusted dependency: R887.

Provisional dependencies: none.

This is an insufficiency fence only. It does not rule out a stronger absorber using the full literal T-rail, R2025/R2026 cap packet, or smallest-counterexample ancestry.

# R2042 — Two-vertex source-exposure four-cap cage

**Status:** PASS
**Source:** Slack workspace R2042

## Statement

In the R2025 source-anchor lift arising from a literal exact two-cover `T` of `G=H-{A,C}`, suppose the exposed source `s` lies on a two-vertex T-rail `{s,z}`. Write the other rail literally as

`Q=(q_0,...,q_k)`, `k>=1`.

Then counterexample status forces all four tight caps

`(s,A,z)`, `(z,C,s)`, `(q_1,q_0,z)`, `(z,q_k,q_{k-1})`.

Moreover R2026 forces at least one of:

1. `(q_0,C,s)` tight;
2. `(s,A,q_k)` tight;
3. `k>=2` and both `(q_1,q_0,C)` and `(A,q_k,q_{k-1})` tight.

Thus every R2034 rigid exception carries a literal complete-reversal-only endpoint cage.

## Proof

Deleting `s` from the two-vertex T-rail and adjoining the retained anchor gives, by R2025,

`N=(A,s,C) | (z) | Q`.

Because `(z)` is a singleton, the four ordered cross-rail joins `z->A`, `C->z`, `z->q_0`, and `q_k->z` each join distinct rails and have exactly one new seam. If any unique seam were tight, that join would yield a spanning exact two-cover of `H`. Therefore the seams

`(z,A,s)`, `(s,C,z)`, `(z,q_0,q_1)`, `(q_{k-1},q_k,z)`

are all bad. Complete-reversal R3 yields respectively

`(s,A,z)`, `(z,C,s)`, `(q_1,q_0,z)`, `(z,q_k,q_{k-1})`.

Now apply R2026 to the edge-bearing rail `Q`. Its three alternatives are exactly `(s,C,q_0)` bad, `(q_k,A,s)` bad, or, when `k>=2`, both `(C,q_0,q_1)` and `(q_{k-1},q_k,A)` bad. Applying complete-reversal R3 gives the displayed second packet.

For the R2034 `E_B` form, deleting the source on the short mixed rail leaves its B-vertex `b` as `z`. If the long rail starts `v,t,...`, then `q_0=v,q_1=t`, so the fixed cap `(q_1,q_0,z)` is `(t,v,b)`. If it ends `...,t,v`, then `q_k=v,q_{k-1}=t`, so `(z,q_k,q_{k-1})=(b,v,t)`. In `E_X`, `z=v`, giving both v-anchor caps plus the two endpoint reverse caps on the long rail.

## Dependencies and scope

Trusted dependencies: R2025, R2026, R3, counterexample status.

Provisional dependencies: none.

No cyclic rotation, rail reversal, R2031, R2033, R2036, R2039, R24, or R5 is used.

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R21.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R21.md -->

# R21 — Puncture Crossing Parent

## Statement

If a retained path is punctured and its surviving part is nonempty, every exact two-cover of the punctured graph selects a state crossing from the surviving carrier to the exterior. More strongly, the number of such crossings is at least the intrinsic path-cover number of the surviving carrier. A non-Hamiltonian survivor therefore forces at least two simultaneous crossings of the same cut.

## Hypotheses


## Scope
For any proper prescribed path removed from a historical cover, every exact two-cover of its complement selects at least the number of surviving historical runs minus two run-crossings. Restoring the prescribed path currentizes the whole packet and all these crossings in one minimum three-cover.


## Applicability


## Persistence


## Exclusions / nonclaims


## Proof
Work in the intended smallest-counterexample puncture setting. Let K be the retained proper graph-intrinsic tight carrier before puncture, let D be the puncture set, assume the surviving carrier S=V(K)\\D is nonempty, and put E=V(H)\\V(K), the original exterior. Let T be any exact two-cover of the punctured graph H-D. The physical partition of V(H-D) is S sqcup E. Because K is a proper tight path in the hypothetical counterexample H, E cannot have path-cover number one: if E admitted a Hamilton tight path Q, then K sqcup Q would be a spanning two-cover of H. Hence pc(H[E])>=2. Apply accepted fully reconstructible intrinsic partition-cover deficit identity R7 to the partition {S,E} and the displayed two-rail cover T. If t is the number of selected states of T crossing S|E, then

t = pc(H[S]) + pc(H[E]) - 2 + sigma

for some representative-relative sigma>=0. Therefore t>=pc(H[S]). Since S is nonempty, pc(H[S])>=1, so every exact two-cover of H-D selects at least one carrier/exterior crossing. If S is non-Hamiltonian, pc(H[S])>=2 and hence at least two selected states cross the same physical cut S|E. This proves the first and stronger clauses of R21. The crossings are current selected states of this exact cover T; no orientation or endpoint role beyond the cut is inferred.

For the historical-run formulation, let a proper prescribed tight path P be removed from a historical spanning cover and split the surviving historical material into its maximal nonempty historical runs. Let T be any exact two-cover of H-V(P). Accepted reconstructed fragmentation identity R20, applied to this historical run coloring and the two current rails of T, says that the number of selected states joining distinct historical runs is at least r-2, where r is the number of surviving historical runs. Finally restore P beside the two exact complement rails. The literal union P sqcup T is a spanning three-cover of H; because H is a counterexample with no spanning two-cover, this displayed three-cover is minimum. Every selected crossing counted in T remains selected in this same restored representative, so the prescribed path and the full crossing packet are current together. This is exactly the second R21 clause. The two arguments determine only crossing multiplicity/currentness, not orientations, endpoint roles, or additional ancestry.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R21.md -->

For three distinct vertices, an ordered triple is tight exactly when its complete reversal is bad.

## Scope

## Persistence

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R322.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R322.md -->

# R322 — Dual-clique density principle for locally sparse uniform families

## Statement
Let r>=k+1, let B be a family of k-subsets of an r-element ground set, write b=|B|, M=binom(r,k), and p=b/M. Assume every (k+1)-subset contains at most t members of B. Then (r-k+1)p^2-p <= t(t-1)(r-k)/(k(k+1)), hence p <= [1+sqrt(1+4t(t-1)(r-k)(r-k+1)/(k(k+1)))]/[2(r-k+1)]. For t>=2, equality can occur only if every (k+1)-set contains exactly t members of B and every (k-1)-set lies in the same number kb/binom(r,k-1) of members of B. The case k=5,t=2 is exactly the structural inequality underlying R320.

## Hypotheses
Integers r>=k+1 and 0<=t<=k+1; B is a family of k-subsets of an r-element ground set; every (k+1)-set contains at most t members of B. Equality regularity clause is for t>=2.

## Scope
Pure order-free extremal set-system theorem. Generalizes the dual Johnson-clique mechanism behind R320 from 5-uniform families to arbitrary uniformity k.

## Applicability
Use whenever a support problem supplies a local cap on how many k-supports from a distinguished family may lie inside one (k+1)-set. Converts the local cap to a global density ceiling and exposes design-like equality structure.

## Persistence
The family B and its union- and intersection-indexed occupancy profiles are intrinsic finite-set data.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not assert equality designs exist. Does not imply path growth or Strong-specific closure. No quantitative near-equality stability is claimed.

## Proof
For each (k+1)-set U let y_U=|B intersect binom(U,k)|. Every edge of J(r,k) has a unique union U, so e(B)=sum_U binom(y_U,2)<=binom(r,k+1)binom(t,2). For each (k-1)-set S let x_S=|{F in B:S subset F}|. Every Johnson edge has a unique intersection S, so e(B)=sum_S binom(x_S,2)=(sum_S x_S^2-kb)/2 because sum_S x_S=kb. Cauchy gives sum_S x_S^2>=k^2 b^2/binom(r,k-1), hence e(B)>=[k^2 b^2/binom(r,k-1)-kb]/2. Compare with the upper bound and use binom(r,k-1)=binom(r,k)k/(r-k+1), binom(r,k+1)=binom(r,k)(r-k)/(k+1), b=p binom(r,k), obtaining (r-k+1)p^2-p<=t(t-1)(r-k)/(k(k+1)). The positive quadratic root gives the stated ceiling. If t>=2 and equality holds, every y_U must equal t and Cauchy must be equality, so all x_S are equal.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R322.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R325.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R325.md -->

# R325 — Dual-clique defect identity and extremal stability

## Statement
Let B be a family of k-subsets of an r-element ground set, r>=k+1, and assume every (k+1)-set contains at most t members of B. Write b=|B|. For each (k-1)-set S let x_S be the number of members of B containing S, let mu=kb/binom(r,k-1), and define the intersection-core variance V:=sum_S (x_S-mu)^2. For each (k+1)-set U let y_U be the number of members of B contained in U, and define the union-clique deficit D:=sum_U [binom(t,2)-binom(y_U,2)]. Then V,D>=0 and the exact identity\n\nV+2D = 2 binom(r,k+1)binom(t,2) + kb - k^2b^2/binom(r,k-1)\n\nholds. Equivalently, for p=b/binom(r,k),\n\nV+2D = k binom(r,k) * [ t(t-1)(r-k)/(k(k+1)) + p - (r-k+1)p^2 ].\n\nThus the density inequality of R322 is exactly the nonnegativity shadow of two structural defects. Equality forces V=D=0; more generally any family whose density is close to the R322 ceiling must simultaneously have nearly uniform (k-1)-core occupancies and nearly maximally filled (k+1)-union cliques in the explicit quantitative sense given by the identity.

## Hypotheses
Integers r>=k+1 and 0<=t<=k+1; B is a k-uniform family; every (k+1)-set contains at most t members of B.

## Scope
Pure finite-set stability theorem refining R322. It retains both physical localization channels instead of collapsing them into a scalar density ceiling.

## Applicability
Use when a support family is close to the dual-clique density ceiling. The identity tells whether residual slack is carried by uneven (k-1)-core concentration or by underfilled (k+1)-local cells, giving two concrete structural branches to attack.

## Persistence
The occupancy vectors x_S,y_U and defects V,D are intrinsic to the set family B.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not assert a universal small-error classification beyond the exact identity. Does not imply realizability or uniqueness of equality designs. Does not by itself produce Strong-specific path growth or two-cover closure.

## Proof
Let e=e(B) be the number of Johnson edges induced by B. Intersection decomposition gives 2e=sum_S x_S(x_S-1)=sum_S x_S^2-kb. Since sum_S x_S=kb and mu=kb/N_- with N_-=binom(r,k-1), sum_S x_S^2=V+N_-mu^2=V+k^2b^2/N_-. Hence 2e=V+k^2b^2/N_- -kb. Union decomposition gives e=sum_U binom(y_U,2)=N_+binom(t,2)-D with N_+=binom(r,k+1). Therefore 2N_+binom(t,2)-2D=V+k^2b^2/N_- -kb, which rearranges to the claimed identity. The normalized form follows from N_-=binom(r,k)k/(r-k+1), N_+=binom(r,k)(r-k)/(k+1), and b=p binom(r,k). Nonnegativity of V and D recovers R322; equality in the density ceiling is equivalent to V=D=0.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R325.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R326.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R326.md -->

# R326 — Johnson local-clique degree density principle

## Statement
Let B be a family of k-subsets of an r-element ground set, r>=k+1, and suppose every (k+1)-set contains at most t members of B. Write p=|B|/binom(r,k). Then\n\np <= [k+(t-1)(r-k)]/[k(r-k+1)].\n\nMore precisely, the induced subgraph J(r,k)[B] has maximum degree at most (t-1)(r-k), while the intersection-clique decomposition forces average degree at least k(r-k+1)p-k. Comparing them gives the stated ceiling. Equality requires both mechanisms to be tight: every member F of B must lie in exactly t members of B inside every (k+1)-superset U of F, and the (k-1)-core occupancies x_S=|{F in B:S subset F}| must all be equal. For k=2,t=2 the bound becomes p<=r/[2(r-1)], the usual Mantel density scale. For k=5,t=2 it gives p<=r/[5(r-4)].

## Hypotheses
Integers r>=k+1 and 1<=t<=k+1; B subseteq binom([r],k); every (k+1)-set contains at most t members of B.

## Scope
Pure finite-set / Johnson-graph theorem. Stronger parent of the R322 quadratic dual-clique ceiling; it uses the same two clique systems but retains the local degree information instead of averaging it away.

## Applicability
Use whenever a support family has a local occupancy cap inside every one-vertex extension. Especially useful when t is small. The theorem turns a local forbidden-density rule into a sharp-scale global density ceiling and equality regularity.

## Persistence
The family B, induced Johnson graph, union-clique local occupancies, and intersection-core occupancies are intrinsic finite combinatorial data.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not assert equality configurations exist for general parameters. Does not imply path growth or Strong-specific closure. Does not invalidate R322/R325; those remain distinct structural/stability and spectral proof resources.

## Proof
Let b=|B| and M=binom(r,k). Fix F in B. Every Johnson neighbor G of F has a unique union U=F union G of size k+1. There are r-k such supersets U of F, and each contains at most t members of B total, hence contributes at most t-1 neighbors G of F. Thus deg_B(F)<= (t-1)(r-k), so 2e(B)<=b(t-1)(r-k). For each (k-1)-set S let x_S count members of B containing S. The intersection-clique decomposition gives 2e(B)=sum_S x_S(x_S-1)=sum_S x_S^2-kb. Since sum_S x_S=kb, Cauchy gives sum_S x_S^2>=k^2b^2/binom(r,k-1). Hence 2e(B)>=k^2b^2/binom(r,k-1)-kb. Comparing and dividing by b>0 gives k^2b/binom(r,k-1)-k <= (t-1)(r-k). Using binom(r,k-1)=M*k/(r-k+1) and p=b/M yields k(r-k+1)p-k <= (t-1)(r-k), hence the claimed bound. Equality forces equality in the pointwise degree bound for every F and equality in Cauchy, giving the stated regularity.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R326.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R341.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R341.md -->

# R341 — Hamilton-five density equality gives regular triangle-free trimer bad graphs with exact edge routing

## Statement
Assume equality in the Hamilton-five bad-family ceiling of accepted R331 on an r-vertex set W, and let B be the family of five-subsets of W that do not support a tight P5. Put q=r/5, so r is divisible by five. Fix any tight trimer support P subset W and let X=W\\P. Form the bad-extension graph G_P on X by joining distinct x,y exactly when P union {x,y} belongs to B. Then G_P is q-regular and triangle-free on r-3=5q-3 vertices. Moreover every bad edge xy has the following exact routing property. For each z in X\\{x,y}, the six-set U=P union {x,y,z} contains exactly one bad five-set other than P union {x,y}. If xz or yz is a bad edge of G_P, then exactly one of them is bad and that corresponding P-extension is the unique partner. If neither xz nor yz is bad, then exactly one of the three five-sets (P\\{p}) union {x,y,z}, p in P, is bad. Thus every equality-case bad edge routes each third outside vertex either to one adjacent bad edge in the fixed-trimer graph or uniquely through one deleted vertex of the trimer.

## Hypotheses
The bad five-set family B on W attains equality in accepted R331; P is a tight trimer support contained in W.

## Scope
Extremal structural refinement of R331 using the fixed-trimer Mantel theorem R328.

## Applicability
Use only in the exact R331 equality case. It converts the global paired 4-design-like normal form into a local regular triangle-free graph at every fixed trimer, together with an exact rule linking that graph to neighboring trimer supports.

## Persistence
B, q, the trimer support P, the graph G_P, its degrees, and the six-set partner assignments are graph-intrinsic combinatorial data on W.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not assert that equality actually occurs in a smallest counterexample. Does not classify q-regular triangle-free graphs. Does not force bipartiteness, a P6, or a two-cover. The routing partner that drops a trimer vertex need not preserve the same trimer P.

## Proof
By R331, equality implies r=5q, every four-subset S of W lies in exactly q bad five-subsets, and every six-set containing one bad block contains exactly two bad blocks. Fix a tight trimer P and x in X. Bad neighbors y of x in G_P are in bijection with bad blocks containing the four-core P union {x}, so deg(x)=q. By R328 the graph is triangle-free. Now fix a bad edge xy and z outside P union {x,y}. The six-set U=P union {x,y,z} is occupied, hence by R331 has exactly one bad five-subset besides P union {x,y}. Its five alternatives are P union {x,z}, P union {y,z}, and the three sets (P\\{p}) union {x,y,z}. Since G_P is triangle-free, the first two cannot both be bad. Therefore if one is bad it is the unique partner; if neither is bad, exactly one of the three trimer-vertex-drop alternatives is bad.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R341.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R348.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R348.md -->

# R348 — Seven-vertex Mantel equality around a fixed trimer forces a P6

## Statement
Let P be a tight trimer support in a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament and let X be four further vertices disjoint from P. Form the fixed-trimer bad-extension graph G_bad on X, joining x,y when P∪{x,y} does not support a tight P5. If G_bad attains the R328 Mantel maximum of four edges, equivalently G_bad is K_{2,2}, then the seven-set P∪X supports a tight P6. Thus at the first nontrivial four-outside-vertex level, exact Mantel equality is a genuine path-growth certificate even though the one-edge-below patterns are not, as witnessed by R347.

## Hypotheses
Finite SAT certificate. By R328 equality, relabel X={3,4,5,6} with bad cross edges 35,36,45,46 and good within-part pairs 34,56; relabel P={0,1,2} with (0,1,2) tight. Encode the 105 reversal pairs by Boolean turn variables and assume no P6. Add 5040 no-P6 clauses (one per ordered six-tuple), 480 bad-P5 clauses (four bad supports times 120 orders), and for each good support 120 auxiliary path witnesses with three implication clauses each plus one 120-literal existence clause; add the unit clause fixing (0,1,2). The resulting 345-variable, 6243-clause CNF is UNSAT under an independent DPLL SAT solver. An independently generated binary MILP encoding of the same constraints is also infeasible.

## Scope
Pure seven-vertex local amplification at exact R328 equality.

## Applicability
Use when a fixed trimer has four outside vertices and its bad-extension graph is Mantel-extremal. It distinguishes exact extremal structure from merely high Hamilton-five density.

## Persistence
The conclusion is graph-intrinsic on the seven vertices.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not generalize automatically to larger outside sets or near-equality graphs. Does not say high P5 density alone forces P6. Does not use smallest-counterexample or exact-cover structure.

## Proof
By R328, equality in the four-vertex bad-extension graph means that after relabeling X={3,4,5,6}, the bad pairs are exactly 35,36,45,46 and the good pairs are exactly 34,56. Relabel the fixed tight trimer as P={0,1,2} with (0,1,2) tight.

Encode boundary antisymmetry on the seven vertices by one Boolean variable for each complete-reversal pair {(a,b,c),(c,b,a)} of ordered triples of distinct vertices. There are 210 ordered triples and hence 105 such variables. Choose the lexicographically smaller ordered triple in each reversal pair as the positive literal; the reverse turn is the negative literal.

Impose absence of a tight P6 as follows. For each ordered six-tuple q=(q1,...,q6) of distinct vertices, add the clause saying that not all four consecutive turns q1q2q3, q2q3q4, q3q4q5, q4q5q6 are tight. There are 7P6=5040 such four-literal clauses.

For each bad pair xy in {35,36,45,46}, and for each of the 5!=120 orders of P∪{x,y}, add the clause saying that not all three consecutive turns of that order are tight. This contributes 4·120=480 three-literal clauses.

For each good pair xy in {34,56}, introduce one auxiliary Boolean w_q for each of the 120 orders q of P∪{x,y}. Add the three implications w_q => each of q's three consecutive turns, and add one 120-literal clause asserting that at least one w_q is true. This contributes 240 auxiliary variables, 720 implication clauses, and two existence clauses. Finally add the unit clause asserting (0,1,2) tight. The resulting formula therefore has 105+240=345 variables and 5040+480+720+2+1=6243 clauses, exactly as recorded in R348.

This CNF is UNSAT by a complete deterministic DPLL search. A reconstructible search rule is: repeatedly apply unit propagation; if no unit remains, choose an unassigned variable maximizing its occurrence count with weight 4 on literals occurring in currently shortest clauses and weight 1 on all other occurrences, breaking ties by the smaller variable index; branch False before True. Number the 105 turn variables by lexicographic order of their canonical reversal-pair representatives, then the 240 witness variables first for support P∪{3,4} and then P∪{5,6}, with the 120 permutations in lexicographic order. This exhaustive search closes every branch with contradiction; an independent rerun visited 18,393 DPLL nodes to maximum branch depth 32 and found no satisfying leaf. As a separate check, translating every clause l1∨...∨lk into the equivalent binary linear inequality sum_{positive xi} xi + sum_{negative xi}(1-xi) >= 1 gives an infeasible 345-variable binary MILP.

Hence there is no Strong Level-(1) assignment on the seven vertices having the K2,2 bad-extension pattern and no tight P6. Therefore exact Mantel equality around the fixed trimer forces a tight P6. The only mathematical dependency is R328 for the equality-to-K2,2 relabeling; all remaining work is the explicit finite exhaustive verification above.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R348.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R355.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R355.md -->

# R355 — Hamilton-five global density equality has a parity fence

## Statement
Assume equality in the accepted R331 Hamilton-five bad-family ceiling on an r-vertex set W with r>=6. Write r=5q, so every four-set lies in exactly q bad five-sets and every six-set contains either zero or exactly two bad five-sets. Then q must be even. Consequently, combining with the accepted R346 condition q≠2 mod3, one has q≡0 or 4 mod6 and therefore r≡0 or 20 mod30. In particular global density equality is impossible at r=15 and, more generally, at every r divisible by five but not congruent to 0 or 20 modulo 30.

## Hypotheses
Equality holds in R331 on an r-vertex set W with r>=6; B denotes the bad five-set family and q=r/5.

## Scope
Parity realizability fence for the R331 paired four-design normal form.

## Applicability
Use before attempting structural analysis of the global Johnson equality branch. It removes all odd q and combines with R346 to leave only two residue classes modulo 30.

## Persistence
The bad-support family, its four-core occupancies, and six-set occupancies are graph-intrinsic.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Necessary condition only. Does not assert equality is realizable for q≡0 or4 mod6.

## Proof
Fix any five-set F. Let x_S=|{G∈B:S⊂G}| for four-sets S and y_U=|{G∈B:G⊂U}| for six-sets U. Modulo two, Σ_{U⊃F} y_U + Σ_{S⊂F,|S|=4} x_S equals r·1_B(F): a block G=F is counted r-5 times in the first sum and 5 times in the second; a block G sharing exactly four vertices with F is counted once in each; all other G are counted zero times. R331 equality gives y_U∈{0,2} and x_S=q, so the left side is 0+5q≡q. As r=5q, the right side is q·1_B(F). If q is odd, every F is bad, contradicting R195. Thus q is even. R346 excludes q≡2 mod3, leaving q≡0,4 mod6 and r≡0,20 mod30.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R355.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R362.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R362.md -->

# R362 — Global Hamilton-five Johnson equality forces a tight P6

## Statement
Assume equality in the global Hamilton-five bad-family ceiling R326/R331 on an r-vertex Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament W, r>=6. Write r=5q. Then W contains a tight P6. Indeed R346 and R355 imply q is even and q is congruent to 0 or 1 modulo 3, so q=2,3 are impossible and the first possible value is q=4. Fix any tight trimer support P in W and form the equality-case bad-extension graph G_P from R341. It is q-regular and triangle-free on n=5q-3 vertices. Suppose G_P has no 4-cycle. For any vertex v, triangle-freeness makes N(v) independent, and C4-freeness makes the q sets N(u)-{v}, u in N(v), pairwise disjoint and disjoint from {v} union N(v). Hence n>=1+q+q(q-1)=q^2+1. Since n=5q-3, this gives (q-1)(q-4)<=0, so q<=4. Thus only q=4 remains. In that case n=17=q^2+1, so equality in the Moore count holds around every vertex: every nonadjacent pair has exactly one common neighbor and every adjacent pair has none. Hence G_P would be strongly regular with parameters (17,4,0,1). Its adjacency matrix A would satisfy A^2=3I-A+J. On the 16-dimensional all-ones-orthogonal subspace every eigenvalue satisfies t^2+t-3=0. The two irrational conjugate roots must have equal multiplicity 8, but then trace(A)=4+8(-1)=-4, contradicting trace(A)=0. Therefore G_P contains a C4. Since G_P is triangle-free, the four cycle vertices induce exactly K_{2,2}; accepted R348 applied to P and those four outside vertices yields a tight P6 in W.

## Hypotheses
W is an r-vertex Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament, r>=6; equality holds in the global R326/R331 Hamilton-five bad-family density ceiling.

## Scope
Exact equality-case path-growth theorem. It uses the global equality design and fixed-trimer regularity, not Hamilton-five density alone.

## Applicability
Use to eliminate P6-free equality cases of the Johnson density bound. In a smallest-counterexample application, exact global density equality automatically enters any existing P6/contact machinery.

## Persistence
The bad family, fixed-trimer graph, and resulting P6 support are graph-intrinsic. The spectral contradiction is only for the hypothetical q=4 C4-free equality graph.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not say near-equality forces P6. Does not contradict R321/R335/R347 density-only or one-edge-below counterexamples. Does not claim a P6 itself closes O4.

## Proof
Assume global R331 equality and write r=5q. R346 and R355 force q even and q≡0 or1 mod3, so q>=4. Fix any tight trimer P. R341 gives a q-regular triangle-free bad graph G_P on m=5q-3 vertices. If G_P has a C4, R348 gives a P6. Otherwise G_P has girth at least five. R363 gives q<=sqrt(m-1)=sqrt(5q-4), hence q<=4. Therefore q=4 and equality holds in R363, so G_P has exact Moore geometry of degree 4. But R369 forbids degree 4 for a diameter-two girth-five Moore graph. Contradiction. Hence G_P contains a C4 and R348 yields a tight P6.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R362.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R363.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R363.md -->

# R363 — Girth-five Moore edge bound

## Statement
Let G be a finite simple graph on m>=2 vertices with no triangles and no 4-cycles. Then |E(G)| <= m*sqrt(m-1)/2. Equality can occur only when m-1 is a perfect square d^2, G is d-regular, and for every vertex v the radius-two Moore count is exact: {v}, N(v), and the sets N(u)\\{v} for u in N(v) partition V(G). Equivalently every two nonadjacent vertices have exactly one common neighbor and G is a diameter-two girth-five Moore graph at the support level.

## Hypotheses
G is a finite simple graph with girth at least five.

## Scope
Pure finite graph theorem, independent of Strong Level-(1).

## Applicability
Use whenever a local obstruction graph is known triangle-free and C4-free. It converts local forbidden 3/4-cycles into an O(m^{3/2}) edge ceiling and gives rigid equality geometry.

## Persistence
Graph-intrinsic degree/neighborhood data.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not classify all Moore graphs or assert equality exists for every square m-1.

## Proof
For each vertex v, triangle-freeness makes N(v) independent, and C4-freeness makes the sets N(u)\\{v}, u in N(v), pairwise disjoint. They are also disjoint from N(v). Hence 1+sum_{u in N(v)} d(u) <= m for every v. Summing over v gives sum_u d(u)^2 <= m(m-1). Cauchy gives (2e)^2=(sum d)^2 <= m sum d^2 <= m^2(m-1), so e<=m sqrt(m-1)/2. Equality forces equality in every local count and in Cauchy, hence regularity d=sqrt(m-1) and exact radius-two partitions around every vertex.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R363.md -->


---

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R366.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R366.md -->

# R366 — Fixed-trimer P6-or-square-root bad-graph dichotomy

## Statement
Let P be a tight trimer in a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament and let X be any set of m>=3 vertices disjoint from P. Form the bad-extension graph G_P on X, joining x,y exactly when V(P) union {x,y} does not support a tight P5. Then at least one of the following conclusions is guaranteed: (i) V(P) union X contains a tight P6; or (ii) G_P has girth at least five and |E(G_P)| <= m*sqrt(m-1)/2, so at least [1-1/sqrt(m-1)]*binom(m,2) pairs of X extend P to a tight P5. More sharply, if |E(G_P)| exceeds the Moore bound then conclusion (i) must occur. Equality in the edge bound forces the Moore-type radius-two geometry of R363.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1); P is a tight trimer; X is disjoint from P.

## Scope
Order-free local growth-or-density theorem.

## Applicability
Use as a local dichotomy: either a P6 is already present on the trimer plus outside set, or the bad P5-extension graph is square-root sparse.

## Persistence
The bad-extension graph and path-support conclusions are graph-intrinsic.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not say the two branches are mutually exclusive: a P6 may coexist with a sparse bad graph. Does not claim high P5 density alone forces P6.

## Proof
By R328 G_P is triangle-free. If it contains a 4-cycle on x1,x2,x3,x4, then neither diagonal can be present, so the restriction is exactly K_{2,2}; R348 forces a tight P6 on P together with those four vertices. If no 4-cycle exists, G_P has girth at least five and R363 gives e<=m sqrt(m-1)/2, hence bad-pair density at most 1/sqrt(m-1).

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R366.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R367.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R367.md -->

# R367 — P6-free Strong systems have asymptotically unit Hamilton-five density

## Statement
Let W be an r-vertex subset, r>=6, of a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament. Then either W supports a tight P6 or the family B of five-subsets of W that do not support a tight P5 satisfies |B|/binom(r,5) <= 1/sqrt(r-4). Equivalently, every r-set satisfies the dichotomy: tight P6 exists, or Hamilton-five support density is at least 1-1/sqrt(r-4). Combining with the unconditional Johnson ceiling R326, in the no-P6 branch the bad density is at most min(r/[5(r-4)],1/sqrt(r-4)); the square-root bound is strictly stronger for r>20 and equal at r=20.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1); W is any r-set, r>=6.

## Scope
Order-free global growth-or-density corollary.

## Applicability
Use when a proof can exploit either a P6 or extremely high P5 support density. The theorem is especially strong on large sets where P6 is excluded for some independent reason.

## Persistence
The path-support family is graph-intrinsic.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not infer P6 from high density alone; the no-P6 branch may have density 1 at small order as in R335.

## Proof
If W has a P6 we are in the first branch. Otherwise every physical three-set P supports a tight trimer by R8 and R366 gives at most (r-3)sqrt(r-4)/2 bad pairs outside P. Summing over all binom(r,3) triples counts each bad five-set exactly 10 times, so 10|B|<=binom(r,3)(r-3)sqrt(r-4)/2. Divide by binom(r,5) to obtain bad density <=1/sqrt(r-4). Compare with R326 as stated.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R367.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R369.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R369.md -->

# R369 — Spectral degree restriction for diameter-two girth-five Moore graphs

## Statement
Let G be a finite simple d-regular graph, d>=2, with girth at least five and exact Moore order |V(G)|=d^2+1, equivalently diameter two with every nonadjacent pair having exactly one common neighbor. Then d belongs to {2,3,7,57}.

## Hypotheses
G is d-regular, d>=2, triangle-free, C4-free, and has d^2+1 vertices with exact radius-two Moore geometry.

## Scope
Pure finite graph spectral theorem.

## Applicability
Use whenever equality in a girth-five Moore bound produces a regular diameter-two graph. It gives an immediate arithmetic obstruction on the degree before any graph-specific classification.

## Persistence
Graph-intrinsic adjacency spectrum.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not assert existence for d=57 and does not classify the graphs for the allowed degrees.

## Proof
Exact Moore geometry gives A^2=(d-1)I-A+J. Besides the trivial eigenvalue d, every eigenvalue satisfies t^2+t-(d-1)=0, so the two roots are (-1±Delta)/2 with Delta=sqrt(4d-3). Their multiplicities are m_±=d^2/2 ± d(d-2)/(2Delta). For d=2 this gives the allowed exceptional degree 2. For d>=3, the multiplicities are rational integers, so Delta must be rational and hence an odd integer q. Then q^2=4d-3 and d=(q^2+3)/4. Integrality of the multiplicities gives q | d(d-2). Modulo q, 4d≡3 and 4(d-2)≡-5, so gcd(q,d) divides 3 and gcd(q,d-2) divides 5. Hence q divides 15. With q odd positive and d>=3, q∈{3,5,15}, giving d∈{3,7,57}. Together with d=2 this yields {2,3,7,57}.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R369.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R380.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R380.md -->

# R380 — Johnson paired-design equality has a biregular girth-eight Levi geometry

## Statement
Assume the t=2 equality setting of R375 and write r=kq. Form the bipartite incidence graph Lambda whose left vertices are the selected k-sets F in B, whose right vertices are all physical (k-1)-subsets S of the ground set, and where F is adjacent to S exactly when S subset F. Then Lambda is (k,q)-biregular: every selected block contains k cores and every core lies in q selected blocks. Moreover Lambda has girth at least eight. Equivalently it has no 4-cycles and no 6-cycles. The point graph on the left side is exactly the induced Johnson graph from R379, while the line-intersection graph on the right is q(k-1)-regular with each core-neighborhood decomposing into q cliques K_{k-1}.

## Hypotheses
Finite k-uniform family in the t=2 equality case of R375; r=kq.

## Scope
Pure finite incidence-geometry theorem.

## Applicability
Use to study equality families via biregular girth methods, incidence spectra, partial linear spaces, or generalized-polygon style constraints.

## Persistence
The incidence graph and its point/line graphs are intrinsic finite combinatorial data.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not assert the Levi graph has girth greater than eight or classify all such incidence geometries.

## Proof
Biregularity follows from R375: every selected k-set contains k different (k-1)-cores and every core lies in q=r/k selected blocks. A 4-cycle would give two distinct selected k-sets containing two distinct common (k-1)-cores; the union of those two cores has size k, forcing the two k-sets to coincide, contradiction. A 6-cycle would give three selected blocks F1,F2,F3 that are pairwise Johnson-adjacent through three distinct cores. In J(r,k), a triangle not contained in one core-clique is necessarily a top triangle: there is a (k+1)-set U with Fi=U\\{u_i} for three distinct omitted vertices. Then U contains three selected k-sets, contradicting the local occupancy cap two. Hence girth is at least eight. For the right-side line-intersection graph, fix a core S. Its q incident selected blocks each contain k-1 other cores; cores arising from the same block form a K_{k-1}, while cores arising from different blocks cannot be adjacent through a second selected block without creating a 4-cycle in Lambda. Thus the neighborhood is q disjoint K_{k-1} and the degree is q(k-1).
