# R393 — Universal O4 interaction-or-endpoint-universality reduction

## Statement
Let H be a hypothetical smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample beyond order ten. Then, unless H has a spanning two-cover, exactly the following global residual dichotomy is sufficient for the generic program. Either (A) there exists a proper tight trimer J=(a,x,c) whose all-internal return yields the source-trimer-localized R389/R160 historical signed-support/anchor or cross-generation pair interaction at middle x; or (B) for every physical pair {a,c} and every x outside that pair, some exact two-cover of H-{a,c} exposes x as a rail endpoint. In branch (B), orienting the unique x-middle tight trimer on {a,x,c} and applying R358 supplies a literal R173-admissible mate clause for every such triple. Thus, after the universal trimer return is consumed, the generic O4 problem reduces globally to either one localized source-trimer historical interaction or the endpoint-universal pair-deletion regime.

## Hypotheses
H is a hypothetical smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample beyond order ten; provisional R390/R392.

## Scope
Top-level structural strengthening of R391. It replaces the local mate-clause alternative by the stronger global exact-cover property that necessarily holds if no source-trimer historical interaction exists anywhere.

## Applicability
Use as the preferred generic frontier if R389-R392 audit successfully. The two remaining targets are qualitatively different: consume one source-trimer-localized historical interaction, or contradict/exploit universal endpoint exposure in every pair-deletion subsystem.

## Persistence
Branch (A) retains its source trimer, middle, residual terminal roles, and historical interaction ancestry. Branch (B) is existential separately for each pair and exposed vertex; exact covers need not coincide. Its mate clauses remain individually certified by literal R358 proposals.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not assert endpoint universality closes the conjecture, that one exact cover exposes all vertices, or that the mate clauses are linked into a physical mate cycle. Does not assert the historical interaction is already closure.

## Proof
Let H satisfy R393. Fix distinct physical vertices a,c and x outside {a,c}. Boundary antisymmetry R3 says exactly one of the complete-reversal x-middle orders (a,x,c),(c,x,a) is tight. Relabel the outer vertices if needed and write the resulting proper tight trimer as J=(a,x,c). Apply the accepted R24-free universal return theorem R920 to J.\n\nIf every physical pair {a,c} and every x outside it lies in R920 endpoint-return regime, then for every such pair/x there exists an exact two-cover of H-{a,c} exposing x at a rail endpoint. This is exactly R393 branch (B). The endpoint-return compiler built into R920/P992 also supplies the literal one-hole or two-hole R173-admissible mate certificate for each oriented x-middle tight trimer, so the branch-(B) mate assertion follows without R358.\n\nOtherwise fix one tight trimer J=(a,x,c) in R920 all-internal regime. The proof P992 chooses an exact source two-cover U sqcup V of H-J and proves directly that both U and V have order at least three, with no use of R168. Write U=(u0,u1,...,ur) and V=(v0,v1,...,vs), r,s>=2. Since every H-{a,c} return keeps x internal, attaching x directly to the left end of either source rail would create a forbidden endpoint return. P992 therefore forces, by R3, the reverse-left shield turns (u1,u0,x) and (v1,v0,x) tight. Hence D_U=(u1,u0) and D_V=(v1,v0) are tail-signed dimers witnessed by x. Both are nontrivial and are physically disjoint from J.\n\nThe fixed source trimer J=(a,x,c) has head-signed terminal dimer M=(x,c), witnessed by a, with signed anchor x. Consequently D_U and M are disjoint signed supports of opposite polarity, hence a graph-intrinsic balanced opposite-sign pair birth Pi_U; likewise D_V and M give a second birth Pi_V. Retain Pi_U first and Pi_V later before unrelated reset. Each birth has two nontrivial dimer supports, and each uses the same terminal dimer M of the same fixed trimer J with a partner support disjoint from J.\n\nThese are precisely the hypotheses of R160. For proof-awareness, use its accepted fully reconstructible alternate route P562: P562 applies the corrected cross-generation theorem R441 to the earlier and later nontrivial pair births. If the generations overlap, R441/R436 gives explicit historical signed-support/anchor contact, growth, cycle/reversal, or signed-side descent; if they are cross-generation disjoint, R441/R440 gives the cross-generation pair interaction/descent certificate. In the present fixed-trimer situation the repeated terminal dimer M already supplies cross-generation overlap at the fixed signed anchor x, so in particular the later birth cannot be quiet and R160 yields the historical signed-support/anchor interaction required by R393, localized to J and middle x. Thus branch (A) holds.\n\nTherefore either some all-internal R920 return gives branch (A) through R160/P562, or no all-internal return exists and all pair/x choices give branch (B), with mate certificates supplied by R920. This proves R393 using only R3,R920,R160. The historical chain R358,R359,R389,R390,R392 and its R168,R5,R24 ancestry are not used.

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R4.md -->

# R4 — Smallest-counterexample minimality

## Statement
In a smallest counterexample H, pc(H)=3 and every nonempty proper induced subsystem has path-cover number at most two. Every proper graph-intrinsic tight path has an exact two-cover of its complement, and restoring it gives a minimum spanning three-cover containing it literally.

## Hypotheses


## Scope
A smallest counterexample to Strong Level-(1) two-cover.

## Applicability


## Persistence


## Exclusions / nonclaims


## Proof
Let H be chosen with minimum vertex order among counterexamples to the Strong Level-(1) spanning two-cover conjecture. By definition H itself has no spanning cover by at most two tight paths. Every nonempty proper induced subgraph H[S] has smaller order, so it is not a counterexample and therefore has a spanning cover by at most two tight paths.

H nevertheless has a spanning cover by three tight paths: choose any vertex v. The proper induced graph H-v has a cover by at most two tight paths by the preceding paragraph, and adjoining the singleton path (v) gives a cover of H by at most three paths. Since H has no two-cover, its path-cover number is therefore exactly three.

Now let K be any proper graph-intrinsic tight path of H. Its complement H-V(K) is a proper induced subgraph, so it has a cover by at most two tight paths. It cannot be Hamiltonian: if one tight path Q covered H-V(K), then K and Q would be a spanning two-cover of H. Thus the complement has path-cover number exactly two. Restoring K literally to any exact two-cover of its complement gives a spanning three-cover of H containing K as the specified current component; because the path-cover number of H is exactly three, that restored cover is minimum. No endpoint prescription or other current state is asserted. This proves the full R4 contract from the definition of a minimum-order counterexample and the elementary fact that a singleton is a tight path.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R4.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R413.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R413.md -->

# R413 — Endpoint-universal pair-deletion partitions glue globally unless a cross-state balanced pair is born

## Statement
Let H be a hypothetical smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample of order n>=11 and assume the endpoint-universal branch of accepted R393: for every physical pair D={a,c} and every x outside D, some exact two-cover of H-D exposes x as a rail endpoint. Then either H has a spanning two-cover, or H contains a graph-intrinsic balanced opposite-sign pair arising from the R176 cross-state comparison of two exact two-covers of one common proper residue. More structurally, if no such R176 pair occurs in any comparison used below, then for every pair D all exact two-covers of H-D induce one canonical unordered rail-support partition pi_D, these pair-deletion partitions agree on every triple overlap, and they glue to one global bipartition V(H)=A sqcup B such that every exact two-cover of H-D has rail supports A\\D and B\\D. The pair-deletion rail floor then forces |A|,|B|>=3. Deleting two vertices of A gives an exact cover whose untouched B-rail is a Hamilton tight path on all of B; deleting two vertices of B similarly gives a Hamilton tight path on all of A. Those two full-block Hamilton paths form a spanning two-cover of H, contradiction. Hence the endpoint-universal branch cannot persist without producing an R176 common-shadow cross-state balanced pair.

## Hypotheses
H is a hypothetical smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample with n>=11; accepted endpoint universality R393, pair-deletion rail floor R168, cross-state upgrade R176, and partition rigidity R410.

## Scope
Global gluing theorem for the endpoint-universal branch. No capture, first-contact, density, or longest-path hypothesis.

## Applicability
Use as the preferred global consumer of endpoint universality. It replaces arbitrary endpoint-return multiplicity by either an R176 cross-state balanced pair with common-shadow provenance or an impossible global two-block decomposition whose blocks are both Hamiltonian.

## Persistence
The canonical partitions pi_D and global blocks A,B are conclusions only in the no-R176-pair branch. The R176 balanced pair is graph-intrinsic historical information. The Hamilton paths on A and B used at the end may come from different pair-deletion representatives, which is harmless because their supports are disjoint and graph-intrinsic.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not claim the R176 balanced pair itself closes the conjecture or preserves a prescribed puncture. Does not assert canonical path orders within A or B. The gluing uses endpoint universality to obtain common triple-deletion covers and fails without that hypothesis.

## Proof
Assume the endpoint-universal property explicitly stated in R413, and assume no comparison produces the balanced pair supplied by R410 through its R176 mechanism. For a fixed pair D, R410 implies that all exact two-covers of H-D have one canonical unordered support partition pi_D; otherwise R410 already gives the desired pair. Now take distinct a,c,d. Endpoint universality for {a,c} gives an exact two-cover of H-{a,c} exposing d at a rail endpoint. The d-rail cannot be the singleton (d): if it were, the other rail would be Hamiltonian on H-{a,c,d}, while R3 supplies a tight trimer on {a,c,d}; those two disjoint paths would span H. Hence deleting endpoint d leaves two nonempty paths and therefore an exact two-cover T1 of H-{a,c,d}. Similarly endpoint universality for {a,d}, followed by trimming c, gives an exact two-cover T2 of the same residue. R410 applied to T1,T2 says either the desired balanced pair occurs or their support partitions agree. Thus pi_{a,c} and pi_{a,d}, restricted to the common triple-deletion residue, agree up to exchange. Define u~v when, for any deletion pair D disjoint from {u,v}, u and v lie in the same block of pi_D. The preceding overlap identity makes this well defined because the two-subset graph of V(H)-{u,v} is connected by single-vertex exchanges. Transitivity is checked inside one pi_D disjoint from any tested triple. There are exactly two equivalence classes A,B: at least two because every pi_D has two nonempty blocks, and at most two because any three vertices survive some pi_D, which has only two blocks. Therefore pi_D={A-D,B-D} for every pair D. Since exact two-covers have two nonempty rails, |A| and |B| are at least three: if a class had size one or two, choose a deletion pair containing that entire class, making its corresponding block empty. Choose distinct a1,a2 in A. Endpoint universality ensures an exact cover of H-{a1,a2}; its supports are A-{a1,a2} and B, so B itself has a Hamilton tight path. Likewise deleting two vertices of B gives a Hamilton tight path on all of A. The two full-block paths are disjoint and together span H, contradiction. Hence endpoint universality yields either the R410/R176 balanced pair or closure. Direct dependencies are only R3 and R410. R168, R393, R5, and R24 are not used.

# R415 — Certificate-retaining balanced-pair descent to the both-singleton floor

## Statement
Let H be a hypothetical smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample and let Pi be a historical balanced opposite-sign pair equipped with a retained physical birth/refund certificate stack in the sense of the signed-support payment machinery. Then there is a chosen certificate-retaining continuation along which either H acquires a spanning two-cover or the active pair support mass descends to two, so both active signed supports are singletons. Every credited mass decrease is backed by a named physical turn/selected outside boundary/Signed-Interval Rebirth certificate, and the pre-existing graph-intrinsic birth ancestry of Pi remains retained as historical certificate data throughout the chosen descent. In particular the endpoint case with one singleton support and one nontrivial support admits a direct one-unit refund using one selected boundary of a nontrivial outside rail; the complementary outside-cover shapes are handled by the previously audited singleton analysis. The resulting both-singleton label by itself is not a contradiction and may be formally cheap; the durable output is the both-singleton floor together with the full retained birth/refund ancestry stack.

## Hypotheses
H is a hypothetical smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample; Pi is an ancestry-bearing balanced opposite-sign pair in the accepted historical signed-support convention; the standard certificate-retaining pair-payment/refund machinery is available.

## Scope
Historical Strong Level-(1) signed-payment theorem. The continuation is lineage-relative and preserves graph-intrinsic certificate ancestry, not one current cover through all steps.

## Applicability
Use after an R176 cross-state pair or any other balanced-pair birth whose provenance matters. It converts pair birth into a finite paid checkpoint: spanning two-cover or ancestry-bearing both-singleton floor. Do not use bare pair mass as a global monotone across unrelated births.

## Persistence
The initial pair birth certificate, any cross-state/reverse-trimer orientation supplied at birth, each chosen refund marker/blade, descendant signed intervals, and final singleton supports are retained as historical truth in the chosen ledger. Active representatives may change.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not close the both-singleton layer. Does not claim pair mass is globally monotone across unrelated remints. Does not assert all balanced-pair continuations follow the same representatives. Does not permit discarding the birth/cross-state ancestry and retaining only anonymous singleton labels.

## Proof
Let Pi be the given ancestry-bearing balanced opposite-sign pair with retained birth/refund certificate stack. If both active supports are already singleton, the conclusion holds. If one support is singleton and the other is nontrivial, apply fully reconstructible R428. Along its chosen nonclosing continuation the singleton support is preserved, the opposite support strictly shortens at each refund, and either a spanning two-cover occurs or both supports become singleton; its refund/rebirth certificates append to the incoming Pi ledger. Suppose instead that no support is singleton. While both supports have order at least three, apply fully reconstructible R426. Its global fixed-witness descent gives either a spanning two-cover or a strict descendant balanced pair, recording each mass decrease by an explicit reverse-trimer shell/refund certificate and retaining the pre-existing pair ancestry. Iterating this chosen nonclosing phase terminates with at least one support of order at most two. If a singleton has appeared, apply R428 to the singleton/nontrivial pair, unless both supports are already singleton. Otherwise some support has order exactly two. Apply fully reconstructible R427 to that ancestry-bearing pair. It gives either a spanning two-cover or a descendant balanced pair with a singleton support, retaining the old dimer, swallowing/reverse-trimer data, and the prior ancestry stack. In the nonclosing branch apply R428 to that singleton/nontrivial pair; if the opposite support is already singleton there is nothing to do, otherwise R428 terminates at a both-singleton pair while preserving the fixed singleton and appending its ordered refund ledger. Thus in every case there is a finite chosen continuation ending in a spanning two-cover or active pair mass two. Every credited mass decrease is certified by one of R426,R427,R428, and concatenating their persistence ledgers retains the initial pair birth plus all subsequent physical refund/rebirth certificates as historical truth. Because the continuation is chosen lineage-relative, this proves no global monotonicity across unrelated pair births or remints, exactly as fenced in R415.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R415.md -->

# R42 — Captured-anchor first-contact control

## Statement

After choosing one actual capture descendant and one designated quiet continuation, the captured anchor remains protected until it reaches the named target role or the first later event touching it is exposed. If a later operation uses a signed support containing that anchor, the operation cannot be a quiet unrelated epoch: an earlier contact was already exposed or the operation itself is the first contact.

## Hypotheses


## Scope
This theorem begins only after an actual protected continuation has been chosen. It does not upgrade every historical capture to current protection, and it does not preserve unrelated current return geometry.


## Applicability


## Persistence


## Exclusions / nonclaims


## Proof
Let e be the physical endpoint captured in the chosen actual-capture descendant, and retain the graph-intrinsic signed support S_0 whose signed endpoint is e. Choose the continuation now, at this capture event. Maintain the invariant that before the named target role is reached, either a first contact with e has already been exposed or the continuation retains a historical signed descendant S_i with the same anchor e. Consider the next support/marker path Q used by a quiet macro. If Q is disjoint from S_i, keep S_i. If Q meets S_i but avoids e, apply the first branch of R436: replace S_i by the nonempty signed-side prefix/suffix ending before the first Q-contact. This is a strictly shorter signed support with the same anchor e, so the invariant persists. If Q contains e, the at-anchor branch of R436 gives strict path growth, tight cycle, or a reverse contact/reversal cell, except for exact stationary singleton replay; in every genuine touching operation this is the exposed first-contact event and the protected-quiet branch stops. Exact replay does not erase the anchor and therefore leaves the invariant unchanged. Thus no chosen quiet operation can silently remove e. The captured anchor remains protected along the designated continuation until the continuation reaches its named target role or the first later genuine event touching e is exposed. In particular a later operation using a signed support containing e cannot constitute a new unrelated quiet epoch: either an earlier first contact already stopped the protected branch or that operation is itself the first contact.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R42.md -->

# R423 — Fixed-Turn Singleton-Checkpoint Reentry

## Statement
Let H be a hypothetical smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample. Fix an arbitrarily preselected retained proper tight turn J=(a,b,c). From any ancestry-bearing both-singleton floor (p),(t), there is a finite chosen continuation which, unless a spanning two-cover or an accepted explicit historical pair/contact exit occurs first, steers the active floor to (a),(c). In the exact aligned pair-deletion frame H-{a,c}=U sqcup V, selected predecessor/successor incidence at b yields an endpoint-anchored signed dimer at a or c; each quiet aligned reentry captures a previously uncaptured endpoint of J. Hence at most two aligned reentries are quiet, and every later aligned reentry yields a spanning two-cover or an explicit historical signed-support contact / cross-generation pair interaction.

## Hypotheses
H is a hypothetical smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample; J=(a,b,c) is any preselected proper tight turn retained as a graph-intrinsic lineage coordinate; an ancestry-bearing both-singleton floor exists. The theorem uses Complete Floor Pair Steering, Pair-Deletion Rigidity, the audited selected-incidence endpoint-anchor extraction, actualization, and the Fixed-Turn Common-Frame Endpoint Budget.

## Scope
Strong Level-(1), arbitrary order. The quantifiers are turn-first and floor-independent: J may be fixed before the floor is chosen/produced, and the incoming ancestry-bearing floor need not already use a or c. This is the historically audited fixed-turn reentry composition.

## Applicability
Use when a desired physical pair {a,c} is the outer pair of a chosen proper turn J and an ancestry-bearing mass-two floor is already available. Along a chosen nonclosing/non-exit continuation, the floor can be aligned to {a,c} without requiring compatibility between its original singleton coordinates and J.

## Persistence
The physical turn J remains graph-intrinsic and fixed. Complete Floor Pair Steering retains the full physical certificate ledger of the incoming ancestry-bearing floor through singleton replacements, including earlier pair-mass/refund/contact certificates, while the current floor coordinates change. The theorem does not require the original floor representative, original witnesses, or old selected paths to remain current. At the aligned checkpoint the exact pair-deletion frame and subsequent endpoint-capture/contact history belong to the chosen J-lineage.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not assert arbitrary same-representative synchronization; does not promise preservation of fixed witness names during steering; does not say every explicit pair/contact exit closes; does not make Psi_J a global rank across turn switches; does not assert that an arbitrary merely historical pair that is no longer an active retained pair can be attached to J. The exact historical sources explicitly prove the turn-first theorem at the ancestry-bearing both-singleton floor. For a higher-mass pair predating the choice of J, the sources separately prove birth-frame-agnostic retained-turn taxation for later retained pairs, but this proposal does not strengthen the chronology beyond the explicit floor-level theorem.

## Proof
Fix the arbitrary preselected proper turn J=(a,b,c) and any ancestry-bearing both-singleton floor. Apply R432 with target {a,c}. Unless a spanning two-cover occurs, this reaches an aligned floor on {a,c}. Now invoke corrected R434 at every aligned common-frame episode. Its selected-incidence extraction either gives an explicit contact/growth output or, for a fresh endpoint e in {a,c}, starts an R42-protected descendant and returns quietly to another aligned floor only after e has become a retained signed singleton coordinate. Thus a completed quiet episode strictly enlarges the completed-endpoint set A_J subseteq {a,c}. Reuse of an endpoint already in A_J is nonquiet by the explicit anchor-contact/strict-growth clause of R434. Hence at most two aligned episodes are quiet. This proves the historical Fixed-Turn Singleton-Checkpoint Reentry conclusion without using the compressed R172 lex-clock proof as a dependency; R432 supplies arbitrary floor-to-target alignment and R434 supplies the exact finite endpoint budget.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R423.md -->

# R425 — Signed-Interval Rebirth and Tight-Path Cut Memory

## Statement
Let P=(v_0,...,v_k) be a graph-intrinsic tight path. Head form: if P is head-signed by w, meaning (w,v_0,...,v_k) is tight, and S is any vertex set with P-S nonempty, then the first surviving interval I=(v_i,...,v_j) of P-S in the old path order is head-signed. If i=0 the witness remains w; if i>0 then v_{i-1} is deleted and (v_{i-1},I) is tight, so v_{i-1} is a new witness. Tail form is dual: if (v_0,...,v_k,z) is tight, the last surviving interval J=(v_i,...,v_j) after deleting S is tail-signed by z when j=k and otherwise by the immediately following deleted vertex v_{j+1}. More generally every surviving interval remembers both cut neighbors: when i>0, (v_{i-1},I) is tight, and when j<k, (I,v_{j+1}) is tight.

## Hypotheses
P is a tight path; the relevant historical head/tail sign is graph-intrinsic when using the signed forms; S is any vertex set; at least one vertex of P survives.

## Scope
Strong-safe and in fact purely path-order theoretic. No smallest-counterexample, cover, CW, exchange, or bounded-marker hypothesis is required.

## Applicability
Use whenever a physical marker/delete-set meets a historical signed support but does not swallow it. It gives a nested signed descendant and exact cut-side witness information without requiring any later cover to select the descendant states.

## Persistence
The surviving interval is a literal ordered subpath of the old support. The sign is graph-intrinsic. The witness may migrate to the immediately deleted old-path neighbor. Repeated contacts yield a nested support ancestry chain with explicit cut witnesses.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not preserve the original signed endpoint anchor when that endpoint is deleted; does not assert selected-state persistence in later covers; does not make deleted marker vertices current; does not by itself imply a cover or component-count improvement.

## Proof
Write P=(v_0,...,v_k). For a head sign (w;P), let I=(v_i,...,v_j) be the first surviving interval after deleting S. If i=0, (w,I) is a prefix of the certified tight path (w,P). If i>0, first-survival implies v_{i-1} in S, and (v_{i-1},v_i,...,v_j) is a contiguous subpath of P, hence tight. Therefore I is head-signed by v_{i-1}. For a tail sign, take the last surviving interval J=(v_i,...,v_j). If j=k retain z; if j<k, then v_{j+1} is deleted and (v_i,...,v_j,v_{j+1}) is a contiguous subpath of P. The same observations on both ends of an arbitrary surviving interval give Tight-Path Cut Memory. This is the exact historical R11 proof. R12 subsequently audited the head form, tail form, cut memory, and marker-contact descent positively.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R425.md -->

# R427 — Width-Two Signed-Pair Dimension Lowering

## Statement
Let H be a hypothetical smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample and let a graph-intrinsic balanced opposite-sign pair have at least one support of order two. Then there is a finite chosen certificate-retaining continuation yielding either a spanning two-cover or a descendant balanced opposite-sign pair with a singleton support. In the head-signed dimer swallowing case (alpha;(p_0,p_1)), one may choose the relevant outside sandwich head nu distinct from alpha; if p_0p_1nu is bad then nu p_1p_0 is tight, and antisymmetry on the distinct triple {nu,p_0,alpha} supplies a second tight trimer meeting the dimer in exactly p_0. Signed-Interval Rebirth therefore leaves the singleton (p_1) head-signed. The tail-side dual is exact. All other width-two sandwich failures already strictly shrink a support or give a two-cover, so finite repetition reaches a singleton.

## Hypotheses
H is a smallest Strong counterexample; a balanced opposite-sign pair is present; at least one support has order exactly two. Use the historical Pair-Complement Sandwich seam table and choose an outside cover endpoint distinct from the relevant sign witness as in the witness-separation lemma.

## Scope
Strong Level-(1), arbitrary order. This is a chosen certificate-retaining dimension-lowering theorem, not a global scalar monotonicity statement.

## Applicability
Use whenever pair descent reaches a signed dimer. It physically pays the last dimension drop to a singleton without voluntary support truncation and without requiring a two-witness reversed-dimer collision.

## Persistence
Retains the old dimer as historical ancestry, the R12 swallowing reverse trimer, the second witness-separated refund trimer, and graph-intrinsic signs on the descendant pair. The signed endpoint/witness on the opposite support may shift if the marker also contacts that support.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not preserve every original witness or endpoint label forever; does not claim the resulting singleton states are selected in an unrelated cover; does not close the both-singleton layer; does not require or imply Same-Polarity Two-Extension Collision.

## Proof
Historical R13 proof. For head-signed P=(p_0,p_1) with alpha p_0p_1 tight, choose an at-most-two-path cover of the outside reservoir having a nonempty component with head nu != alpha. Such a choice always exists unless H is already two-covered: if a one-path cover begins at alpha, split off alpha; if the reservoir is exactly {alpha}, then (alpha,P) together with the opposite support already two-covers H. In the unique R12 dimer-swallowing case p_0p_1nu is bad, so nu p_1p_0 is tight. Since nu,p_0,alpha are distinct, boundary antisymmetry gives exactly one of nu p_0 alpha and alpha p_0 nu tight. This order-three marker meets P exactly at p_0. Signed-Interval Rebirth therefore leaves P'=(p_1) with a graph-intrinsic head sign. Other R12 bad seams either already reduce the width-two support to one vertex, shrink the opposite support, or close; the only nonterminal repetitions strictly lower total active pair mass. The tail dual is identical. Researcher 14 independently audited Witness-Separated Outside Head, Width-Two Swallow Refund, Width-Two Dimension Lowering, and the composition PASS.

# R428 — Fixed-Singleton Opposite-Support Descent to the Both-Singleton Floor

## Statement
Let H be a hypothetical smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample and let (alpha;(p)),(T;beta) be a balanced opposite-sign pair with one singleton support p and a nontrivial opposite support T. There is a finite chosen certificate-retaining continuation that preserves the singleton support p and yields either a spanning two-cover or an ancestry-bearing balanced pair with both supports singleton. At each nonclosing stage, take an at-most-two-path cover of the outside reservoir. If it contains a nontrivial path, the One-Rail Unsigned-End Refund R175 strictly shortens T while avoiding p; if the reservoir consists of two singleton components, combine them as a tight dimer and apply the same refund; if the reservoir is a single vertex, the two seam tests of the literal candidate (p,u,T) give either a spanning two-cover or a reverse-trimer certificate disjoint from p that strictly shortens T. Hence every nonclosing repeat preserves p and strictly decreases |T|, so the process terminates at the both-singleton floor. The head/tail dual is exact.

## Hypotheses
H is a smallest Strong counterexample; a balanced opposite-sign pair is present with one support the singleton (p) and the other support T nontrivial. The chosen descent retains the singleton side and uses exact outside-reservoir covers.

## Scope
Strong Level-(1), arbitrary order. This is the historical singleton/nontrivial direct-descent package used by Complete Floor Pair Steering.

## Applicability
Use after any operation has installed a desired singleton coordinate in an ancestry-bearing balanced pair. It pays the opposite support to singleton width while keeping that coordinate fixed, unless a spanning two-cover occurs.

## Persistence
The singleton support p is unchanged throughout the chosen nonclosing continuation. Retain nested descendants of T, the graph-intrinsic sign witnesses supplied by Signed-Interval Rebirth, and the ordered trimer/outside-boundary refund ledger. The witness on T may shift when certified rebirth requires it.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not preserve an unrelated source cover or all original witnesses; does not make pair mass globally monotone across arbitrary resets; does not close the final both-singleton floor; does not claim every historical refund marker remains selected.

## Proof
Let O be the outside reservoir. Minimality gives an at-most-two-path cover. Any nontrivial outside component triggers R175. Two singleton components are combined into a dimer. The sole remaining one-vertex reservoir is handled by the exact two seam tests of (p,u,T); every bad case is either an immediate two-cover or a physical marker disjoint from p that clips two unsigned T vertices. Iterate.

# R432 — Complete Floor Pair Steering

## Statement
Let H be a hypothetical smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample and let S={p,t} be the two singleton supports of any ancestry-bearing mass-two balanced opposite-sign floor. Fix any prescribed target pair T={a,c} of distinct vertices. Then there is a finite chosen ancestry-retaining continuation, using at most two singleton-replacement macros, which yields either a spanning two-cover or an ancestry-bearing mass-two floor whose singleton supports are exactly {a,c}. Equivalently, with delta_T(S)=2-|S intersect T|, every nonclosing replacement macro strictly lowers delta_T by one until delta_T=0. If one current singleton already belongs to T, it may be preserved while the other coordinate is replaced by the missing target vertex; if S is disjoint from T, first install one target vertex and then preserve it while installing the other.

## Hypotheses
H is a smallest Strong counterexample; an ancestry-bearing both-singleton balanced-pair floor S={p,t} is active; T={a,c} is any prescribed pair of distinct physical vertices. The historical singleton signs and pair ancestry are available to the replacement macro.

## Scope
Strong Level-(1), arbitrary order and arbitrary prescribed target pair. The target pair may be fixed independently of the incoming floor. No compatibility, capture-history, order-ten, or representative-overlap hypothesis is required.

## Applicability
Use whenever an ancestry-bearing mass-two floor exists and a proof needs to place its two singleton supports on an independently prescribed physical pair. This is the target-coordinate engine behind the historical fixed-turn reentry theorem R423.

## Persistence
The steering continuation retains the full physical ancestry ledger of the incoming paid floor: original pair birth and earlier refund/contact certificates, the actualizing dimer/orientation used for each replacement, its pair-deletion rails and marker-actualization certificate, the fixed singleton during each one-coordinate descent, successive floor coordinates, and final target-aligned pair-deletion frame. Witness names may change under certified rebirth. The source representative and old selected rails need not remain current.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not imply the target floor is in the same representative as the incoming floor; does not preserve arbitrary witness names, old rails, crossings, or seams as current; does not close the target floor; does not make target distance a monotone under arbitrary unrelated proof operations; does not permit a bare formal relabeling without the physical replacement certificates.

## Proof
Let the active ancestry-bearing floor be S={p,t} and the prescribed target pair be T={a,c}. If S=T, stop. If |S intersect T|=1, relabel the common coordinate as p and the missing target as x. Apply R433 to obtain a two-cover or the exact floor (p),(x)=T. If S and T are disjoint, first apply R433 while retaining p and prescribing x=a, obtaining a two-cover or floor (p),(a). Now retain a and use the exact head/tail dual of R433 to replace p by c, obtaining a two-cover or floor (a),(c). Thus at most two replacement macros suffice. At every nonclosing macro the intersection with the target pair grows by exactly one, so delta_T(S)=2-|S intersect T| decreases exactly by one. The retained ledger is the concatenation of the incoming floor ancestry and the one or two R433 replacement certificates. No claim is made that an additional protected/current role on a fixed singleton survives unless a separate protection theorem supplies it.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R432.md -->

# R434 — Fixed-Turn Selected-Incidence Endpoint Budget Package

## Statement
Let H be a hypothetical smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample, let J=(a,b,c) be a fixed proper tight turn, and work at an aligned exact pair-deletion frame H-{a,c}=U sqcup V. Let A_J subseteq {a,c} record the outer endpoints for which an earlier quiet selected-incidence episode has been completed all the way back to an aligned floor with that endpoint retained as a signed singleton coordinate. Then: (i) every selected predecessor r->b yields a graph-intrinsic signed dimer whose signed endpoint is a, and every selected successor b->s yields one whose signed endpoint is c; (ii) each such dimer gives either a spanning two-cover during actualization or a balanced pair birth retaining that endpoint-anchored dimer; (iii) if the anchored endpoint e already lies in A_J, the new nontrivial dimer containing the retained historical singleton anchor e is an explicit anchor-contact/strict-growth event and the episode is nonquiet; (iv) if e is fresh, immediately designate the return-to-aligned-floor continuation as an R42 protected continuation. Along that continuation either a first event touching e is exposed, or pair descent reaches a both-singleton floor with e itself as one singleton; R433 then restores the other outer endpoint while preserving e, completing a new aligned floor and enlarging A_J by e. Consequently every completed quiet aligned episode strictly enlarges A_J, so at most two such episodes are quiet for one fixed turn.

## Hypotheses
H is a smallest Strong counterexample; J=(a,b,c) is retained; the current floor is aligned on {a,c}; H-{a,c}=U sqcup V is an exact two-cover; selected predecessor/successor incidence at b is taken from that frame. For a fresh endpoint capture, the descendant continuation is designated immediately at the actual capture event as protected in the sense of R42 and follows the stated R427/R428/R433 return protocol.

## Scope
Strong Level-(1), arbitrary order. This packages the historical Left/Right Selected-Incidence Endpoint-Anchor Extraction, Selected-Incidence Endpoint Pair Birth, and the weaker endpoint-budget content of Fixed-Turn Common-Frame Endpoint Budget. It does not include the stronger internal-middle immediate two-pair collision conclusion.

## Applicability
Use at a target-aligned fixed-turn floor to obtain a genuine two-element quiet-episode budget without treating bare historical capture or exact certificate replay as progress.

## Persistence
Retain J, the aligned frame used for the episode, the selected incidence, exact endpoint-anchored signed dimer and witness, its pair-deletion/actualization certificate, and A_J. In a fresh quiet episode retain the R42 protected continuation until the captured endpoint e has become a signed singleton; R428/R433 then preserve that singleton through return to the aligned floor. A_J records only endpoints that have completed this protected return, not arbitrary historical captures. Source rails and unrelated selected states need not survive.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not claim every historical capture is protected. Does not count exact certificate-stationary replay as fresh progress. Does not assert all episode representatives coexist. A first contact is an explicit output, not automatic conjecture closure. The stronger internal-middle simultaneous two-pair collision theorem is not included.

## Proof
Let the aligned floor be {a,c}. Pair-Deletion Rigidity R429 gives two nontrivial rails, so the rail containing b supplies a selected predecessor or successor. Left predecessor r->b: R3 says exactly one of r a b and b a r is tight, producing respectively the tail-signed dimer (r,a) with witness b or (b,a) with witness r; both have signed endpoint a. The successor case is the exact dual at c. Delete the resulting dimer D. R429 gives two nontrivial rails; exactly one contains its sign witness, and the other is a nontrivial disjoint marker. Test its terminal marker seam directly with R3, obtaining either the whole rail or the standard short opposite-polarity support. Thus either a spanning two-cover has already occurred in the accepted actualization branch or a balanced pair birth retaining D is obtained. Now let e be the signed endpoint of D. If e is already in A_J, an earlier quiet episode ended at an aligned floor with e retained as a signed singleton support. The new dimer D is a nontrivial proper tight path containing that singleton anchor, so R436 gives an explicit at-anchor contact/strict-growth output; this episode is nonquiet. Suppose e is fresh. At this actual capture/birth event immediately designate the following descendant route as the R42 protected continuation, with target role: e is a literal signed singleton at the next aligned floor. First run the finite R427 width-two pair descent. If any step genuinely touches e, R42 exposes the first contact and the episode is nonquiet. Otherwise e remains the anchor of the retained descendant of D. If R427 makes that descendant singleton, it must therefore be exactly (e). If instead R427 first makes the opposite support singleton, apply R428 with that singleton fixed and the e-containing support as the nontrivial side. Again any touch of e is an R42 first-contact exit; in the quiet arm the e-containing support is shortened without losing e and eventually becomes the singleton (e). If the opposite support is still nontrivial, R428 with (e) fixed pays it to singleton width or closes. We now have a both-singleton floor containing (e), with e still the completed protected endpoint of this episode. Let f be the other member of {a,c}. Apply R433 to replace the other singleton by f while preserving (e); this returns to an aligned {a,c} floor. Record e in A_J. Therefore every completed quiet aligned episode strictly enlarges A_J. Since A_J is a subset of {a,c}, at most two completed aligned episodes are quiet. No claim is made that bare historical capture, without this protected return protocol, spends the budget.

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R435.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R435.md -->

# R435 — Reverse Ear Lemma

## Statement
Let P=(v_0,...,v_k) and K be vertex-simple tight paths. Let E be a K-subpath from v_i to v_j such that v_i,v_j are consecutive K-contacts with P, so every internal vertex of E lies outside P, and assume i>j. If E is the single state v_i v_j with i=j+1, K already contains the reversal of the old P-state v_j v_i. Otherwise one obtains either a tight reverse trimer at one of the two P/E seams or a vertex-simple tight cycle formed by E together with the old P-segment from v_j through v_{i-1}. Consequently, outside a reversal/reverse-trimer or proper-cycle output, the P-vertices encountered along any tight path K occur in increasing P-order.

## Hypotheses
P and K are vertex-simple tight paths in a finite Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament. The displayed contacts v_i,v_j are consecutive along K and occur in reverse P-order i>j.

## Scope
Pure Strong Level-(1) path-interaction lemma. No smallest-counterexample, completion, CW, boundedness, selected-state persistence, or contradiction-from-cycle hypothesis.

## Applicability
Use to compare an ancestral path with a later path/marker. It converts a reverse-order encounter into an explicit reverse local cell or a constructive proper cycle, and otherwise gives order alignment.

## Persistence
The output reverse trimer/reversal cell and proper cycle are graph-intrinsic once exhibited. The theorem does not assert that either input path remains selected in later covers.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
A proper tight cycle is a constructive output, not a contradiction. If K has a bounded order, the reverse local cell is correspondingly bounded; the cycle itself need not be bounded. No representative synchronization is asserted.

## Proof
Let E be the K-subpath from v_i to v_j with no internal P-vertex and i>j. If E is exactly the state v_i v_j and i=j+1, this is already the reversal of the old P-state v_j v_i. Otherwise let x be the successor of v_i on E and y the predecessor of v_j on E; in the one-state nonadjacent case x=v_j and y=v_i. Since i>j, v_{i-1} and v_{j+1} exist. Test v_{i-1} v_i x and y v_j v_{j+1}. If the first is bad, R3 gives x v_i v_{i-1} tight. If the second is bad, R3 gives v_{j+1} v_j y tight. If both are tight, traverse E from v_i to v_j, then the old P-segment v_j,v_{j+1},...,v_{i-1}, and use the first tested seam to close back to v_i. Every turn is either on E, on P, or one of the tested seams, and vertex simplicity follows from the no-internal-P-contact condition. Thus a tight cycle results. Hence outside these outputs reverse-order consecutive contacts cannot occur, so all P-contacts along K follow increasing P-order.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R435.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R436.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R436.md -->

# R436 — General Tight-Path Contact and Historical Anchor Protection

## Statement
Let (w;P) be a graph-intrinsic head-signed tight path, P=(v_0,...,v_k), and let Q be any proper tight path meeting P. If Q avoids the signed anchor v_0, let i=min{j : v_j lies in V(Q)}; then i>=1 and the head-containing prefix (v_0,...,v_{i-1}) is a nonempty strictly shorter head-signed support disjoint from Q. If Q contains v_0, then, except for the vacuous exact replay of the same singleton support with no new certificate data, one obtains at least one of: strict full-P tight-path growth, strict Q growth, a vertex-simple tight cycle, or a three-vertex reverse contact/reversal cell. The tail-signed dual is exact. Consequently, outside those explicit outputs, a genuinely later signed support or marker cannot contain the anchor of an older historical signed support; quiet contacts away from the anchor may only shorten the old support on its signed side and therefore retain that anchor.

## Hypotheses
A graph-intrinsic head- or tail-signed tight support is given, together with a proper tight path Q meeting it. For the historical-anchor corollary, Q is a genuinely later support/marker rather than mere re-display of the identical singleton certificate.

## Scope
Strong Level-(1), graph-intrinsic path-contact theorem. No smallest-counterexample, completion, bounded-marker, CW, current-selection, or representative-persistence assumption is needed. The exact-replay fence is explicit.

## Applicability
Use to normalize later contact with historical signed supports and, in particular, to protect a historical signed endpoint against silent later support/marker reuse. It is the local parent behind Captured-Anchor First-Contact Control.

## Persistence
When contact is away from the signed anchor, the retained descendant is literally the signed-side prefix/suffix of the old support and keeps the old anchor. At-anchor contact is exposed as a graph-intrinsic growth/cycle/reversal event. Witnesses and selected representatives need not persist beyond what the displayed paths certify.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not declare a proper cycle contradictory. Does not turn bare historical capture into current protection. Does not count exact stationary replay of the same singleton support/certificate as fresh progress. Does not assert later paths are current in a common cover.

## Proof
Head case. Let (w,v_0,...,v_k) be tight. If Q avoids v_0, let i=min{j : v_j lies in V(Q)}; then i>=1. Then P^-=(v_0,...,v_{i-1}) is nonempty, disjoint from Q, and (w,P^-) is a prefix of the old signed extension, so P^- is a strictly shorter head-signed support with the same anchor. Now suppose Q contains v_0. If k=0, then a nontrivial Q strictly grows the singleton P; if Q=(v_0) and no new certificate is present this is only stationary replay, while the old dimer (w,v_0) is available but is not credited as a new event. Assume k>=1. Apply R435 to P and Q. Outside a reverse cell or proper cycle, P-vertices occur in increasing P-order along Q, so v_0 is the first P-vertex of Q. If Q has a predecessor a before v_0, test a v_0 v_1. Tightness concatenates the Q-prefix through v_0 with all of P, strictly extending P; badness gives v_1 v_0 a tight by R3. If v_0 is the head of Q and Q is the singleton, (w,v_0) strictly extends Q unless this is the stationary singleton replay just fenced. Otherwise Q=(v_0,q_1,...). If w is outside Q, test w v_0 q_1: tightness makes (w,Q) a strict extension of Q, badness gives q_1 v_0 w tight by R3. If w lies on Q after v_0, compare the two tight paths (w,P) and Q: they contain w and v_0 in opposite orders, so R435 gives a reverse cell or a proper cycle. This exhausts the head case. Reverse all orders for the tail case. The historical-anchor statement follows: a genuinely later support/marker containing the old signed endpoint is the at-anchor case above, while contact away from the endpoint can only replace the old support by the signed-side descendant and therefore does not erase its anchor.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R436.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R44.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R44.md -->

# R44 — Global-longest two-path endpoint gap parent

## Statement

Let a globally longest tight path be disjoint from another tight path. At either end, the outer attachment of the shorter path to the longer path is bad. If the inner attachment is tight, transferring that endpoint gives the exact size bound forced by global longestness; if it is bad, boundary antisymmetry gives a reverse four-vertex path.

## Hypotheses


## Scope
Applying the two end tests together gives:

- equal orders: both reverse four-paths occur;
- order gap one: at least one reverse four-path occurs;
- order gap two: either a reverse four-path occurs or the endpoint transfers produce a second globally longest path.

When the two paths are the exact complement of a marker, the transfers are literal reversible exact-cover exchanges, preserve the marker, and have zero cycle debt. In the gap-two double-tight face, the two endpoint moves commute, forming a four-cover square.

This is a global-longest parent, not the older lexicographically maximal cover theorem. It subsumes the older gap-zero, gap-one, and gap-two turn geometry for the two largest components, but the lexicographic theorem remains available when selected-cover ownership or boundary ancestry is needed.


## Applicability


## Persistence


## Exclusions / nonclaims


## Proof
Let A=(a_0,...,a_{m-1}) be a globally longest tight path and B=(b_0,...,b_{n-1}) a disjoint tight path, with m>=n and n>=2 in the nontrivial endpoint-test case. At the left end of A, the outer attachment (b_{n-1},a_0,a_1) is bad: if it were tight, (b_{n-1},a_0,...,a_{m-1}) would be a tight path of order m+1, contradicting global longestness. Hence R3 gives the reverse turn (a_1,a_0,b_{n-1}) tight. Test the inner attachment I_L=(b_{n-2},b_{n-1},a_0). If I_L is tight, then B_L=(b_0,...,b_{n-1},a_0) is a tight path of order n+1, obtained by transferring the endpoint a_0 from A to B; global longestness gives n+1<=m. If I_L is bad, R3 gives (a_0,b_{n-1},b_{n-2}) tight, and together with (a_1,a_0,b_{n-1}) this makes the literal reverse four-path (a_1,a_0,b_{n-1},b_{n-2}).

The right end is dual. The outer attachment (a_{m-2},a_{m-1},b_0) is bad, so R3 gives (b_0,a_{m-1},a_{m-2}) tight. Test I_R=(a_{m-1},b_0,b_1). If I_R is tight, then B_R=(a_{m-1},b_0,...,b_{n-1}) is a tight path of order n+1 and global longestness again gives n+1<=m. If I_R is bad, R3 gives (b_1,b_0,a_{m-1}) tight, producing the reverse four-path (b_1,b_0,a_{m-1},a_{m-2}).

Now compare the orders. If m=n, either inner attachment would create a path of order m+1, so both are bad and both reverse P4s occur. If m=n+1 and both inner attachments were tight, then the combined path (a_{m-1},b_0,...,b_{n-1},a_0) would have order n+2=m+1, contradicting global longestness; hence at least one inner attachment is bad and at least one reverse P4 occurs. If m=n+2, then either one inner attachment is bad and gives a reverse P4, or both are tight; in the latter case the combined path (a_{m-1},b_0,...,b_{n-1},a_0) has order n+2=m and is therefore a second globally longest path.

When A and B are the two rails of the exact complement of a fixed marker, a tight I_L gives the literal cover exchange A|B -> (a_1,...,a_{m-1}) | (b_0,...,b_{n-1},a_0), and a tight I_R gives A|B -> (a_0,...,a_{m-2}) | (a_{m-1},b_0,...,b_{n-1}). These are state-for-state endpoint transfers inside the same vertex set and preserve the external marker. If both apply, performing both yields (a_1,...,a_{m-2}) | (a_{m-1},b_0,...,b_{n-1},a_0) regardless of order, so the two moves commute and form the four-cover square. All four displayed objects are literal path covers; no cycle is created or consumed, hence the cycle-debt contribution is zero. This proves the complete R44 parent.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R44.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R444.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R444.md -->

# R444 — Bare Both-Singleton Degeneracy

## Statement
Let p and t be distinct vertices of any Level-(1) boundary tournament. Under the accepted graph-intrinsic signed-support convention, the singleton supports (p) and (t) admit a formal balanced opposite-sign labelling: (t;(p)) is a head sign on (p) with witness t, and ((t);p) is a tail sign on (t) with witness p. This uses only that every ordered two-vertex path is automatically tight because it has no internal turn. Consequently the bare both-singleton balanced-pair label carries no turn information by itself. Any productive use of a mass-two floor must retain additional physical ancestry/certificates; distinct historical certificate labels on the same singleton cannot be declared a collision solely from singleton sign labels.

## Hypotheses
p and t are distinct vertices. The standard signed-support convention allows the witness of one singleton support to lie on the opposite support, while remaining outside its own support.

## Scope
Level-(1)-universal negative/degeneracy theorem. No smallest-counterexample, cover, payment, or CW hypothesis. Historically proved by R17 and independently audited in the subsequent R18/R20 audit chain.

## Applicability
Use as a guardrail whenever a signed-support or cross-generation argument reaches width one. It prevents treating an anonymous both-singleton pair, or mere reminting of sign certificates on a singleton, as new geometric progress without retained ancestry.

## Persistence
The statement is graph-intrinsic and representation-independent. If a particular floor has stronger birth/payment/capture ancestry, that ancestry remains separately available and may support stronger consumers.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not say an ancestry-bearing mass-two floor is useless. Does not say every later event involving the same singleton is quiet. Does not rule out same-polarity singleton collision from distinct physical witnesses when an actual three-vertex turn is tested. It only says singleton sign labels alone impose no internal-turn geometry and do not justify a universal opposite-polarity same-singleton collision theorem.

## Proof
Take distinct p,t. The ordered path (t,p) has two vertices and therefore has no internal turn to check, so it is tight. Hence (t;(p)) is a valid head-signed singleton with witness t. The same two-vertex path is also exactly the certificate required for ((t);p), so (t) is tail-signed by witness p. The supports are disjoint and the witnesses lie outside their own supports, so these form a formal balanced opposite-sign pair. Since the proof used no triple of vertices, the bare pair certifies no turn. Thus any later theorem claiming productivity from a both-singleton label must consume additional ancestry rather than the labels alone.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R444.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R452.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R452.md -->

# R452 — Directed-state rigidity modulo same-support collision

## Statement
Let H be a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament and let e=(u,v) be a directed physical state. Among vertex-simple tight paths containing e in this orientation, either the same physical dimer (u,v) carries a same-polarity two-witness interaction of R38, or the immediate successor of e is unique whenever it exists and the immediate predecessor of e is unique whenever it exists. Consequently, if two vertex-simple tight paths P,Q contain the same directed state (u,v) in the same orientation and have the same ordered head and tail endpoints, then either an R38 same-support interaction occurs on (u,v) or P=Q as literal ordered paths. More generally, outside R38 interaction, a directed state together with any one reachable terminal endpoint determines the corresponding one-sided continuation uniquely.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1); P,Q and all compared paths are vertex-simple tight paths; the shared state (u,v) is used in the same orientation. R38 is available.

## Scope
Order-free graph-intrinsic stationary-state rigidity. This is a new canonical rederivation of the useful mathematical content associated with the legacy stationary-state/end-window gap; it does not claim to reconstruct every stronger historical first-divergence variant recorded in M12.

## Applicability
Use when several current or historical path representatives share one directed state. It converts ambiguity of predecessor/successor into an explicit same-support sign interaction, and outside that output lets endpoints plus one state freeze a rail.

## Persistence
The shared directed state and any R38 sign certificates are graph-intrinsic. Equality P=Q is literal for the two compared ordered paths under the no-interaction alternative; no statement is made about unrelated representatives not containing the state.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not assert two paths sharing only an unordered edge coincide. Does not compare opposite orientations of the state. Does not exclude productive R38 collision. Does not reconstruct the unavailable historical stationary end-window theorem beyond the stated uniqueness consequence.

## Proof
Suppose two tight paths contain the directed state (u,v) and have distinct immediate successors a and b. Then (u,v,a) and (u,v,b) are both tight, so the same physical dimer (u,v) is tail-signed by the distinct witnesses a,b with the same polarity. R38 gives the same-support two-witness interaction. Therefore outside R38 interaction the successor is unique. Dually, if distinct immediate predecessors a,b occur then (a,u,v) and (b,u,v) are tight, so (u,v) is head-signed by two distinct witnesses and R38 applies; hence the predecessor is unique outside interaction. Now let P,Q contain (u,v) in the same orientation and have the same ordered head and tail. If no R38 interaction occurs, repeatedly apply successor uniqueness from (u,v): the next vertex agrees, then the next directed state agrees, so induction forces the entire suffix through the common tail to agree. Vertex-simplicity prevents one path from passing the common tail and later returning to it. Applying predecessor uniqueness backward forces the prefixes through the common head to agree. Hence P=Q literally. The one-sided endpoint version is the same induction in one direction.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R452.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R460.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/ACTIVE/R460.md -->

# R460 — Native three-cover splice fan is mate-complement-free

## Statement
Let H=A sqcup B sqcup C be a literal spanning three-cover by nontrivial vertex-simple tight paths, and form the six native R453 ordered-pair splice clauses. The twelve turn literals occurring in those clauses are pairwise distinct and belong to twelve distinct boundary-antisymmetry pairs. Hence the six clauses are propositionally separable: no literal or its antisymmetric complement occurs in two different native clauses, no nontrivial resolution step is available between native clauses, and after imposing only boundary antisymmetry R3 plus the six R453 disjunctions there are 2^6 consistent local exact-one valuations obtained by choosing independently one tight literal in each clause. In particular, for every native splice literal L there is such a valuation satisfying all six clauses with L bad, so the native fan alone forces neither a specific native turn nor a contradiction. In the all-internal R359 specialization H=J sqcup U sqcup V, the two splice disjunctions used by R455 are exactly the native U-to-V and V-to-U members of this same separable R453 fan. R455 becomes productive only because R359 supplies four additional non-native shield turns sharing the relevant oriented terminal dimers, allowing whichever seam mate fires to be interpreted by R38 as a same-support collision. Thus R455 does not repair the native R173 mate-linkage obstruction: any Physical Mate-Cycle forcing still requires an additional physically certified proposal introducing an exact complementary literal, or some genuinely non-propositional structural input.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1); H=A sqcup B sqcup C is a literal spanning three-cover by nontrivial vertex-simple tight paths; accepted R3 and R173. For the R455 specialization, H is a hypothetical smallest counterexample in the all-internal R359 regime and pending R453/R455 are used provisionally with exact revision IDs.

## Scope
Order-free adversarial fence strengthening the native-splice obstruction. The 2^6 valuations are local truth assignments on the twelve antisymmetry pairs appearing in the fan, not asserted realizable as complete boundary tournaments with pc(H)>2.

## Applicability
Use before any propositional, SAT-like, or R173-resolution attempt on a fixed native three-cover fan. Clause abundance alone has zero cross-clause linkage. For R455, credit the progress specifically to the imported R359 shield geometry and the R38 collision compiler, not to new mate-cycle structure among the native splice clauses.

## Persistence
The separability statement depends only on the fixed literal ordered source paths and their endpoint identities. The R455 interpretation retains the exact source currentization, the two residual-rail splice proposals, and the four R359 shield turns as physical certificate data.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not construct a global Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament realizing any of the 2^6 local valuations. Does not claim the six clauses are independent after arbitrary additional graph constraints are imported. Does not invalidate R455 or say its R38 collisions are vacuous. Does not rule out R173 after component surgery, an alternate path representative, endpoint-return machinery, or another physically certified proposal supplies a complementary literal.

## Proof
Fix the literal spanning three-cover H=A sqcup B sqcup C by nontrivial vertex-simple tight paths and the six native ordered-pair splice clauses named in the statement. We first prove the separability assertion directly from the literal endpoint data of those six clauses; no theorem about how they were originally obtained is needed.\n\nTake two distinct source components X=(x_0,...,x_m) and Y=(y_0,...,y_n), with m,n>=1. The X-to-Y native concatenation has seam holes h_1=(x_{m-1},x_m,y_0) and h_2=(x_m,y_0,y_1), so its two mate literals are L^1_{XY}=bar(h_1)=(y_0,x_m,x_{m-1}) and L^2_{XY}=bar(h_2)=(y_1,y_0,x_m). Record only the source-component membership of the three coordinates. These words are YXX and YYX. Because A,B,C are pairwise vertex-disjoint, equality of ordered turn literals forces equality of their component-membership words. As X,Y range over the six ordered pairs of distinct source components, the word YXX uniquely identifies the ordered pair together with the first literal, and YYX uniquely identifies the same ordered pair together with the second literal. Hence the twelve native clause literals are pairwise distinct.\n\nNow compare their R3 reversals. The reversal of L^1_{XY} is (x_{m-1},x_m,y_0), with component word XXY. The only native literal having word XXY is the second literal in the reverse Y-to-X clause, namely (x_1,x_0,y_n). Exact equality would force x_m=x_0, impossible because X is nontrivial and vertex-simple. Likewise bar(L^2_{XY})=(x_m,y_0,y_1) has word XYY. The only native literal with that word is the first literal in the reverse Y-to-X clause, (x_0,y_n,y_{n-1}); equality again forces x_m=x_0. Therefore no native literal is the complete reversal of any other native literal. The twelve literals lie in twelve distinct boundary-antisymmetry pairs.\n\nIntroduce the tight/bad truth value of each native literal as one Boolean variable, with R3 fixing its unlisted reverse to the opposite value. Each of the six already-formed native clauses is a disjunction of two variables that occur in no other native clause, and no complement of either variable occurs in another clause. Thus there is no nontrivial resolution pivot between two distinct native clauses. More concretely, choose exactly one tight literal in each clause and declare its partner bad. Since the twelve R3 pairs are distinct, the six choices are mutually compatible and give 2^6 local exact-one valuations. Given any particular native literal L, choose its clause partner tight and L bad, then choose one tight literal arbitrarily in each other clause. Hence the native fan alone forces neither L nor a propositional contradiction. This is only a local valuation of the clause/antisymmetry data, exactly as fenced in the statement; no global tournament realization is asserted.\n\nNow reconstruct the all-internal specialization without R359, R453, or R455. Assume the specialization setup of the statement, so H is a hypothetical smallest counterexample with proper tight trimer J=(a,x,c) and fixed all-internal source currentization H=J sqcup U sqcup V. Apply current accepted R920 to this same named source state. Its direct proof gives |U|,|V|>=3 and the four tight reverse shields. Writing U=(u_1,...,u_r), V=(v_1,...,v_s), the two shields relevant to U-to-V are (x,u_r,u_{r-1}) and (v_2,v_1,x), and the dual pair is available for V-to-U.\n\nBecause pc(H)=3, the literal proposal obtained by concatenating U followed by V while retaining J as the other path cannot be a spanning two-cover. It inherits every old turn of U and V and has exactly two new seam turns h_1=(u_{r-1},u_r,v_1) and h_2=(u_r,v_1,v_2). Therefore at least one hole is bad, and R3 gives exactly the native U-to-V disjunction A OR B, with A=(v_1,u_r,u_{r-1}) and B=(v_2,v_1,u_r). The V-to-U proposal gives the symmetric native clause. Thus the two directional disjunctions historically used by R455 are indeed members of the same six-clause native fan, now reconstructed directly rather than imported through R453.\n\nThe reason these two clauses become productive is the non-native shield geometry supplied by R920. If A fires, then A=(v_1,u_r,u_{r-1}) and the shield (x,u_r,u_{r-1}) are two head certificates on the identical tested oriented dimer (u_r,u_{r-1}) with distinct witnesses v_1,x, so current reconstructible R523 gives the same-support collision packet. If B fires, then B=(v_2,v_1,u_r) and the shield (v_2,v_1,x) are two tail certificates on the identical tested oriented dimer (v_2,v_1) with distinct witnesses u_r,x, so R523 gives the collision. The V-to-U direction is symmetric. Hence the extra information comes from imported non-native shields, not from any complement linkage among native clauses.\n\nConsequently the native fan itself remains mate-complement-free and propositionally separable. Any forcing mechanism that needs complementary mate linkage must add a genuinely new physically certified proposal or other non-propositional structural input. This proves every assertion of R460 using only R3, R523, and R920. No R173, R359, R453, R455, R168, R5, R24, or P22 dependency is used.

# R463 — Physical Mate-Cycle Forcing

## Statement
Let H satisfy pc(H)>k. Call {A,B} a physically certified mate clause when a displayed literal spanning k-cover proposal has complete hole set exactly {bar(A),bar(B)}, where bar denotes exact boundary-antisymmetric reversal. For any finite family F of such clauses, form the directed physical implication graph G_F on turn literals by inserting, for every certified clause {A,B}, the two labeled arcs bar(A)->B and bar(B)->A, each retaining the underlying proposal and its exact two-hole certificate.

(1) Tightness propagates along every directed path of G_F. Hence if G_F contains a directed path bar(X)->...->X, then X is tight.

(2) Call a literal L collision-decorated when either L=(w,p,q) and a retained tight turn (w',p,q) with w' distinct from w is available, or L=(p,q,w) and a retained tight turn (p,q,w') with w' distinct from w is available. Thus, if L becomes tight, R38 gives a same-polarity two-witness collision on the oriented support (p,q). If one certified clause {A,B} has a directed path from A to a collision-decorated literal L_A and a directed path from B to a collision-decorated literal L_B (paths of length zero allowed), then H carries a named R38 same-support collision, with the realized implication path and every proposal/hole certificate on that path retained.

The R173 Physical Mate-Cycle is the special case in which the clauses give the path bar(X_0)->X_1->...->X_r->X_0. In the all-internal R359 currentization H=J sqcup U sqcup V, each directional residual-rail R453 splice clause is already doubly collision-decorated by the two relevant R359 shield turns, so part (2) recovers the partner-only residual-terminal collision conclusion of R455 without requiring a mate cycle.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1) boundary antisymmetry R3; pc(H)>k; every implication edge comes from a displayed literal spanning k-cover proposal whose complete hole set is exactly the two reversed endpoint literals. For part (2), the sink decorations are retained tight turns on the identical oriented physical dimer and with distinct witnesses, in the tested order required by R38. The R359/R453 specialization assumes the all-internal proper-trimer currentization and nontrivial residual rails in the scope of those revisions.

## Scope
Order-free, CW-free, certificate-preserving parent compiler for physical two-hole clause systems. It strengthens the cycle-only interface of R173 to arbitrary directed reachability and adds collision-decorated sinks. The abstract graph never replaces the underlying path-cover certificates: every arc is labeled by its literal proposal and exact hole pair.

## Applicability
Use when physical mate clauses are abundant but direct complement cycles are absent. Search for one or more additional certified proposals that create directed reachability between native clause literals, or for structural shield turns that decorate reachable literals. This reframes the R453/R460 bottleneck from 'build a full mate cycle' to 'connect both branches of one live physical clause to productive sinks.'

## Persistence
Forced turn conclusions and R38 collisions are graph-intrinsic once obtained. Every implication step retains the exact proposal and two-hole certificate that justified it; collision sinks retain the oriented physical support and both witness identities. Alternative proposal representatives need not remain simultaneously current.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
An abstract Boolean clause, SAT implication, Hall edge, or unlabeled resolution step is insufficient: every graph arc must retain a literal physical k-cover proposal with its complete two-hole set. The theorem does not create new proposals, does not assert the native R453 fan has nontrivial reachability beyond its six clauses, and does not claim an R38 collision alone closes H. Collision decoration requires identical oriented support, same polarity/tested order, and distinct witnesses; mere support overlap is insufficient.

## Proof
Fix a finite family F of physically certified mate clauses in the sense of R463. For one clause {A,B}, retain its displayed spanning k-cover proposal. By definition the complete unresolved hole set of that proposal is exactly {bar(A),bar(B)}. Because pc(H)>k, those two hole turns cannot both be tight. Hence at least one of bar(A),bar(B) is bad. By boundary antisymmetry R3, at least one of A,B is tight. Thus the physically certified disjunction A OR B holds, with the literal proposal and its complete two-hole certificate retained.\n\nIf bar(A) is tight, then R3 says A is bad. Since A OR B holds, B is tight. Therefore the labelled arc bar(A)->B is a sound tightness implication. Symmetrically bar(B)->A is sound. Repeating this one-clause argument along a directed path in G_F proves tightness propagation while retaining every proposal/hole certificate labelling the path.\n\nFor part (1), suppose G_F contains a directed path bar(X)->...->X. If X were bad, R3 would make bar(X) tight, and path propagation would then make X tight, contradiction. Therefore X is tight. The R173 mate-cycle pattern is exactly the special case whose certified clauses provide the successive labelled arcs bar(X_0)->X_1, X_1->X_2, ..., X_r->X_0, so the same argument recovers that forcing directly; R173 itself is not used as a dependency.\n\nFor part (2), let L be collision-decorated. In the head case L=(w,p,q) and a retained turn S=(w',p,q) is tight with w' distinct from w. Once L is tight, L and S are two head certificates on the identical tested oriented dimer (p,q), with distinct witnesses. Current reconstructible R523 therefore gives exactly the named same-support two-head collision packet. In the tail case L=(p,q,w), S=(p,q,w') the TT clause of R523 gives the corresponding two-tail collision. Now let {A,B} be a certified source clause with directed paths A->...->L_A and B->...->L_B to collision-decorated sinks. The already-proved disjunction A OR B makes at least one source endpoint tight. Propagation along its designated labelled path makes the corresponding sink tight, and R523 then gives the named collision. Every implication proposal, hole pair, tested support, and witness identity on the realized route is retained.\n\nIt remains only to reconstruct the all-internal specialization without the historical R359/R453 route. Assume the specialization hypotheses of R463, so H is the hypothetical smallest counterexample in the all-internal proper-trimer source geometry with J=(a,x,c) and a fixed literal currentization H=J sqcup U sqcup V. Write U=(u_1,...,u_r), V=(v_1,...,v_s). Apply current accepted R920 to this same named trimer and source currentization. Its direct all-internal proof gives |U|,|V|>=3 and the four tight reverse shields (u_2,u_1,x), (x,u_r,u_{r-1}), (v_2,v_1,x), (x,v_s,v_{s-1}). No singleton-floor theorem is involved.\n\nTest the literal U-to-V concatenation while keeping J as the second path. Every old turn of U and V is inherited; the complete new hole set is exactly h_1=(u_{r-1},u_r,v_1) and h_2=(u_r,v_1,v_2). If both were tight, (u_1,...,u_r,v_1,...,v_s) together with J would be a spanning two-cover of H, contradicting pc(H)=3. Thus one hole is bad. R3 gives the physically certified mate clause A OR B with A=bar(h_1)=(v_1,u_r,u_{r-1}) and B=bar(h_2)=(v_2,v_1,u_r). This is precisely the native directional clause historically supplied by R453, now proved directly.\n\nBoth endpoints are already collision-decorated with zero-length implication paths. For A, the tested oriented dimer is (u_r,u_{r-1}); A is a head certificate with witness v_1, while R920 supplies the tight head shield (x,u_r,u_{r-1}) with distinct witness x. For B, the tested oriented dimer is (v_2,v_1); B is a tail certificate with witness u_r, while R920 supplies the tight tail shield (v_2,v_1,x) with distinct witness x. The witnesses are distinct because J,U,V are vertex-disjoint literal paths. Therefore part (2), using R523 on the exact tested orientations, forces one of the two named residual-terminal collision packets. Exchanging U and V gives the symmetric directional channel. This is exactly the partner-only collision content asserted in the final specialization of R463.\n\nThus every conclusion of R463 follows from R3, R523, and R920. The historical R38 role is supplied by its current fully reconstructible replacement R523, while the historical R359/R453 specialization is reconstructed directly from R920 plus the literal two-hole seam proposal. No R359, R453, R168, R5, R24, or P22 dependency is used.
