# R275 — No-P4 double-contact four-cell has a unique Strong orientation signature

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Let X={a,b,c,d} be a four-vertex Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament satisfying the double-contact packet from R274: the turns (a,b,c), (a,b,d), (d,b,c), (d,c,b), and (b,a,d) are tight. If X has no Hamilton tight P4, then every remaining reversal-pair choice is forced. Precisely, the tight ordered triples on X are exactly (a,b,c), (a,b,d), (a,c,b), (b,a,c), (b,a,d), (b,d,a), (c,a,d), (c,d,a), (c,d,b), (d,b,c), (d,c,a), and (d,c,b), together with no others except these same listed orientations. Equivalently, the local tournament orders at the four possible middle vertices are: middle a: b>c>d; middle b: a>d>c; middle c: d>a>b; middle d: c>b>a. Thus the non-P4 branch of R274 is one unique labeled antisymmetric four-cell, not a family of residual orientations.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1) boundary antisymmetry on four vertices; the five displayed R274 double-contact turns are tight; no Hamilton tight P4 exists on X.

## Scope
Pure finite four-vertex graph-intrinsic classification. No smallest-counterexample, cover, capture, payment, or historical hypothesis is required beyond the displayed double-contact turns.

## Applicability
Use after R274 in its non-P4 branch. It replaces an underdetermined bounded contact label by one exact 12-turn orientation signature, suitable for comparison with historical no-Hamilton K4 modules or direct fifth-vertex analysis.

## Persistence
The complete orientation signature is graph-intrinsic on the physical four-set X.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not identify this cell with the historical cyclic matching-block K4 without a separate equivalence proof. Does not assert universal fifth-vertex Hamilton extension, a two-cover, or any cover currentization. Does not use or claim a computational proof.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Unique no-P4 double-contact signature is a narrow one-consumer local classification; retain proof history and let broader four-cell parents carry canonical visibility.
- **Curation note:** Unique no-P4 double-contact signature is a narrow one-consumer local classification; retain proof history and let broader four-cell parents carry canonical visibility.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** The conditional finite four-cell classification is correct and now has an independent R3-only proof; it does not rely on R274 being accepted.

## Proof
Assume the five displayed turns abc, abd, dbc, dcb, bad are tight and no tight P4 exists. Boundary antisymmetry fixes their reverses as bad. Force the remaining reversal pairs as follows. (1) In (a,b,d,c), abd is tight, so bdc must be bad; hence cdb is tight. (2) In (a,c,d,b), cdb is tight, so acd must be bad; hence dca is tight. (3) In (a,d,b,c), dbc is tight, so adb must be bad; hence bda is tight. (4) In (a,d,c,b), dcb is tight, so adc must be bad; hence cda is tight. (5) In (b,d,a,c), bda is tight, so dac must be bad; hence cad is tight. (6) In (b,c,a,d), cad is tight, so bca must be bad; hence acb is tight. (7) In (c,a,b,d), abd is tight, so cab must be bad; hence bac is tight. These seven forced choices, together with the five initial turns, determine all twelve reversal pairs. The tight orientations are exactly abc, abd, acb, bac, bad, bda, cad, cda, cdb, dbc, dca, dcb. Grouped by middle vertex, the local orders are: middle a: b>c>d; middle b: a>d>c; middle c: d>a>b; middle d: c>b>a. Thus the no-P4 double-contact cell has the claimed unique orientation signature.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R275.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R276.md

# R276 — Rigid double-contact cell has transitive perfect-matching quotient

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
In the unique no-P4 double-contact four-cell of R275 on X={a,b,c,d}, partition the six physical dimers into the three opposite-edge perfect matchings B_1={{a,b},{c,d}}, B_2={{a,c},{b,d}}, and B_3={{a,d},{b,c}}. At every physical vertex, the three incident dimers inherit the same strict local order B_1>B_2>B_3 from the tight-turn signature of R275. Explicitly: at a, ab>ac>ad; at b, ab>bd>bc; at c, cd>ac>bc; at d, cd>bd>ad. Hence the four-cell has a uniform transitive three-block quotient. In particular it is not a cyclic-quotient matching-block cell.

## Hypotheses
The exact R275 orientation signature on four vertices.

## Scope
Pure finite graph-intrinsic reformulation of R275 in perfect-matching quotient coordinates. No historical K4 classification is used as a premise.

## Applicability
Use to compare the R274/R275 residual with matching-block K4 technology. It routes the residue to the transitive quotient branch and explicitly rules out direct use of cyclic-quotient fifth-vertex extension theorems.

## Persistence
The physical matching partition and quotient order are graph-intrinsic on X.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not assert that every transitive matching-block K4 has the R275 signature beyond the displayed relabelling. Does not provide a fifth-vertex extension theorem, shell success, or two-cover. Historical matching-block classification is not used as a dependency.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Finite perfect-matching quotient reformulation of one rigid four-cell residue. Fully correct but branch-specific, zero-consumer, and mainly a routing observation to transitive rather than cyclic quotient technology.
- **Curation note:** Finite perfect-matching quotient reformulation of one rigid four-cell residue. Fully correct but branch-specific, zero-consumer, and mainly a routing observation to transitive rather than cyclic quotient technology.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Valid transitive perfect-matching quotient of the R275 signature.

## Proof
From R275, the local neighbor orders are: middle a: b>c>d; middle b: a>d>c; middle c: d>a>b; middle d: c>b>a. Define B1={{a,b},{c,d}}, B2={{a,c},{b,d}}, B3={{a,d},{b,c}}. At vertex a the incident edges are ab in B1, ac in B2, ad in B3, so the local order is B1>B2>B3. At b the incident edges are ba=ab in B1, bd in B2, bc in B3; the R275 order a>d>c again gives B1>B2>B3. At c the incident edges cd in B1, ca=ac in B2, cb=bc in B3; d>a>b gives B1>B2>B3. At d the incident edges dc=cd in B1, db=bd in B2, da=ad in B3; c>b>a gives B1>B2>B3. Thus orientation between matching blocks is uniform and the quotient is the transitive order B1>B2>B3. A cyclic quotient would require a directed 3-cycle among the three block labels, so this cell is not cyclic.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R276.md -->

# R28 — Same-rail endpoint absorption

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement

For a current rail endpoint and an internal prescribed vertex on the same other rail, boundary antisymmetry chooses one of two antisymmetric endpoint trimers. # R285 — Bilateral four-core capture yields an anchored carrier-spoke interaction fan

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Let K=(v_0,...,v_m) be a tight path in a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament, let d be a vertex outside K, and let B be any set of internal vertices of K. For each b=v_i in B with carrier neighbors l_b=v_{i-1} and r_b=v_{i+1}, the physical spoke {b,d} carries two signed certificates with the distinct witnesses l_b and r_b. Consequently R38 forces on every such spoke either the same-polarity two-extension collision package or the opposite-polarity strict two-ended signed-path interaction. Thus one fixed exterior anchor d supports an R38-productive spoke at every chosen internal carrier position. In the historical R250 repeated-dimer setting this applies to every internal member of the class B, hence at at least |B|-2 positions.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1) boundary antisymmetry; K is a graph-intrinsic tight path; d is outside K; B consists of internal vertices of K.

## Scope
Order-free capture-free replacement for the invalid R251 capture-to-spoke proof.

## Applicability
Use wherever the old R251 interaction fan was consumed only for its signed-spoke/R38 conclusion. The R250 class-size count may still be imported, but no capture ancestry is attached to the fresh spokes.

## Persistence
K, d, the carrier neighbors, centered trimer certificates, spoke supports, witnesses, and R38 interaction outputs are graph-intrinsic. Any unrelated historical captures at the same carrier vertices remain separate ancestry facts.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not claim that any historical capture reenters {b,d}; does not invoke R155; does not make different R38 descendants simultaneous; does not currentize a whole fan.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Fresh anchored carrier-spoke R38 fan is capture-free and follows from local carrier-neighbor trimers; it does not transport the historical captures that motivated it. With C264/C265/C267 active, this zero-/single-use role-blind existence interface need not remain canonical.
- **Curation note:** Fresh anchored carrier-spoke R38 fan is capture-free and follows from local carrier-neighbor trimers; it does not transport the historical captures that motivated it. With C264/C265/C267 active, this zero-/single-use role-blind existence interface need not remain canonical.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Valid capture-free replacement for the old R251 spoke-interaction content.

## Proof
Fix b=v_i. Boundary antisymmetry gives exactly one tight b-middle orientation of {l_b,b,d}; whichever orientation is tight, its terminal dimer {b,d} has l_b as the opposite outer witness under R41. Likewise the unique b-middle tight trimer on {r_b,b,d} signs the same physical spoke with witness r_b. Since l_b and r_b are distinct, R38 applies to these two tested certificates. This is independent of any capture event or representative. Repeating independently over B gives the fixed-anchor fan. In the R250 setting only the at most two endpoints of K fail internality, so at least |B|-2 class vertices contribute.

The canonical one-hole proposals around the middle pivot have exact one-hole or two-hole counts. When the middle turn is tight, the two mates concatenate into a tight four-path. Four explicit minimum three-cover mate-packet representatives exist and each preserves the opposite source splice.

Same-end mate/splice incompatibility rules out a previously tempting target: these canonical packets cannot contain one mate packet together with both source splices as a path forest. This deletes that synchronization branch; it is not merely a failure to find a construction.

The central internal-singleton representative and the deepest transfer coordinate are related by a neutral two-for-two switch with zero cycle debt, but they are exclusive resources. In the tight sign the conflict is a transfer-coordinate conflict; in the bad sign it is a shielding-bad-turn conflict.

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R302.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R302.md -->

# R302 — Bare R38 interaction existence is universal and is not a progress alternative

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Let H be any Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament and let D={u,v} be any physical dimer with two distinct witnesses x,y outside D. Then D carries one signed certificate with witness x and one signed certificate with witness y, so R38 forces a same-support two-witness interaction on D. Consequently every Strong Level-(1) system of order at least four already contains an R38 interaction. Therefore a theorem alternative stated only as either an R38 same-support interaction exists or some residue holds is logically vacuous in its first branch unless the interaction is localized by specified physical support, specified witnesses, ancestry, currentness, or another consumer-relevant coordinate.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1) boundary antisymmetry; accepted R3, R38, and the terminal-dimer sign convention R41.

## Scope
Order-free proof-design correction and local theorem. It concerns bare existential R38-productivity, not coordinate-localized R38 certificates.

## Applicability
Use when evaluating claimed progress whose output is merely existence of some R38 same-support two-witness interaction. Such existence is free once four vertices are present. Useful descendants must retain nontrivial support/witness identity, ancestry, polarity branch, current geometry, or an explicit path/contact output.

## Persistence
The chosen dimer D, witnesses x,y, and their R38 interaction are graph-intrinsic.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not say R38 is useless. Coordinate-localized R38 interactions, forced polarity, explicit strict P4 outputs, collision ancestry, or interactions on strategically constrained supports may be highly productive. Does not assert closure of the Strong conjecture.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Historical warning that bare R38 interaction is ubiquitous; current focus already treats generic interaction/contact as non-progress.
- **Curation note:** Project-wide role-consumption correction: bare R38 interaction exists universally and is not itself progress.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Accepted correction: bare existence of an R38 interaction is universal on any dimer with two outside witnesses and is not by itself a progress alternative.

## Proof
Fix D={u,v} and distinct x,y outside D. By R3, exactly one of (u,v,x) and (x,v,u) is tight. In either case the terminal physical dimer {u,v}, with the tested order inherited from that tight trimer, is signed by witness x in the sense used by R41/R38. Likewise exactly one of (u,v,y) and (y,v,u) is tight, giving a second signed certificate on the same physical support D with distinct witness y. R38 therefore applies: if the two certificates have the same polarity, the same-polarity two-extension collision package occurs; if they have opposite polarities, the strict two-ended signed-path interaction occurs. Hence bare existence of an R38 interaction is automatic on every physical dimer having two outside vertices. In any system of order at least four such a choice exists.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R302.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R304.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R304.md -->

# R304 — Fresh-triple R38 manufacture is role-blind and does not synchronize historical ancestry

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Suppose x and y are two distinct physical vertices carrying any historical roles whatsoever, for example alternative floor coordinates, captured carrier indices, crossing endpoints, paid descendants, or unrelated labels. If an argument obtains a same-support R38 interaction by choosing fresh vertices u,v and applying only boundary antisymmetry to the triples {u,v,x} and {u,v,y}, then the resulting signed certificates use x and y only as physical witness identities. Their historical roles are not consumed or transported into the R38 certificate. The identical proof works for any two distinct vertices. Therefore such a construction is a role-blind coordinate-labeled interaction, not by itself a synchronization of the histories that happened to name x and y. In particular the fresh-triple mismatch steps in R300 and the first two mismatch steps of R303 are mathematically valid but do not couple paid-floor or puncture-capture ancestry unless a downstream theorem separately consumes the special witness roles.

## Hypotheses
Accepted R3,R38,R41. Historical coordinates x,y may come from arbitrary prior lineages; no same-representative assumption is made.

## Scope
Order-free provenance/synchronization fence. Distinguishes graph-intrinsic witness identity from inheritance of a witness special historical role.

## Applicability
Use when evaluating synchronization arguments that manufacture new signed certificates from historical coordinates by fresh boundary-antisymmetry triples. Such certificates are useful only to the extent a consumer needs those exact physical witness identities; they cannot be cited as evidence that the source histories themselves have merged, interacted, become simultaneous, or transported ancestry.

## Persistence
The newly manufactured signs and R38 interaction are graph-intrinsic. The source historical roles of x,y persist only in their own ancestry ledgers and are not imported into the new signs by this construction.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not invalidate R300 or R303 as literal existence theorems. Does not prevent a later role-sensitive consumer from exploiting the fact that the physical witnesses happen to equal historically important coordinates. Does not apply when the signed certificates themselves arise through ancestry-preserving transport rather than fresh R3 manufacture.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Historical fresh-triple R38 role-blindness warning; no live use remains.
- **Curation note:** Project-wide ancestry correction: fresh R38 manufacture does not transport historical roles.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Accepted provenance correction distinguishing physical witness identity from transport of historical role/ancestry.

## Proof
Fix distinct physical vertices x,y and choose a physical dimer D={u,v} disjoint from them. By R3, one of (u,v,x),(x,v,u) is tight, giving through R41 a signed certificate on D with witness x. Likewise one of (u,v,y),(y,v,u) is tight, giving a second certificate on D with witness y. R38 applies. No step references any source floor, capture, crossing, payment, selected support, or ancestry property of x or y. Hence the certificate depends only on their physical distinctness. If x and y are renamed to any other distinct vertices, the same proof goes through verbatim. Therefore historical labels attached to x,y are not transported into the newly manufactured R38 packet. R300 and the floor/capture mismatch steps of R303 use exactly this proof pattern, so their interactions are coordinate-labeled but role-blind unless a later consumer explicitly uses the witnesses historical roles.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R304.md -->

# R305 — Every six vertices carry a capture-free fixed-trimer nonquiet interaction packet

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Let H be any Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament and let b,d_1,d_2,y,r,s be six distinct vertices. Then there exist signed spokes S_1={b,d_1}, S_2={b,d_2}, both with common witness y, and one fixed tight trimer T on {r,y,s}, such that each S_i forms a direct mass-four balanced pair with a terminal dimer of T of opposite polarity. After declaring one pair birth first, the second birth through the same fixed T is nonquiet by R160 and forces the accepted historical signed-support/anchor interaction or cross-generation pair interaction before unrelated reset. Consequently every Strong Level-(1) system of order at least six contains a fixed-trimer nonquiet packet. The bare existence of such a packet is therefore not smallest-counterexample progress and is not evidence of puncture/capture synchronization.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1) boundary antisymmetry; six distinct vertices; accepted R3,R39,R41,R160.

## Scope
Pure six-vertex local theorem. No path, cover, smallest-counterexample, capture, exterior-floor, payment, or puncture hypothesis is required.

## Applicability
Use to simplify R291-style constructions and to prevent counting an unlocalized fixed-trimer nonquiet packet as structural progress. A useful consumer must exploit special identities/ancestry of b,d_i,y,T, force a specific interaction output, or connect the packet to current cover geometry.

## Persistence
The two spoke signs, fixed trimer, direct pair births, and R160 historical interaction are graph-intrinsic/historical as in their parent theorems.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not say R160 is useless. A packet on prescribed supports or witnesses, tied to capture/payment/current geometry, may carry genuine information. Does not assert the R160 interaction is a contradiction or a spanning two-cover.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Historical six-vertex fixed-trimer interaction packet countermodel; no live use remains.
- **Curation note:** Universal six-vertex ubiquity theorem showing fixed-trimer nonquiet packets are role-blind and therefore not progress by bare existence.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Accepted universal six-vertex capture-free fixed-trimer nonquiet packet; useful primarily as a fence against counting unlocalized R160 packets as structural progress.

## Proof
For i=1,2, boundary antisymmetry R3 gives exactly one tight orientation of the triple {b,d_i,y} with middle d_i, namely either (b,d_i,y) or (y,d_i,b). By R41 the terminal physical spoke S_i={b,d_i} therefore carries a signed certificate with witness y. Independently, R3 gives exactly one tight orientation T of {r,y,s} with middle y. Its two terminal dimers have opposite polarities by R41. For each i choose the terminal dimer M_i of T whose polarity is opposite to that of S_i. The supports S_i and M_i are disjoint because the six vertices are distinct, so R39 gives a direct mass-four balanced pair (S_i,M_i). Declare the first birth historical. The second birth also uses a signed dimer disjoint from the same fixed trimer T and one of T terminal dimers, so R160 says it cannot begin a quiet independent pair epoch before unrelated reset: the accepted historical signed-support/anchor interaction or cross-generation pair interaction is forced. No carrier or capture fact was used.

The four reverse root-cap turns over one transfer edge force the fixed deleted vertex to be blocked at both ends of both common-shadow rails. # R312 — Protected capture plus lawful old-carrier mirror reentry forces first contact

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Let A be a retained historical tight carrier path, D={x,z} a physical crossing of A, and suppose x has a valid historical capture certificate through D. Assume x has at least one genuine historical carrier adjacency E={p,x} on A. Choose one actual capture descendant and one designated quiet continuation to which accepted R42 applies. Then invoking accepted R155 on the same retained packet (A,D,capture) with the old adjacency E is a lawful mirror reentry and cannot be a quiet unrelated epoch: either an earlier event touching the protected anchor x has already been exposed, or this R155 mirror-reentry operation itself is the first contact at x. The later mirror trimer retains the capture event as ancestry. Thus any captured anchor lying on a nontrivial retained historical carrier has an explicit first-contact probe using an actual old carrier edge; no capture transport to a fresh path is required.

## Hypotheses
Smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample; A,D,x form a valid capture packet in the exact scope of R155; x has a historical adjacency E on A; one actual capture descendant and designated quiet continuation are chosen as required by R42; accepted correction R277.

## Scope
Order-free ancestry/contact compiler staying entirely inside the genuine retained historical carrier.

## Applicability
Use after any lawful capture when the captured vertex has at least one old carrier adjacency. It converts the otherwise static capture event into a forced first-contact alternative.

## Persistence
A,D,x,E and the historical capture event are retained. The chosen protected continuation is lineage-relative. The R155 mirror trimer is a later representative and retains capture ancestry as stated by R155.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not apply by substituting a newly invented carrier. Does not say the first contact closes the conjecture. Does not claim capture protection survives after the first contact has been exposed. Does not require two carrier neighbors.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** R312 is the old protected-capture first-contact compiler. Protected-contact production is no longer a live frontier and no current consumer remains.
- **Curation note:** Ancestry-sensitive first-contact consumer: protected capture plus lawful old-carrier mirror reentry forces first contact.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Accepted lawful protected-contact compiler. After choosing an R42 continuation, old-carrier R155 mirror reentry exposes an earlier contact or is itself the first contact.

## Proof
Retain the exact R312 packet: a historical tight carrier A, physical crossing D={x,z} with x in A and z outside A, a valid historical capture of x through D, and a genuine carrier adjacency E={p,x} on A. Choose one actual capture descendant and designated quiet continuation in the scope of accepted R42. Since A is a certified historical carrier crossed by D and E is one of its genuine adjacencies, accepted fully reconstructible R155 applies. It gives a later minimum three-cover whose mirror trimer through x has D and E as its two boundary physical supports, while the capture event remains historical ancestry. This later operation uses signed/physical supports containing the protected anchor x. Accepted R42 therefore rules out treating it as a quiet unrelated epoch along the chosen protected continuation: either some earlier operation already touched x, in which case that earlier contact is exposed, or the R155 mirror-reentry operation itself is the first contact at x. This is exactly the R312 dichotomy. No substitution of a fresh carrier is made, and no old selected orientation, old residual rail, or protection after first contact is claimed.

# R314 — Smallest-counterexample order is at most twice longest proper-path order plus one

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Let H be a smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample of order n, and let L be the maximum order of a proper tight path in H. Then n<=2L+1. For any vertex v, minimality gives a spanning two-cover of H-v by two tight paths P,Q. Both are proper tight paths of H, so |P|,|Q|<=L, while |P|+|Q|=n-1. Hence n-1<=2L. In particular L<=5 implies n<=11.

## Hypotheses
H is a smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample; L is the maximum order of a proper tight path in H.

## Scope
Order-free minimality/size inequality.

## Applicability
Use whenever another theorem bounds the global longest proper-path order.

## Persistence
The inequality depends only on n,L and smallest-counterexample minimality.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not itself bound L or close any fixed order.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** superseded
- **Lifecycle note:** The bound n<=2L+1 is the immediate one-vertex-deletion size consequence of smallest-counterexample minimality R4; retain it historically but not as a separate canonical theorem.
- **Curation note:** The bound n<=2L+1 is the immediate one-vertex-deletion size consequence of smallest-counterexample minimality R4; retain it historically but not as a separate canonical theorem.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Accepted minimality inequality n<=2L+1.

## Proof
Fix v in V(H). Since H is a smallest counterexample, the proper induced subsystem H-v has a spanning cover by at most two tight paths P,Q. Each nonempty P,Q is also a tight path of H and is proper because v is omitted, so each has order at most L. Their vertex sets cover H-v and are disjoint as a path cover, hence |P|+|Q|=n-1. Therefore n-1<=2L and n<=2L+1.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R314.md -->

# R316 — Order-eleven longest-five residue has exact 5+5 cover after every vertex deletion

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Let H be a smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample of order 11 whose maximum proper tight-path order is five. Then for every vertex v in V(H), every spanning two-cover of H-v supplied by minimality consists of exactly two vertex-disjoint tight P5s. In particular H-v has a literal exact 5+5 cover, and both five-path supports are global-longest supports in H. Thus every vertex v is the unique omitted vertex of at least one pair of disjoint global-longest P5 supports whose union is V(H)\\{v}.

## Hypotheses
H is a smallest Strong Level-(1) counterexample; |H|=11; maximum proper tight-path order is five.

## Scope
Finite order-eleven exact-deletion structure.

## Applicability
Use in the finite residual branch of R315. It converts minimality into eleven literal 5+5 deletion roots.

## Persistence
For each v, existence of the two disjoint global-longest supports is graph-intrinsic; a chosen ordering/cover representative is deletion-root-relative.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not synchronize the eleven deletion roots. Does not say the two supports in different roots intersect or coincide in any prescribed way. Does not by itself close order eleven.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Order-eleven exact 5+5 deletion-root structure. Mathematically substantive but special-order, single-use residue analysis no longer on the active arbitrary-order spine; preserve accepted history.
- **Curation note:** Order-eleven exact 5+5 deletion-root structure. Mathematically substantive but special-order, single-use residue analysis no longer on the active arbitrary-order spine; preserve accepted history.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Accepted finite residue theorem: in the n=11,L=5 branch every vertex deletion has an exact 5+5 cover by two global-longest paths.

## Proof
Fix v. By smallest-counterexample minimality, H-v has a spanning two-cover by tight paths P,Q. Since every proper tight path of H has order at most five and |H-v|=10, we have 10=|P|+|Q| with |P|,|Q|<=5. Therefore |P|=|Q|=5. Their supports are disjoint and cover V(H)\\{v}. Because the maximum proper path order in H is five, each is global-longest. This holds for every v.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R316.md -->

# R32 — Root basins and extremal transfer components

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement

A cover is isolated in the fixed-root transfer graph exactly when every endpoint is completely shielded. The whole graph is edgeless exactly when every exact deletion cover is completely shielded. If an edge exists, that edge enters the accepted good-splice/root-mate basin without importing selected states from its endpoints.

## Scope
Within one transfer component, maximize the rail-size gap. No transfer can move an endpoint from the shorter rail to the longer rail there, so the longer rail is triply shielded at both ends; at least one transfer from longer to shorter remains. The minimum-gap dual is valid only when the minimum gap is at least two. Extremality belongs to the chosen component and representative, not to the entire transfer universe.

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R320.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R320.md -->

# R320 — Dual-clique Hamilton-five density amplification

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Let W be any r-vertex subset, r>=6, of a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament. Let B be the family of five-subsets of W that do not support a tight P5, and write b=|B| and M=binom(r,5). Then\n\n b/M <= beta_r := [15 + sqrt(225+60(r-4)(r-5))]/[30(r-4)].\n\nEquivalently the Hamiltonian five-support density is at least 1-beta_r. Combining with R216 gives bad-density at most min(1/3,beta_r). For every r>10 one has beta_r<1/3, so this strictly improves the two-thirds Hamilton-five density theorem. In particular for r=11, b<=148 and therefore at least 314 of the 462 five-subsets support tight P5s. As r tends to infinity, beta_r tends to 1/sqrt(15), so the Hamiltonian five-support density is asymptotically at least 1-1/sqrt(15) approximately 0.7418.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1) boundary antisymmetry; W is an r-set with r>=6; accepted four-of-six Hamilton-five density R195.

## Scope
Order-free support-density theorem. Pure finite set-system/Johnson-graph counting; no smallest-counterexample, carrier, deletion, sign, payment, or representative hypotheses.

## Applicability
Use for higher-order exterior/residual sets when the coarse R216 two-thirds density is insufficient. The structural proof retains both union-six-set and intersection-four-core clique localization, making it suitable for occupancy/generalization arguments. A separate spectral proof route should also be retained because it may generalize differently.

## Persistence
The bad-support family B, its Johnson edges, six-set clique occupancies, and four-core occupancies are graph-intrinsic finite-set data.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not force P6 or longer paths, does not prescribe compatible P5 orderings, does not by itself yield a two-cover, and does not assert the density bound is sharp. For r<=10 the displayed beta_r bound need not improve R216, so the combined min(1/3,beta_r) is the recommended numerical form.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** superseded
- **Lifecycle note:** The quadratic dual-clique density amplification is strictly weaker than the later conditional Johnson-degree density hierarchy; preserve its proof technology historically, but keep C281 canonical.
- **Curation note:** The quadratic dual-clique density amplification is strictly weaker than the later conditional Johnson-degree density hierarchy; preserve its proof technology historically, but keep C281 canonical.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Dual-clique Hamilton-five density amplification is correct. The structural proof establishes the full r>=6 scope and the numerical beta_r consequences.

## Proof
Write B for the non-Hamiltonian five-subsets of W and b=|B|. Regard the five-subsets as vertices of J(r,5). Every Johnson edge A-Aprime has |A union Aprime|=6 and belongs to the unique union-indexed K6 consisting of the six five-subsets of that six-set. By R195, every six-set contains at most two bad five-subsets, hence each such K6 contains at most one edge of the induced graph on B. Therefore e(B)<=binom(r,6). Now decompose the same Johnson edges by their unique four-set intersection. For each four-set S subset W put x_S=|{A in B:S subset A}|. The five-sets containing S form a clique K_{r-4}, and every Johnson edge has exactly one four-set intersection, so e(B)=sum_S binom(x_S,2). Also sum_S x_S=5b because each bad five-set contains five four-sets. Hence 2e(B)=sum_S x_S^2-5b >= (sum_S x_S)^2/binom(r,4)-5b =25b^2/binom(r,4)-5b by Cauchy. Combining with e(B)<=binom(r,6) gives 25b^2/binom(r,4)-5b<=2binom(r,6). Put M=binom(r,5), use binom(r,4)=5M/(r-4) and binom(r,6)=(r-5)M/6, and set alpha=b/M. After division by M this becomes 15(r-4)alpha^2-15alpha-(r-5)<=0. The positive root is beta_r=[15+sqrt(225+60(r-4)(r-5))]/[30(r-4)], proving alpha<=beta_r. At r=11 the resulting real upper bound is b<149, so b<=148 and h_5(W)>=462-148=314. Finally beta_r<1/3 exactly when r>10, and beta_r tends to 1/sqrt(15).

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R320.md -->

# R321 — Seven vertices need not contain a tight P6

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
The explicit seven-vertex Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament of R230 has maximum tight-path order exactly five and nevertheless 18 of its 21 physical five-subsets support tight P5s. Thus a P6-free Strong system can have Hamilton-five support density 18/21=6/7. In particular no theorem whose only hypothesis is a Hamilton-five density lower bound at or below 6/7 can force a P6, even locally on seven vertices. This sharply fences attempts to turn R216 or R320 density alone into path-length growth.

## Hypotheses
The explicit seven-vertex turn table and exhaustive P6-free verification of accepted R230.

## Scope
Order-free local negative result strengthening R230 with exact P5-density data. It is a regression fence, not a smallest-counterexample model.

## Applicability
Use when evaluating density-to-growth strategies. R320 gives a stronger universal lower density than R216 for large r, but density alone is not the missing carrier-growth mechanism.

## Persistence
The explicit seven-vertex turn table and the list/count of Hamiltonian five-subsets are graph-intrinsic and finitely reconstructible.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not show 6/7 is the maximum P5 density of P6-free Strong systems, does not construct arbitrarily large P6-free examples, and does not refute a density-plus-minimality, carrier, exact-cover, or ancestry theorem.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Historical seven-vertex P6 counterexample; global path-length fences R823/R829 now carry the durable warning.
- **Curation note:** Explicit seven-vertex P6-free system with P5 density 6/7; quantitative density-to-growth barrier.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Strengthened R230 negative result is correct: the explicit seven-vertex P6-free model has Hamilton-five density exactly 18/21=6/7.

## Proof
Use the explicit local tournaments recorded in R230. Exhaustive enumeration of all 21 physical five-subsets shows that exactly three fail to support a tight P5 and the remaining eighteen do. The same accepted R230 enumeration verifies that every ordered six-tuple has a bad consecutive turn, so the maximum tight-path order remains five. Hence the P5-support density is 18/21=6/7 in a genuinely P6-free Strong Level-(1) system.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R321.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R327.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R327.md -->

# R327 — Dual-clique conditional Hamilton-five density hierarchy

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Let W be an r-vertex subset, r>=6, of a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament, and fix S subseteq W of size s in {0,1,2,3}. Among the five-subsets F of W containing S, the fraction that fail to support a tight P5 is at most\n\n(r-s)/[(5-s)(r-4)].\n\nEquivalently\n\nh_5(W;S) >= [1-(r-s)/((5-s)(r-4))] binom(r-s,5-s).\n\nFor s=0 this gives global Hamilton-five density at least 4(r-5)/[5(r-4)], tending to 4/5. For fixed vertex, pair, and triple the asymptotic guaranteed densities tend respectively to 3/4, 2/3, and 1/2. For every r>10 these bounds strictly improve the older R228 fractions 2/3,3/5,1/2,1/3 and the earlier quadratic R324 bounds. In particular for r=11 at least 317 of the 462 five-subsets support tight P5s.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament; W any r-set with r>=6; S subseteq W with |S| in {0,1,2,3}; accepted R195 local four-of-six Hamilton-five theorem; Johnson local-clique degree principle R326.

## Scope
Order-free quantitative strengthening of R228 and prior revision R324. Preserves a fixed physical vertex, pair, or triple while obtaining the stronger Johnson-degree density ceiling.

## Applicability
Use when a named physical vertex/dimer/trimer must occur in many Hamiltonian P5 supports. This is the preferred conditional-density estimate, while R324 remains a distinct quadratic/defect-compatible proof route.

## Persistence
Pure graph-intrinsic support counting through the fixed subset S; no ordering synchronization or representative currentness.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not prescribe P5 orderings or force P6/path growth. Density-only growth remains blocked by R321. Fixed four-sets receive no nontrivial bound from this t=2 quotient argument.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** The conditional Hamilton-five density hierarchy is a direct quotient-and-apply-R326 corollary of the general Johnson density theorem plus R195; preserve historically, but not as separate canonical mathematics.
- **Curation note:** The conditional Hamilton-five density hierarchy is a direct quotient-and-apply-R326 corollary of the general Johnson density theorem plus R195; preserve historically, but not as separate canonical mathematics.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Strengthened fixed-S Hamilton-five density hierarchy is correct; it improves R228 and R324 for r>10 and gives at least 317 Hamiltonian five-subsets when r=11,s=0.

## Proof
Let B_S={F\\S:S subseteq F subseteq W, |F|=5, F non-Hamiltonian}. Then B_S is k=(5-s)-uniform on N=r-s vertices. Every (k+1)=(6-s)-set U in W\\S gives a six-set S union U, and R195 says at most two of its five-subsets are bad, so U contains at most t=2 members of B_S. R326 gives p_bad<= [k+(N-k)]/[k(N-k+1)]=N/[k(N-k+1)]. Substituting N=r-s, k=5-s, and N-k+1=r-4 yields (r-s)/[(5-s)(r-4)]. The displayed Hamiltonian density and asymptotic values follow by complementation. For r>10 direct comparison gives strict improvement over R228; at r=11,s=0 the bad count is at most floor((11/35)*462)=145, hence at least 317 good five-sets.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R327.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R328.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R328.md -->

# R328 — Fixed-trimer bad-extension graph is triangle-free

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Let P be a tight trimer in a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament and let X be any set of m>=3 vertices disjoint from P. Form a graph G_bad on X by joining x,y when the five-set V(P) union {x,y} does not support a tight P5. Then G_bad is triangle-free. Consequently |E(G_bad)|<=floor(m^2/4), so at least binom(m,2)-floor(m^2/4) pairs {x,y} extend P to a Hamiltonian five-support. Equality in the bad-pair bound forces the Mantel extremal structure: G_bad is a complete bipartite graph with part sizes floor(m/2),ceil(m/2). Equivalently, in the equality case the outside vertices split into two nearly equal classes and every within-class pair extends P to a tight P5.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament; P is any tight trimer; X is any m-set disjoint from P, m>=3; accepted three-exterior pair extension theorem R146.

## Scope
Order-free exact structural strengthening of the fixed-trimer s=3 density specialization. Recasts R146 as a triangle-free bad-extension graph and imports the sharp Mantel extremal/equality picture.

## Applicability
Use whenever one fixed tight trimer is retained and many outside vertices are available. The theorem gives an exact extension count and, near/equality, a two-class structure on outside vertices that may be exploitable by sign, carrier, or cover arguments.

## Persistence
The bad-extension graph on the physical outside vertices is graph-intrinsic. No P5 ordering synchronization is claimed.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not say which P5 ordering occurs on a good pair. Does not force P6. Equality of the Mantel bound is a set-system structure, not a two-cover contradiction by itself.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** superseded
- **Lifecycle note:** Fixed-trimer bad-extension graph triangle-freeness is exactly the graph reformulation of C143: a bad triangle would be three exterior vertices for which all three pair extensions fail. Keep C143 canonical and preserve the graph reformulation historically.
- **Curation note:** Fixed-trimer bad-extension graph triangle-freeness is exactly the graph reformulation of C143: a bad triangle would be three exterior vertices for which all three pair extensions fail. Keep C143 canonical and preserve the graph reformulation historically.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Fixed-trimer bad-extension graph is triangle-free by R146, with the sharp Mantel bound and equality partition.

## Proof
For any three distinct x,y,z in X, R146 applied to P,x,y,z says at least one of Pxy,Pxz,Pyz supports a tight P5. Therefore not all three pairs xy,xz,yz can be edges of G_bad, so G_bad is triangle-free. Mantel gives |E(G_bad)|<=floor(m^2/4), with equality exactly for the balanced complete bipartite graph K_{floor(m/2),ceil(m/2)}. The complementary good-pair count is binom(m,2)-|E(G_bad)|. In the equality case every within-part pair is absent from G_bad and hence is a good P5 extension of P.

# R33 — Attachment-fiber and endcap saturation

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement

In a crossed fiber, the normalized endpoint covers are obtained by exchanging rail labels only; current paths are not reversed. The central one-hole path has one exact hole, its opposite mate aligns with a current reverse-boundary collision, and two arm trimers have exact complements. The two arm retractions are neutral and reversible.

## Scope
At an endcap, tight signs give two-for-two root-mate retractions. They commute to restore the original local rails while preserving the opposite attachment path. Bad signs have explicit singleton blocker sets and one-for-one outputs; the two bad-sign restorations also commute. This saturates local rail restoration only, not every cross-coupled use of the fixed-shadow packet.

The higher accepted parent is a six-pair absorption/retraction family with opposite-polarity cap factorization. Exactly one absorption coordinate preserves a given transfer edge, and the local moves form a reversible restoration cube. This does not reproduce the older ancestry carried by R20/R19 or R28 through R34.

# R331 — Hamilton-five density equality forces a paired four-design normal form

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Let W be an r-vertex subset, r>=6, of a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament, and let B be the family of five-subsets of W that do not support a tight P5. Then |B|/binom(r,5)<=r/[5(r-4)]. If equality holds, necessarily 5 divides r, every four-subset S of W lies in exactly r/5 members of B, and every six-subset U that contains at least one member of B contains exactly two members of B. Equivalently the extremal bad family is a 4-(r,5,r/5) design at the core-incidence level and is locally paired inside every occupied six-set. Hence failure of either core regularity or six-set pairing gives a strict density improvement below the R326 ceiling.

## Hypotheses
Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament; W any r-set; R195 gives at most two bad five-subsets in every six-set; R326 Johnson local-clique degree density principle and its equality conditions.

## Scope
Order-free structural equality corollary for Hamilton-five support density. Converts the scalar 4/5-asymptotic ceiling into a concrete design-like extremal normal form.

## Applicability
Use when a support-counting argument approaches the R326 ceiling. Instead of squeezing constants further, attack the forced four-core regularity or the exact two-bad-per-occupied-six-set pairing.

## Persistence
The bad-support family and its four-core/six-set incidence pattern are graph-intrinsic.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not assert such extremal designs exist or are realizable by Strong Level-(1) systems. Does not classify near-equality families quantitatively. Does not imply P6.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** superseded
- **Lifecycle note:** Hamilton-five paired four-design equality normal form is the k=5 Strong specialization of the general Johnson t=2 equality theorem C325/R375. R331 remains a useful heavily consumed proof interface, but canonical mathematical discovery should point to the general parent.
- **Curation note:** Hamilton-five paired four-design equality normal form is the k=5 Strong specialization of the general Johnson t=2 equality theorem C325/R375. R331 remains a useful heavily consumed proof interface, but canonical mathematical discovery should point to the general parent.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Hamilton-five density equality forces the claimed design-like four-core regularity and exact local pairing in every occupied six-set.

## Proof
For the bad Hamilton-five family B, R195 supplies local six-set occupancy at most two. Equality in the R326 bad-density ceiling is therefore exactly the t=2 equality setting of R375 with k=5. Hence 5 divides r, every four-set lies in exactly r/5 bad five-sets, and every occupied six-set contains exactly two bad five-sets. This is precisely the paired four-design normal form asserted by R331.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R331.md -->

# R332 — Boundary antisymmetry permits unit Hamilton-five density

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
For every finite vertex set V with a fixed total order <, define a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament by declaring an ordered triple (a,b,c) tight exactly when a<c. Then complete reversal (c,b,a) is tight exactly when c<a, so boundary antisymmetry holds. Moreover every nonempty vertex subset W admits a tight Hamilton path by listing its vertices increasingly. In particular every five-subset supports a tight P5, so Hamilton-five support density can equal 1 in a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament. Therefore no upper obstruction to very high P5 density follows from boundary antisymmetry alone; any theorem forcing near-unit P5 density in a smallest counterexample must use global minimality/extremality or exact-cover structure.

## Hypotheses
Finite vertex set with a chosen total order.

## Scope
Order-free explicit Strong Level-(1) construction; strategic density fence, not a smallest-counterexample model.

## Applicability
Use when assessing whether very high Hamilton-five density is locally possible. It is: density one occurs. The research problem is forcing such density under smallest-counterexample hypotheses.

## Persistence
The construction and Hamiltonicity statement are graph-intrinsic.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not produce a smallest counterexample and does not imply a smallest counterexample can have density one.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Historical unit Hamilton-five density example; no live route depends on this local density fence.
- **Curation note:** Explicit Strong construction showing boundary antisymmetry permits Hamilton-five density one.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Accepted. The total-order construction satisfies boundary antisymmetry and has an increasing Hamilton path on every subset, so Hamilton-five density one is locally possible.

## Proof
Fix the chosen total order < on V and declare (a,b,c) tight iff a<c. For any three distinct a,b,c, exactly one of a<c and c<a holds. Hence exactly one of (a,b,c) and its complete reversal (c,b,a) is tight, so the declared turn system satisfies Strong Level-(1) boundary antisymmetry. Now let W be any nonempty subset and list its vertices increasingly as w_1<...<w_k. For every consecutive triple w_i,w_{i+1},w_{i+2}, the first entry is smaller than the third, so (w_i,w_{i+1},w_{i+2}) is tight. Thus the increasing listing is a tight Hamilton path of W. In particular each five-subset has a tight P5, so the Hamilton-five support density is exactly 1. Therefore boundary antisymmetry alone cannot impose any upper obstruction below density one. No prior theorem is used; the proof is a direct verification from the displayed construction.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R332.md -->

# R335 — Unit Hamilton-five density does not force a tight P6

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
There exists a six-vertex Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament on V={0,1,2,3,4,5} in which every one of the six physical five-subsets supports a tight P5, but V itself supports no tight P6. Thus even Hamilton-five support density 1 does not force path growth from order five to order six. Consequently any generalization of the order-ten proof that needs P5 density to force longer-path existence must use additional structure beyond the density statistic itself, even if that density were strengthened all the way to 100%.

## Hypotheses
Explicit six-vertex Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament. For each middle b, notation a>c means (a,b,c) is tight. The local tournaments are: T0: 1>2,1>3,1>4,5>1,3>2,4>2,5>2,3>4,5>3,5>4. T1: 0>2,3>0,0>4,5>0,3>2,4>2,5>2,3>4,5>3,5>4. T2: 1>0,3>0,4>0,5>0,3>1,4>1,5>1,4>3,5>3,4>5. T3: 1>0,0>2,4>0,0>5,1>2,4>1,5>1,4>2,5>2,4>5. T4: 0>1,2>0,3>0,5>0,2>1,3>1,1>5,3>2,2>5,3>5. T5: 1>0,0>2,0>3,0>4,1>2,1>3,1>4,3>2,2>4,3>4.

## Scope
Explicit local regression fence for density-only path-growth arguments. No smallest-counterexample hypothesis.

## Applicability
Use to reject any inference of the form sufficiently high Hamilton-five density alone forces a tight P6. The obstruction survives even at density one.

## Persistence
The explicit turn table and Hamiltonicity/non-Hamiltonicity statements are graph-intrinsic and finitely checkable.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not refute a theorem using smallest-counterexample exact-cover structure, role-bearing ancestry, or other information in addition to P5 density. Does not assert the example is a smallest counterexample.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Historical unit Hamilton-five-density/P6 counterexample; no live route depends on it.
- **Curation note:** Explicit six-vertex counterexample: unit Hamilton-five density does not force P6.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Accepted after independent exhaustive verification. The explicit six-vertex system has Hamilton-five density 1 and no tight P6.

## Proof
Boundary antisymmetry is built into the displayed local-tournament encoding: each unordered outer pair at each middle has exactly one orientation. P5 witnesses, indexed by their five-set, are: {0,1,2,3,4}: (3,0,4,1,2); {0,1,2,3,5}: (0,3,5,2,1); {0,1,2,4,5}: (1,5,4,0,2); {0,1,3,4,5}: (0,5,3,1,4); {0,2,3,4,5}: (3,5,4,0,2); {1,2,3,4,5}: (4,3,5,2,1). Direct finite enumeration of all 6!=720 vertex orderings against the displayed turn table finds zero tight P6 orderings. Hence all six five-subsets are Hamiltonian while the six-set is not.

# R342 — Every equality-case trimer bad edge has a balanced five-way routing partition

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Assume the equality-case fixed-trimer setup of provisional R341. Thus r=5q, P={p_1,p_2,p_3} is a tight trimer, and G_P is the q-regular triangle-free bad-extension graph on X=W\\P. Fix any bad edge xy of G_P. Then the remaining vertex set X\\{x,y} partitions canonically into five classes, each of cardinality q-1: N(x)\\{y}; N(y)\\{x}; and, for i=1,2,3, the class A_i of vertices z adjacent to neither x nor y for which the unique paired bad five-set in the occupied six-set P union {x,y,z} is (P\\{p_i}) union {x,y,z}. In particular every bad edge sees exactly q-1 third vertices routed through each of the five possible replacement channels: swap y along an x-neighbor, swap x along a y-neighbor, or delete one of the three trimer vertices.

## Hypotheses
The exact R331 equality case holds and provisional R341 is available; xy is an edge of the fixed-trimer bad graph G_P.

## Scope
Exact local balance refinement of the R331/R341 equality normal form.

## Applicability
Use in attempts to classify or exclude the R331 equality case. It replaces an unstructured bad-edge neighborhood by a canonical five-way equipartition.

## Persistence
The graph G_P, edge xy, and five routing classes are graph-intrinsic combinatorial data determined by the bad-five family B and trimer P.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not assert that these partitions are globally consistent from edge to edge, that G_P is bipartite or multipartite, or that the equality case exists. Does not force a P6 or a two-cover.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Balanced five-way routing partition is a finely structured equality-case combinatorial corollary, but has no live consumers and no demonstrated independent use outside that equality branch. Preserve R342/P348 historically.
- **Curation note:** Balanced five-way routing partition is a finely structured equality-case combinatorial corollary, but has no live consumers and no demonstrated independent use outside that equality branch. Preserve R342/P348 historically.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Correct balanced five-way routing partition around every bad edge in the R331 equality case.

## Proof
Fix bad edge xy. Since G_P is q-regular and triangle-free, x and y have no common neighbor; excluding each other leaves two disjoint neighbor classes of size q-1. For p_i in P let S_i=(P\\{p_i}) union {x,y}. R331 says exactly q bad five-sets contain S_i. One is S_i union {p_i}=P union {x,y}; hence there are exactly q-1 other bad blocks S_i union {z}. For each such z, the six-set P union {x,y,z} has P union {x,y} as one bad block and S_i union {z} as the unique partner, so R341 places z in A_i. Conversely every z routed through deletion p_i gives one such bad block. Thus |A_i|=q-1. The routing uniqueness makes A_1,A_2,A_3 disjoint and disjoint from the two graph-neighbor classes. Their sizes sum to 5(q-1)=5q-5=|X\\{x,y}|, so they partition the remainder.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R342.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R346.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R346.md -->

# R346 — Hamilton-five density equality has an order congruence fence

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Assume equality in the accepted R326/R331 Hamilton-five bad-family density ceiling on an r-vertex set W. Then r is congruent to 0 or 5 modulo 15. More precisely, R331 already gives r=5q and a 4-(r,5,q) design on the bad five-sets. In any 4-(r,5,q) design, the number lambda_2 of bad blocks through a fixed physical pair is lambda_2=q*binom(r-2,2)/binom(3,2)=q(r-2)(r-3)/6, hence an integer. If q is congruent to 2 modulo 3, then r=5q is congruent to 1 modulo 3, so q(r-2)(r-3) is congruent to 2*2*1=1 modulo 3, contradiction. Therefore q is congruent to 0 or 1 modulo 3, equivalently r is congruent to 0 or 5 modulo 15. In particular at every order r congruent to 10 modulo 15 the R326 density bound is necessarily strict.

## Hypotheses
Accepted R331 equality normal form for the bad five-set family.

## Scope
Pure design-integrality consequence of the accepted extremal density normal form. No Strong turn geometry beyond R331 is used.

## Applicability
Use when testing whether the R331 extremal bad-family structure can actually occur at a given order. It removes all r=10 mod 15 equality candidates immediately.

## Persistence
Order arithmetic only.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not rule out equality for r congruent to 0 or 5 modulo 15. Does not improve the asymptotic 4/5 density constant by itself and does not force path growth.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** superseded
- **Lifecycle note:** The r mod 15 equality fence is the k=5 lambda_2 integrality instance of the full lower-incidence divisibility tower C327/R377. Preserve R346 as shorthand dependency, route discovery to C327.
- **Curation note:** The r mod 15 equality fence is the k=5 lambda_2 integrality instance of the full lower-incidence divisibility tower C327/R377. Preserve R346 as shorthand dependency, route discovery to C327.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Valid design-integrality congruence fence r=0 or 5 mod 15.

## Proof
By R331, equality implies 5 divides r; write r=5q, and the bad family is a 4-(r,5,q) design. Fix a two-subset S of W. Double-count pairs (B,T) where B is a bad block containing S and T is a four-subset with S subset T subset B. On one hand each block B through S contains binom(3,2)=3 such four-subsets T. On the other hand there are binom(r-2,2) four-subsets T containing S and each lies in exactly q bad blocks. Thus 3 lambda_2=q binom(r-2,2), so lambda_2=q(r-2)(r-3)/6 is an integer. Suppose q=2 mod 3. Since r=5q=2q mod 3, r=1 mod 3, hence r-2=2 mod 3 and r-3=1 mod 3. Therefore q(r-2)(r-3)=2*2*1=1 mod 3, impossible because divisibility by 6 in particular requires divisibility by 3. Hence q is not 2 mod 3. Thus q=0 or 1 mod 3 and r=5q is 0 or 5 mod 15. The strictness statement for r=10 mod 15 follows.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R346.md -->

# R347 — Mantel-near-equality fixed-trimer bad graph need not force P6

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
There exists a seven-vertex Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament with a fixed tight trimer support P={0,1,2} such that the bad-extension graph G_bad on X={3,4,5,6}, where xy is an edge iff P∪{x,y} has no tight P5, is exactly the three-edge star K_{1,3} with center 3, while the whole seven-vertex system has maximum tight-path order exactly five. Concretely P∪{3,4}, P∪{3,5}, P∪{3,6} are non-Hamiltonian five-supports, whereas P∪{4,5}, P∪{4,6}, P∪{5,6} all support tight P5s. No six-vertex support carries a tight P6. Thus R328's Mantel extremal threshold is structurally sharp at m=4: being only one bad edge below the extremal K_{2,2} pattern does not imply path growth.

## Hypotheses
Explicit seven-vertex boundary-antisymmetric turn system on vertices 0,...,6. For each middle vertex b, write a>c when (a,b,c) is tight. T0: 1>2,1>3,1>4,5>1,1>6,2>3,2>4,5>2,2>6,4>3,5>3,6>3,5>4,6>4,5>6. T1: 0>2,0>3,0>4,0>5,6>0,3>2,4>2,2>5,6>2,4>3,3>5,6>3,4>5,4>6,6>5. T2: 0>1,3>0,0>4,5>0,0>6,3>1,1>4,5>1,6>1,3>4,3>5,3>6,5>4,6>4,5>6. T3: 1>0,2>0,4>0,5>0,6>0,2>1,4>1,1>5,6>1,2>4,2>5,2>6,5>4,6>4,6>5. T4: 1>0,0>2,3>0,5>0,6>0,1>2,1>3,1>5,6>1,3>2,5>2,6>2,3>5,6>3,6>5. T5: 0>1,0>2,0>3,0>4,0>6,2>1,3>1,4>1,1>6,2>3,2>4,2>6,4>3,3>6,4>6. T6: 1>0,0>2,3>0,4>0,0>5,1>2,1>3,4>1,1>5,3>2,4>2,2>5,4>3,3>5,4>5. Also (0,1,2) is tight. Exhaustive enumeration of all 120 orders on each P∪{x,y} gives bad exactly for 34,35,36 and good for 45,46,56; example tight P5s are (5,0,1,2,4), (1,0,6,2,4), and (0,2,1,5,6). Exhaustive enumeration of all 5040 ordered six-tuples finds no tight P6.

## Scope
Pure seven-vertex local regression fence for structural-density-to-path-growth arguments.

## Applicability
Use against attempts to infer a P6 from near-Mantel fixed-trimer bad-graph structure. It shows exact extremality, not merely high density, is the first plausible local threshold at four outside vertices.

## Persistence
The explicit turn system and all support/path facts are graph-intrinsic.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not refute R328 or its exact Mantel equality statement. Does not show that exact K_{2,2} equality can be P6-free. Does not model a smallest counterexample or exact-cover ancestry.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Historical Mantel-near-equality P6 countermodel; no live route depends on it.
- **Curation note:** Sharp near-Mantel counterexample: one edge below fixed-trimer equality still need not force P6.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Explicit seven-vertex certificate independently verified: fixed-trimer bad graph is K1,3 and no P6 exists.

## Proof
Use exactly the seven middle-vertex comparison rows written in R347. For each middle b, the row contains one orientation of every unordered pair {a,c} disjoint from b, hence 15 comparisons; taking the reverse orientation false fills all 30 ordered triples with middle b. Across the seven middles this assigns all 210 ordered triples of distinct vertices and, pair by pair, exactly one of (a,b,c),(c,b,a) is tight. Thus the table is a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament. The row for middle 1 contains 0>2, so (0,1,2) is tight.

Now verify the fixed-trimer extension claims by literal enumeration. For a five-vertex support S, enumerate all 5!=120 orders q=(q1,...,q5) and accept q exactly when its three consecutive turns q1q2q3, q2q3q4, q3q4q5 are all tight according to the table. On P={0,1,2}, the supports P∪{3,4}, P∪{3,5}, P∪{3,6} have zero accepted orders, whereas P∪{4,5}, P∪{4,6}, P∪{5,6} have respectively 2, 5, and 4 accepted orders. Concrete witnesses include (5,0,1,2,4), (1,0,6,2,4), and (0,2,1,5,6). Hence G_bad is exactly the star with center 3.

Finally enumerate every ordered six-tuple of distinct vertices. There are 7P6=5040. A six-tuple is tight exactly when its four consecutive turns are tight. Direct lookup in the same table gives zero tight six-tuples. Since the good five-supports above exhibit tight P5s, the maximum tight-path order is exactly five. This finite check is completely reconstructible from the comparison table in R347: it requires only iterating the stated 120- and 5040-element order sets and testing consecutive triples; no external theorem or hidden certificate is used.

# R349 — Fixed-trimer Mantel equality forces local P6 growth at every outside size at least four

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Let P be a tight trimer in a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament and let X be a set of m>=4 vertices disjoint from P. Form the R328 bad-extension graph G_bad on X. If G_bad attains the Mantel extremal bound floor(m^2/4), then V(P)∪X contains a tight P6. Indeed R328 equality makes G_bad a complete bipartite graph with balanced parts, each of size at least two. Choosing two vertices from each part gives a four-vertex subset X_0 on which the restricted bad-extension graph is exactly K_{2,2}; provisional R348 then forces a tight P6 on V(P)∪X_0. Thus exact Mantel equality is a genuine path-growth condition, even though R347 shows one-edge-below equality need not be.

## Hypotheses
P is a tight trimer; X is disjoint from P with |X|>=4; the fixed-trimer bad-extension graph attains Mantel equality.

## Scope
Order-free local extremal-structure-to-path-growth corollary.

## Applicability
Use only at exact R328 equality. It converts the extremal complete-bipartite bad graph into a seven-vertex P6 witness.

## Persistence
The chosen four outside vertices, restricted K2,2 bad graph, and resulting P6 are graph-intrinsic.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not apply to near-equality bad graphs. R347 shows the m=4 one-edge-below case can be P6-free. Does not imply that high Hamilton-five density alone forces growth.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Arbitrary-size fixed-trimer Mantel-equality P6 growth is an immediate corollary of the fixed K2,2 consumer and Mantel equality structure; not independently canonical.
- **Curation note:** Arbitrary-size fixed-trimer Mantel-equality P6 growth is an immediate corollary of the fixed K2,2 consumer and Mantel equality structure; not independently canonical.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Valid extension of the seven-vertex K2,2 result to Mantel equality at all outside sizes m>=4 by restriction to two vertices from each bipartition class.

## Proof
R328 equality gives G_bad=K_{floor(m/2),ceil(m/2)}. Since m>=4 both classes have at least two vertices. Select x1,x2 in one class and y1,y2 in the other. On X_0={x1,x2,y1,y2}, exactly the four cross pairs are bad and the two within-class pairs are good, so the restricted bad graph is K2,2. R348 forces a tight P6 on P∪X_0.

# R353 — Conditional Hamilton-five density equality has divisibility fences

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
In the setting of accepted R327, fix S⊆W with |S|=s∈{0,1,2,3} and suppose equality holds in the conditional bad-five density ceiling p_bad(W;S)=(r-s)/[(5-s)(r-4)]. Then necessarily (5-s) divides (r-s). More precisely, after quotienting out S as in R327, the bad supersets form a k=(5-s)-uniform family on N=r-s vertices attaining equality in R326 with t=2. The R326 equality condition forces every (k-1)-core to have the same occupancy μ=N/k=(r-s)/(5-s), hence μ is an integer. Thus: s=0 requires r≡0 mod5; s=1 requires r≡1 mod4; s=2 requires r≡2 mod3; s=3 requires r odd. If the R327 ceilings are simultaneously attained for all four levels s=0,1,2,3 at one order r, then necessarily r≡5 mod60. Therefore at all other orders at least one level of the conditional density hierarchy is automatically strict.

## Hypotheses
W has r>=6 vertices in a Strong Level-(1) boundary tournament; S⊆W has size s∈{0,1,2,3}; equality holds in the R327 conditional bad-density bound.

## Scope
Equality-realizability fence for the Johnson conditional hierarchy.

## Applicability
Use when a density argument approaches or assumes equality in R327. The congruence conditions identify orders where equality is arithmetically impossible before any turn-structure analysis.

## Persistence
The conclusion concerns the bad-support incidence family and is graph-intrinsic.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
These are necessary conditions only, not existence theorems. Simultaneous equality at r≡5 mod60 is not asserted realizable. Global R331 equality does not imply conditional R327 equality for s>0.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Conditional-density equality divisibility congruences are correct arithmetic consequences of the parent equality theorem, but zero-consumer and mainly equality-case bookkeeping. Preserve in R353/P359 history.
- **Curation note:** Conditional-density equality divisibility congruences are correct arithmetic consequences of the parent equality theorem, but zero-consumer and mainly equality-case bookkeeping. Preserve in R353/P359 history.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Valid necessary divisibility conditions for equality in each conditional R327 density level and simultaneous CRT residue r=5 mod 60.

## Proof
With N=r-s and k=5-s, R327 equality has p=N/[k(N-k+1)]. R326 equality forces x_T constant over all (k-1)-cores T, with mean μ=k|B|/binom(N,k-1)=p(N-k+1)=N/k=(r-s)/(5-s). Since each x_T is an integer, k divides N. The four congruences follow. Solving r≡0 mod5, r≡1 mod4, r≡2 mod3, and r≡1 mod2 gives r≡5 mod60.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R353.md -->

# R354 — Global Johnson equality is locally far from fixed-trimer Mantel equality

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Assume equality in the global Hamilton-five bad-family ceiling R331 on an r-vertex set W, and write r=5q. For any tight trimer support P⊆W, accepted R341 gives a q-regular triangle-free fixed-trimer bad-extension graph G_P on n=5q-3 outside vertices, hence |E(G_P)|=q(5q-3)/2. If q>1 then 2q<5q-3=n, so |E(G_P)|<n^2/4 and therefore G_P is strictly below the R328 Mantel extremal edge count floor(n^2/4). In particular the exact-Mantel path-growth theorem R349 cannot be applied merely from global R331 equality. Combining with the R346 congruence fence, every nontrivial arithmetically admissible global equality case has q>=3 and therefore |E(G_P)|/(n^2/4)=2q/(5q-3)<=1/2. Thus global Johnson extremality produces a regular routed local structure that is quantitatively far from local Mantel extremality; these are genuinely different structural regimes.

## Hypotheses
Equality holds in R331 on W; q=r/5; P is any tight trimer support in W.

## Scope
Equality-regime separation between the Johnson density program and fixed-trimer Mantel path-growth.

## Applicability
Use to prevent feeding R331 equality directly into R328/R349. Any path-growth consumer of the global equality design must use the q-regular routing structure of R341/R342 rather than local Mantel extremality.

## Persistence
The fixed-trimer bad graph and its degree/edge count are graph-intrinsic support-family data.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not say R331 equality is realizable or P6-free. Does not rule out path growth from the stronger routing/design structure. It only separates two notions of extremality.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Global-Johnson-versus-local-Mantel extremality separation is a correct interpretive equality corollary with no consumer. The substantive equality path-growth theorem C314 remains active.
- **Curation note:** Global-Johnson-versus-local-Mantel extremality separation is a correct interpretive equality corollary with no consumer. The substantive equality path-growth theorem C314 remains active.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Valid separation of global Johnson equality from local fixed-trimer Mantel equality; the local q-regular graph is quantitatively far below Mantel extremality.

## Proof
R341 gives n=5q-3 and degree q, so e=qn/2. For q>1, n-2q=3(q-1)>0 and in fact n^2/4-e=n(n-2q)/4=3(5q-3)(q-1)/4>1, hence e<floor(n^2/4). Thus the fixed-trimer graph is strictly below Mantel equality. Combining with R346, every nontrivial arithmetically admissible global equality case has q>=3, and then 2q/n=2q/(5q-3)<=1/2.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R354.md -->

# FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R356.md

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R356.md -->

# R356 — Global Hamilton-five equality is conditionally uniform but never conditionally extremal

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Assume equality in the global R331 Hamilton-five bad-family ceiling on an r-vertex set W, r>5. Then for every fixed subset S⊆W of size s∈{0,1,2,3,4}, the fraction of five-subsets containing S that are bad is exactly the global bad density r/[5(r-4)], independent of S. In particular, for each positive s∈{1,2,3}, this conditional density is strictly below the accepted R327 conditional ceiling (r-s)/[(5-s)(r-4)] by the explicit gap s(r-5)/[5(5-s)(r-4)]. Thus global Johnson equality cannot simultaneously be equality at any positive level of the R327 conditional hierarchy; the equality design is conditionally uniform rather than conditionally extremal.

## Hypotheses
Equality holds in R331 on W; S is any fixed subset of size at most four.

## Scope
Structural separation of global Johnson equality from the conditional density ceilings.

## Applicability
Use to rule out arguments that stack equality in R331 with equality in R327 at fixed vertices, pairs, or triples. Under global equality all such conditional densities are known exactly and have positive slack.

## Persistence
The conditional bad-support counts are graph-intrinsic incidence data of the R331 four-design.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not say the global equality design is realizable. Does not bound conditional densities away from their ceilings outside the global equality branch.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Conditional-uniformity/slack formula under global Johnson equality is a correct derived design corollary but has no live consumer and does not change the canonical equality outcome. Preserve historically.
- **Curation note:** Conditional-uniformity/slack formula under global Johnson equality is a correct derived design corollary but has no live consumer and does not change the canonical equality outcome. Preserve historically.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Valid conditional-uniformity theorem for the global equality 4-design; positive-level R327 bounds have explicit strict slack.

## Proof
Write q=r/5. For |S|=s<=4, the number of bad blocks through S is λ_s=q*binom(r-s,4-s)/binom(5-s,4-s)=q*binom(r-s,4-s)/(5-s). The total number of five-subsets through S is binom(r-s,5-s). Their ratio is q/(r-4)=r/[5(r-4)], independent of s. Subtracting this from the R327 ceiling gives [(r-s)/(5-s)-r/5]/(r-4)=s(r-5)/[5(5-s)(r-4)], positive for s>0 and r>5.

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R356.md -->

<!-- BEGIN FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R357.md -->

# R357 — Johnson density equality has macroscopic dual-clique deficit

**Record status:** `USABLE/LEGACY`

## Statement
Assume equality in the global R326/R331 Hamilton-five bad-family ceiling on an r-vertex set W, and evaluate the R325 defect quantities V,D for k=5,t=2 on the same bad family B. Then V=0 but D is exactly the number of six-subsets containing no bad five-set, namely
D = [2(r-10)/(5(r-4))] * binom(r,6).
Equivalently the occupied six-set fraction is 3r/[5(r-4)] and the empty six-set fraction is 2(r-10)/[5(r-4)]. Thus R326 equality is not a near-equality regime for the weaker R322/R325 dual-clique inequality: after the parity fence R355 the first arithmetically admissible order is r=20, where already one quarter of all six-sets are empty, and the empty fraction tends to 2/5 as r grows. The R331 equality structure is 'uniform four-cores plus perfectly paired occupied six-sets', not 'nearly every six-set maximally filled'. Any use of R325 extremal stability in the R326 equality branch must respect this distinction.

## Hypotheses
Equality holds in R331; V,D are the R325 defects for the bad five-set family with k=5,t=2.

## Scope
Extremality-separation theorem for the quadratic dual-clique and linear Johnson bounds.

## Applicability
Use to prevent transferring R325 near-zero-defect conclusions into R326/R331 equality or near-equality without quantitative justification.

## Persistence
Four-core occupancies and six-set occupancies are graph-intrinsic support-family data.

## Exclusions / nonclaims
Does not refute R325 or R326. It shows their equality notions are different. Does not say R326 near-equality always has exactly this deficit; the formula is for exact R331 equality.

## Record notes
- **Lifecycle:** retired
- **Lifecycle note:** Exact dual-clique deficit formula under Johnson equality is useful equality-analysis detail but zero-consumer and secondary to the active equality parent/path-growth theorems.
- **Curation note:** Exact dual-clique deficit formula under Johnson equality is useful equality-analysis detail but zero-consumer and secondary to the active equality parent/path-growth theorems.
- **Review status:** accepted
- **Review note:** Valid exact R325 defect evaluation under R331 equality; V=0 while a macroscopic fraction of six-sets are empty.

## Proof
R331 gives x_S=r/5 for every four-set, hence V=0. It also gives y_U∈{0,2}; therefore the R325 summand 1-binom(y_U,2) equals 1 exactly on empty six-sets and 0 on occupied ones, so D is the number of empty six-sets. If b=|B| and O is the number of occupied six-sets, then b(r-5)=sum_U y_U=2O. Using b=[r/(5(r-4))]binom(r,5) and binom(r,6)=binom(r,5)(r-5)/6 gives O/binom(r,6)=3r/[5(r-4)]. Subtract from one to obtain D/binom(r,6)=2(r-10)/[5(r-4)].

<!-- END FILE: A7C3/ARCHAEOLOGY/RESULTS/USABLE/LEGACY/R357.md -->
